questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A core services team wants Copilot cloud agent to handle medium-risk logging and test-coverage improvements without allowing unreviewed changes into the default branch. The team needs an SDLC sequence that separates planning from execution and keeps GitHub as the review and audit surface. In what order should the team implement the workflow?
questions.scenario: The repository already uses pull requests, GitHub Actions checks, and CODEOWNERS. The new process should preserve delivery speed while making agent plans, diffs, validations, and approvals inspectable.

options.text: Configure the agent prompt to emit a structured plan before proposing code changes.
Evaluate the PR using required checks, session logs, and human review before merge.
Define task inputs, expected artifacts, success criteria, and approval checkpoints.
Allow approved work to proceed on an agent branch with commits and a PR.
Add repository controls for required PRs, status checks, and CODEOWNERS review.

explanation.whyCorrect: The safest sequence starts by defining the agent task contract, then enforcing repository governance, then requiring a structured plan before execution. Only after the plan is reviewable should the agent act on a branch and open a PR. Evaluation comes through CI, logs, and human review before merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Starting with a prompt before defining task boundaries leaves unclear success criteria and weak approval gates.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Evaluation is necessary, but placing it first does not establish how the agent should plan or act.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Letting the agent write code before plan validation weakens the planning/execution boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Repository controls are important, but they should enforce a task model that has already been defined.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 sequence questions, put policy and task definition before agent execution. Plans, branches, PRs, checks, and review usually form the control path.

questions.stem: A repository administrator reviews a proposed custom agent profile for a triage agent. The agent only needs to read repository files and inspect GitHub issues and pull requests in the source repository. Which replacement best satisfies the requirement with least privilege?
questions.scenario: The organization already allows Copilot cloud agent to use the built-in GitHub MCP server. The administrator wants to avoid adding unnecessary credentials or write-capable tools.

artifact.title: .github/agents/triage.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: triage-agent
description: Reviews bug reports and correlates them with related pull requests.
tools: ["*"]
mcpServers:
  github:
    type: http
    url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
---
You investigate reported defects and summarize likely ownership.

options.text:
---
name: triage-agent
description: Reviews bug reports and correlates them with related pull requests.
tools: ["read", "search", "github/*"]
mcp-servers:
  github:
    tools: ["*"]
---

---
name: triage-agent
description: Reviews bug reports and correlates them with related pull requests.
tools: ["*"]
mcp-servers:
  github:
    type: http
    url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/
---

---
name: triage-agent
description: Reviews bug reports and correlates them with related pull requests.
tools: ["read", "search", "github/issue_read", "github/pull_request_read"]
---

---
name: triage-agent
description: Reviews bug reports and correlates them with related pull requests.
tools: ["read", "search"]
mcpServers:
  github:
    type: http
    url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/
---

explanation.whyCorrect: The corrected profile uses the custom agent tools property to grant only file-reading, search, and the specific GitHub MCP tools needed for issue and pull request inspection. It also avoids unnecessary custom MCP server configuration and credentials because the built-in GitHub MCP server is already available with a source-repository-scoped token.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: It keeps broad tool access, which grants more capabilities than the triage task requires.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: It uses the wrong frontmatter property name for custom-agent MCP configuration and omits GitHub MCP tools from the allowed tool list.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: It exposes all GitHub MCP tools instead of the specific issue and pull request read tools needed for triage.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a GH-600 item shows a custom agent profile, inspect both the YAML property names and the blast radius of the tools list. Broad wildcards often hide over-permissioning.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A repository administrator reviews pilot telemetry for a custom implementation-planner agent. Session logs show the agent repeatedly ran shell commands, generated migration code, and edited production source files, even though the intended outcome was a reviewable implementation plan. Which change best tunes the agent based on the observed failure?
questions.scenario: The administrator must keep the agent useful for exploring the repository and writing a plan, but reduce tool misuse and clarify the expected artifact.

artifact.title: .github/agents/implementation-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: implementation-planner
description: Plans high-risk platform changes and drafts plan documents
tools: ["*"]
---

You are a senior engineer. Take assigned issues and make progress.
If code changes are needed, update the implementation directly.
Use tests and shell commands to validate your work before finishing.
Summarize your approach in the pull request description.

options.text: Remove edit access entirely, keep read and search, and require the plan to be posted as a comment.
Keep shell access, add mandatory test and coverage commands, and block completion until all checks pass.
Limit tools to read, search, and edit; require a structured markdown plan; prohibit source edits unless requested.
Keep all tools enabled, add a reminder to prefer documentation changes, and monitor the next five sessions.

explanation.whyCorrect: The failure is tool misuse plus vague instructions. GitHub custom agent profiles can scope available tools, and the documented implementation-planner pattern uses read, search, and edit to create structured markdown plans rather than implementing code. Adding explicit output constraints directly tunes the behavior that failed.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Monitoring keeps the broad tool surface active and does not correct the vague implementation-oriented prompt that caused the drift.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Removing edit prevents the agent from creating the expected plan file, which is still part of the intended workflow.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: More validation commands improve code execution workflows, but this agent’s intended output is planning, not implementation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When telemetry shows tool misuse, tune both the tool list and the behavioral instructions. Do not add more execution checks when the root problem is that the agent is doing the wrong class of work.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: An organization owner wants to publish a custom performance-investigation agent for all repositories in the organization, but security requires a private validation phase before broad availability. In what order should the owner roll out the agent?
questions.scenario: The organization uses Copilot Business and wants the agent to become discoverable across the organization only after the profile has been tested and approved in GitHub.

options.text: Create the organization `.github-private` repository from the custom agents template.
Test from the agents tab by selecting `.github-private` and reviewing session results.
Move the approved profile into the root `agents` directory and merge it.
Place the draft agent profile under `.github/agents` and merge for private testing.
Iterate on the profile until performance, compliance, and task-fit criteria are satisfied.
Monitor released agent usage with session records and audit log filtering.

explanation.whyCorrect: Organization-level custom agents are prepared in a `.github-private` repository. For a validation phase, the profile is placed under `.github/agents` in that repository and tested from the agents tab. After testing and iteration, moving the profile to the root `agents` directory and merging releases it broadly. Monitoring afterward preserves auditability.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Testing cannot happen until the repository and draft profile exist on the default branch.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Moving to the root `agents` directory releases the agent, so it belongs after validation.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: The draft profile location is correct for testing, but the `.github-private` repository must exist first.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Iteration depends on test results, so it follows an initial test run.
whyDistractorsWrong.F: Monitoring is an operating step after release, not a substitute for validation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For custom-agent rollout questions, distinguish private testing locations from organization-wide release locations. Availability changes when the profile moves from `.github/agents` to root `agents`.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A platform enablement team is reviewing the first pilot week of Copilot cloud agent usage across several internal repositories. Match each observed failure mode to the most appropriate SDLC control or mitigation.
questions.scenario: The team wants to reduce risk without pausing all agent usage. Each mitigation should address the root cause rather than adding after-the-fact reporting only.

options.text: An implementation agent writes code immediately after a vague issue comment, with no reviewable plan artifact.
A migration agent keeps applying conventions from a prior unrelated service to the current repository.
A dependency update agent retries private package installation several times and hides the setup failure in its final summary.
A documentation agent changes agent instructions and setup workflow files without platform-owner review.

matchChoices: Protect agent governance files with CODEOWNERS and required reviews
Add a post-merge dashboard that tracks agent PR counts by repository
Increase the context window and allow direct updates to the default branch
Require a structured plan artifact and human approval before execution
Define deterministic setup steps and expose failures through Actions or session logs
Prune or reset task context and scope memory to task-relevant facts

pairs.row1: Require a structured plan artifact and human approval before execution
pairs.row2: Prune or reset task context and scope memory to task-relevant facts
pairs.row3: Define deterministic setup steps and expose failures through Actions or session logs
pairs.row4: Protect agent governance files with CODEOWNERS and required reviews

explanation.whyCorrect: The first issue is a planning/execution boundary failure, so the control is a structured plan plus approval. The second is context leakage, so the mitigation is pruning or resetting task context. The third combines nondeterministic setup with poor observability, so deterministic setup steps and surfaced logs address it. The fourth concerns governance files, so CODEOWNERS and required reviews are the right repository controls.
explanation.examStrategyNote: In GH-600 matching items, classify the failure before selecting the control. Planning failures need approval gates; context failures need scoping; governance-file changes need GitHub review controls.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A platform team pilots Copilot cloud agent for medium-risk refactoring issues. The first five pull requests pass CI, but reviewers still report that the agent misses architecture constraints and implements changes that do not match its initial plan. What evaluation approach best aligns the signals with the team’s development intent?
questions.scenario: The team wants to decide whether to tune the agent instructions, refine memory, or restrict tools before expanding the pilot to more repositories.

options.text: Count changed files and commits per pull request, then tune the agent to minimize repository churn.
Track CI pass rate and merge lead time only, then expand if both metrics improve over two sprints.
Use reviewer thumbs-up ratings as the primary signal, then tune only when ratings fall below target.
Combine plan-to-diff adherence, scan findings, test results, and recurring review comments for each run.

explanation.whyCorrect: The best evaluation set combines quantitative signals, such as tests and automated security scans, with qualitative signals, such as plan adherence and recurring reviewer feedback. This supports the GH-600 objective to define success criteria, use automated scanning tools as evaluation signals, and analyze failures using plans, logs, outputs, and workflow artifacts.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: CI and lead time are useful quantitative signals, but they miss whether the agent followed the intended architecture and plan.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Changed-file count can indicate scope drift, but optimizing for fewer changes can hide incomplete or incorrectly scoped work.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Reviewer ratings are useful qualitative feedback, but using them alone misses objective scan, test, and plan-adherence evidence.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 evaluation questions, prefer blended signal sets that reflect the task’s intent. Passing tests alone rarely proves that an autonomous agent made the right design decisions.

questions.stem: A reliability team asks Copilot CLI to remediate an incident caused by a failed framework upgrade. The work includes restoring the build, updating generated API clients, rewriting affected unit tests, and producing an incident summary. The API clients depend on the build fix, but the unit tests and summary can proceed after the affected files are identified. Which orchestration approach best balances speed and correctness?
questions.scenario: The team wants to use subagents where useful, but the postmortem must explain which agent changed which artifact and why.

options.text: Use a hybrid orchestrator-worker plan: sequence dependent fixes, then fan out independent test and summary tasks.
Start with a debate pattern where agents independently propose full remediations before any code changes.
Run all four tasks with parallel subagents and merge whichever pull request completes first.
Use one general-purpose agent for the whole incident to avoid inter-agent coordination overhead.

explanation.whyCorrect: The best plan respects task dependencies before parallelizing. GitHub documents that parallel subagents are useful when work can be divided into independent subtasks, while inherently sequential work gains little from parallel execution. Sequencing the build and API-client dependency first, then fanning out independent work, reduces conflict risk while preserving speed and auditability.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Parallelizing dependent work can create conflicting or unusable outputs, especially when generated clients depend on the build fix.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A single agent avoids coordination issues but gives up useful specialization and parallelism for independent incident tasks.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A debate pattern may help compare designs, but this incident needs coordinated remediation with dependency-aware execution.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 orchestration items, identify dependency boundaries first. Parallel fan-out is favored only after the work units are genuinely independent.

questions.stem: An enterprise platform team is preparing to let developers use MCP servers with GitHub Copilot in supported IDEs and Copilot CLI. Security requires developers to discover approved servers from a central catalog, and a locally installed internal MCP server must also be permitted. What should the team configure?
questions.scenario: Several teams currently paste MCP server definitions into local configuration files. The security team wants a preventive control before expanding access.

options.text: Configure each repository's cloud agent MCP JSON and rely on repository administrators to copy the approved server list.
Enable the cloud agent firewall allowlist and add every approved MCP server domain to the network settings.
Publish an MCP registry, set the enterprise policy to Registry only, and include local servers by exact ID.
Require teams to submit MCP server logs weekly and remove any server that appears unapproved.

explanation.whyCorrect: An MCP registry provides the central catalog, and the Registry only access policy restricts MCP usage to servers in that registry. Local servers must be included in the registry with the correct server ID because allowlist enforcement also applies to local servers.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Repository MCP JSON configures cloud agent tools in one repository, but it does not create a central IDE and CLI discovery and access policy.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: The firewall controls network destinations for cloud agent processes, but it is not the MCP registry or allowlist mechanism.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Weekly log review is reactive and leaves unapproved MCP servers usable until after the next review.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 MCP governance questions, prefer preventive policy controls such as registry and allowlist settings over repository-by-repository copying or after-the-fact monitoring.

questions.stem: A search platform team uses Copilot cloud agent to modernize a legacy indexing pipeline across several pull requests. The work often pauses overnight, and resumed sessions sometimes repeat completed refactors or reintroduce decisions that were rejected in the original issue. The team already uses Copilot Memory for repository conventions. What should the team do to improve continuity without misusing memory?
questions.scenario: The team needs resumable execution, clear auditability in GitHub, and protection against context drift during long-running agent work.

options.text: Create an organization vector store for all agent traces, then replay similar traces when the task resumes.
Store completed steps as Copilot Memory facts, then let the next agent session infer unfinished work from memory.
Paste the full prior chat transcript into each prompt, and ask Copilot to continue from that context.
Write structured checkpoints to the PR or branch, then require the agent to read them before acting.

explanation.whyCorrect: Structured checkpoints in a PR description, issue comment, or branch file are durable state artifacts that let an agent resume from the current branch and prior decisions. Copilot Memory is better suited to persistent repository facts and conventions, not task-by-task execution state.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Copilot Memory stores scoped repository facts and validates citations before use; using it as a task progress ledger risks stale or incomplete execution state.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Replaying the full transcript increases noise and token pressure, but does not create a durable, auditable source of truth in the repository workflow.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: An external vector store may be useful for some architectures, but it adds complexity and can conflict with GitHub branch state if not treated as authoritative.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 memory questions, separate durable task state from long-term repository memory. Progress, decisions, and resume points belong in inspectable artifacts tied to the branch or PR.

questions.stem: A release engineering team is configuring a Copilot cloud agent to prepare draft release notes. The agent must call an approved remote MCP server for read-only changelog data, install private npm packages during setup, and run a bash validation command that calls an internal metadata API. Select THREE configuration actions the team should take.
questions.scenario: The team wants the agent to complete the task without exposing broad credentials or allowing arbitrary outbound access.

options.text: Store the MCP token as an Agents secret prefixed with COPILOT_MCP_ and reference it in MCP headers.
Store the MCP token as an Actions secret and reference it directly from the agent profile.
Disable the cloud agent firewall so npm, MCP, and validation traffic share the same network path.
Configure the MCP server tools list with only the read-only changelog tools the agent needs.
Grant the agent all MCP tools and rely on the release note prompt to avoid write operations.
Allowlist the internal metadata API domain for the agent's bash validation network call.

explanation.whyCorrect: MCP configuration can use Agents secrets and variables with the required COPILOT_MCP_ prefix. The MCP tools list should enable only necessary tools because Copilot can use configured MCP tools autonomously. The firewall should allow the internal metadata API domain needed by the agent's bash validation command instead of opening broad outbound access.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Copilot cloud agent has dedicated Agents secrets and variables; MCP configuration requires referenced names to use the COPILOT_MCP_ prefix.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Disabling the firewall increases exfiltration risk and is broader than permitting the specific validation endpoint.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Prompt instructions are not a permission boundary; the MCP tools list should enforce the allowed capabilities.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For environment-permission questions, separate three controls: Agents secrets for sensitive values, MCP tool lists for callable capabilities, and firewall settings for agent-initiated network access.

questions.stem: A platform team added a setup workflow so Copilot cloud agent can install dependencies and run validation consistently before making changes. Copilot sessions still behave inconsistently, and a reviewer notices the following file has not been merged to the default branch. What should the team change?
questions.scenario: The repository is a Node.js service. The goal is deterministic dependency installation and test validation without granting the setup job unnecessary repository or deployment permissions.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  prepare-agent:
    runs-on: macos-latest
    timeout-minutes: 90
    permissions:
      contents: write
      actions: write
      deployments: write
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "20"
          cache: "npm"
      - name: Install and test
        run: npm ci && npm test

options.text: Change timeout to 59 and keep macOS because setup steps support any GitHub-hosted image.
Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps, use Ubuntu or Windows, minimize permissions, and merge to default.
Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps, keep write permissions, and rely on session logs for audit.
Keep current job and permissions; add a required status check to block PRs when setup fails.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot setup steps must be in .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml on the default branch and must contain a single job named copilot-setup-steps. The job should use supported Ubuntu or Windows runners, stay within supported settings such as timeout-minutes, and grant the lowest permissions needed.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: A required status check does not make Copilot pick up a misnamed setup job or fix excessive job permissions.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Reducing the timeout addresses only one issue; macOS is not a supported Copilot cloud agent runner environment.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Renaming the job helps discovery, but retaining broad write and deployment permissions violates least-privilege setup.

explanation.examStrategyNote: On GH-600 configuration artifacts, check both syntax and governance: the correct answer usually fixes the required key names while reducing permissions.

questions.stem: An SRE platform team is building a Copilot SDK incident assistant that can delegate to specialized subagents. During a game day, the rollback agent was selected automatically from a vague prompt and modified files before the incident commander approved the rollback. The team also could not reconstruct which subagent failed because the UI only showed display names. Which change should the team make?
questions.scenario: Rollback is a high-impact recovery action. The incident commander wants automatic triage and patch planning, but rollback must be explicit and the execution tree must be auditable.

artifact.title: incident-session.ts

options.text: Set rollback to explicit invocation, scope its tools, and track started/completed/failed events by toolCallId.
Keep rollback inferable, but add a post-run report that lists changed files by subagent display name.
Remove patch-planner edit access and require triage to generate all remediation and rollback changes.
Preselect the rollback agent at session creation so recovery actions use a consistent agent profile.

explanation.whyCorrect: The rollback agent should not be automatically selected for vague incident prompts. In the Copilot SDK, setting infer to false prevents automatic selection, and tool scoping limits each agent to its intended capabilities. Subagent lifecycle events include toolCallId on started, completed, and failed events, which supports reconstructing the execution tree for audit and incident review.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A post-run report improves review, but it does not prevent unapproved rollback execution or reliably correlate failures.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Preselecting rollback increases the chance of premature recovery actions and bypasses the intended triage-first workflow.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Removing patch-planner edit access blocks legitimate remediation work and overloads the read-only triage role.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a GH-600 question combines recovery risk and observability, choose the option that both constrains invocation and records correlation identifiers for later analysis.

questions.stem: A payments team wants Copilot cloud agent to help with schema refactoring work that can affect checkout availability. The work must stay fast, but the security team requires a visible checkpoint before code changes begin. Which architecture best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The repository already uses pull requests, CODEOWNERS, required checks, and deployment environments. Product managers create GitHub issues containing acceptance criteria and impacted file paths.

options.text: Require a structured issue plan first, approve it, then allow a draft PR governed by checks.
Let the agent open a PR immediately, then ask reviewers to infer the plan from the commit diff.
Limit the agent to analysis only and require developers to manually copy any suggested code changes.
Let the agent implement directly on a protected branch after reading the issue, then request CODEOWNERS review.

explanation.whyCorrect: The best design separates planning from action: the agent first produces an inspectable structured plan from the issue inputs, waits for approval, and then performs implementation through normal PR controls such as checks and review.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Direct implementation on a protected branch collapses planning and action and bypasses the intended checkpoint before code changes begin.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A PR diff alone is a weak planning artifact because reviewers must reconstruct intent after the agent has already acted.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Analysis-only use avoids autonomous risk but sacrifices too much delivery velocity when PR governance can safely control implementation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 architecture questions, favor designs that make the agent's plan inspectable before execution and then use GitHub PR controls for action and evaluation.

questions.stem: A healthcare engineering organization is enabling Copilot cloud agent for repositories that contain regulated application code. The platform team wants Copilot to continue opening draft PRs for routine fixes, but any change to agent instructions, setup permissions, or external tool configuration must require review by the platform-security team. Based on the current CODEOWNERS file, which change best satisfies the requirement without adding unnecessary approval gates?
questions.scenario: The repository ruleset already requires pull request review from Code Owners before merging to the default branch. Required CI and code scanning checks also apply to the default branch.

artifact.title: .github/CODEOWNERS
artifact.content:
# Current ownership rules
/src/payments/ @contoso/payments-service
/src/claims/ @contoso/claims-service
/.github/workflows/* @contoso/devops

options.text: Disable Copilot cloud agent for repositories that contain regulated workloads until quarterly manual reviews finish.
Rely on signed Copilot commits, session logs, and audit-log exports to detect unsafe edits.
Add CODEOWNERS entries for Copilot and MCP configuration files, and require Code Owner review.
Add a ruleset requiring platform-security approval on every branch matching copilot/** before merge.

explanation.whyCorrect: Adding targeted CODEOWNERS entries for Copilot and MCP configuration files uses the existing human review gate only where it materially reduces risk. GitHub recommends protecting important Copilot and MCP configuration files with CODEOWNERS and enabling required Code Owner review. This preserves agent velocity for routine code changes while requiring human judgment for changes that alter the agent's operating constraints.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Disabling the agent is disproportionate because the requirement is to protect sensitive configuration changes, not stop all autonomous draft PR work.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Requiring platform-security approval for every Copilot branch over-gates routine code fixes and fails the goal of minimizing approvals that do not reduce risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Signed commits, session logs, and audit logs improve traceability, but they detect or explain changes after the fact rather than blocking unsafe configuration changes before merge.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 guardrail questions, prefer targeted preventive controls that protect high-risk paths. Avoid answers that either shut down all autonomy or rely only on after-the-fact monitoring.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A tax platform team is onboarding Copilot cloud agent for database migration work. Compliance requires a human to approve the migration plan before any schema or application code file is changed. A repository administrator reviews the custom agent profile below. What change best satisfies the requirement while preserving delivery velocity?
questions.scenario: The team wants the agent to help with analysis and implementation, but audit findings specifically require separation between planning and execution for migration tasks that touch regulated data models.

artifact.title: .github/agents/migration-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: migration-planner
description: Plans and implements database migrations for the tax platform
tools: ["read", "search", "edit"]
---

You are a database migration specialist.

When assigned a migration issue:
1. Inspect the repository and identify affected entities, migrations, tests, and API callers.
2. Create an implementation checklist.
3. Update migration files, data-access code, and related tests.
4. Run the relevant test suite.
5. Open a pull request with a summary of the completed work.

If requirements are incomplete, make reasonable assumptions and continue.

options.text: Allow the current agent to create draft pull requests, then require CODEOWNERS to review database files.
Keep the agent unchanged, but require all copilot/ branches to pass CI before merge.
Add verbose logging and require Copilot to include the session log link before opening the pull request.
Split the workflow: planner uses read/search to publish a structured plan; after human approval, invoke an implementation agent with edit.

explanation.whyCorrect: Option C enforces a planning-to-execution boundary: the first agent is constrained to analysis and structured plan output, and implementation with edit capability is not invoked until a human approves the plan. This aligns with the GH-600 objective to configure planning separately from execution, validate plans, and prevent action until approval.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Logging improves traceability, but it does not prevent the agent from editing schema or application code before plan approval.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Required CI checks are useful evaluation controls, but they occur after code changes and do not separate planning from action.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Draft pull requests and CODEOWNERS reviews add governance after implementation, but the current agent still edits regulated files before approval.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 planning-boundary questions, prefer designs that change the agent workflow or tool scope before execution. Review, CI, and logs are important controls, but they are not substitutes for an explicit pre-action approval gate.

questions.stem: Fabrikam wants organization-level custom agents that engineers can discover, while preventing unreviewed changes to agent prompts and SDLC setup files. Which control design best satisfies the case study requirements?
questions.scenario: The platform-governance team must support self-service use of approved agents without making every developer an owner of agent definitions.

options.text: Move agent files into each app repo and let repository admins approve prompt changes independently.
Store agents in a private wiki and paste prompts into Copilot Chat for each task.
Keep .github-private public internally, but rely on session logs to detect unsafe agent prompts.
Create the .github-private repo from the template, limit visibility, and require CODEOWNERS review.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents using a .github-private repository for organization custom agents with internal or private visibility. CODEOWNERS with required review is the GitHub-native way to make controlled files reviewable by the responsible team before merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Per-repository copies fragment governance and make agent profiles harder to review consistently across the organization.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Session logs help audit behavior, but they do not prevent unreviewed prompt or setup changes from being merged.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A wiki loses GitHub-native review, versioning, and file-based agent configuration for .github/agents/*.agent.md files.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a GH-600 question asks for governance, prefer preventive GitHub controls such as repository visibility, CODEOWNERS, rulesets, and required reviews over after-the-fact monitoring.

questions.stem: Fabrikam is assigning Copilot cloud agent a medium-risk refactor in retail-platform that touches inventory and order-orchestration code. The technical requirements say planning must be validated before implementation. Which workflow should the team use?
questions.scenario: The issue has a business goal and acceptance criteria, but the exact affected files are not yet known.

options.text: Require a plan-only session first; after human approval, start a separate implementation session.
Let Copilot start implementation immediately, then require reviewers to reject PRs that lack a plan.
Disable cloud agent for service repositories until architects manually write all implementation steps.
Create a shared planning issue, but allow the agent to commit once CI can run.

explanation.whyCorrect: This preserves the required boundary between planning and action. Copilot cloud agent supports repository research, plan creation, iteration on the plan, and later implementation after the user is satisfied.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Rejecting poor PRs after implementation is reactive and allows action before the required plan approval checkpoint.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Running CI is useful during evaluation, but it does not validate the proposed implementation approach before code changes.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Manual architecture up front can be appropriate for high-risk work, but it removes useful agent planning instead of governing it.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 planning questions, prefer workflows that make the agent produce an inspectable plan before permitting code changes.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: Fabrikam is defining the standard SDLC flow for medium-risk Copilot cloud agent work in retail-platform. In which order should the team apply the steps?
questions.scenario: The flow must produce inspectable artifacts, preserve the plan-to-action boundary, and end with human-governed review.

options.text: Create or refine the issue with scope, inputs, target files, and measurable acceptance criteria.
Ask Copilot cloud agent to research and produce a plan without making code changes.
Have the owning engineer review the plan and approve the implementation approach in GitHub.
Prompt the agent to implement the approved plan on a copilot branch and open a PR when ready.
Evaluate session logs, diff, status checks, and required reviews before a human merge.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sequence follows a governed plan, act, evaluate lifecycle: define task inputs and success criteria, produce a plan, obtain human validation, implement on a controlled branch, then evaluate logs, code, checks, and reviews before merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-C: Implementing before plan approval violates the case study requirement to validate the plan before action.
whyDistractorsWrong.E-before-D: Evaluation depends on concrete artifacts such as a diff, session log, CI checks, and pull request reviews.
whyDistractorsWrong.B-before-A: Starting research without scoped inputs and acceptance criteria increases ambiguity and weakens later evaluation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Sequence questions often test lifecycle discipline. Anchor the order on inputs first, planning second, action third, and evaluation plus human review last.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: This moves the decision record outside GitHub and relies on copying summaries back after the fact.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: This loses the benefits of Copilot cloud agent sessions, GitHub traceability, and standard PR-based supervision.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Repository custom instructions provide guidance, but they are not the organization-level custom agent profile mechanism.

caseStudies.title: Case Study: Fabrikam Retail Engineering Agent Rollout
caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Fabrikam Retail Engineering owns a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization with 38 application repositories. The organization is piloting GitHub Copilot cloud agent to reduce maintenance backlog in customer-facing retail systems. The first target is the retail-platform repository, which contains inventory, catalog, and order-orchestration services.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The retail-platform repository has required pull requests, CI status checks, and CODEOWNERS review for production service directories. Copilot cloud agent is enabled for a pilot group of senior engineers. Current issues vary in quality: some include acceptance criteria and target files, while others contain only a short problem statement. The team plans to create organization-level custom agents in a .github-private repository and to define agents in .github/agents/*.agent.md files.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: Fabrikam wants agents to handle routine refactoring, test coverage, and documentation tasks without slowing developers. Agent output must remain inspectable in GitHub through issues, plans, branches, pull requests, status checks, and session logs. Engineering managers want custom agents that are easy for teams to discover but not easy to modify without platform review.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: For medium-risk work in retail-platform, the agent must separate planning from implementation. Before code changes, the agent must research the repository and produce a structured implementation plan. A human owner must validate the plan before the agent makes changes. Implementation work must occur on a copilot/ branch or PR head branch and must produce a reviewable pull request with passing checks.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Fabrikam treats agent profiles, repository instructions, and .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml as controlled SDLC assets. Changes to these files require review from the platform-governance team. Agent-created pull requests must be reviewed and merged by a human. The person who triggered an agent-created pull request should not be the sole approver. Administrators must be able to trace who initiated agent work and inspect logs for completed sessions.

caseStudies.title: Case Study: Woodgrove Retail Agentic SDLC Rollout
caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Woodgrove Retail is adopting GitHub Copilot cloud agent and organization-level custom agents for its commerce engineering teams. The initial rollout covers the returns-platform and catalog-api repositories, which receive frequent maintenance requests, test-gap issues, and low-to-medium-risk refactoring work. Woodgrove wants agents to accelerate routine SDLC work while preserving GitHub as the system of record for decisions, proposed changes, approvals, and audit evidence.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The repositories are hosted in a GitHub organization named woodgrove-retail. The organization uses GitHub Copilot Business. Branch protection already requires pull requests, one approving review, required status checks for unit tests and CodeQL, and CODEOWNERS review for .github/**, deployment/**, and src/payments/**. Production deployments use a GitHub environment named production with required reviewers from the release-approvers team. The organization has not yet created its .github-private repository for custom agents.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: Woodgrove wants medium-risk agent work to follow a repeatable Plan -> Act -> Evaluate flow. Engineering managers want agent plans to be visible in GitHub before code changes are made. Developers must be able to approve a plan without creating long manual handoffs. Custom agents should be discoverable across the organization after testing, but proposed agent profiles must be privately validated before they are made broadly available.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: The implementation-planner agent must generate a structured plan that lists inputs, touched areas, test strategy, rollback considerations, and success criteria. The coding agent may create branches and draft pull requests after a plan is accepted. Copilot cloud agent must use a deterministic setup workflow for dependencies when needed. The private package registry is reachable at packages.woodgrove.example.com, and the registry token must be available only to Copilot cloud agent, not to general GitHub Actions workflows.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Agent-created changes must remain reviewable through pull requests, checks, session logs, and commit history. The user who initiates agent work should not be the sole approving reviewer for the resulting pull request. Workflow runs from Copilot-created pull requests must be inspected before privileged workflows are approved. Firewall configuration must minimize data exfiltration risk while allowing required dependency downloads. Changes to .github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, CODEOWNERS, and custom agent profiles require platform team review.

artifacts.title: Woodgrove Agent Governance Standard
artifacts.content:
Medium-risk agent task flow:
1. Capture request as a GitHub issue with inputs, constraints, and acceptance criteria.
2. Ask implementation-planner to produce a structured plan as a GitHub artifact before code changes.
3. Require a human maintainer to approve the plan before coding begins.
4. Let Copilot cloud agent work on a copilot/ branch and open a draft pull request.
5. Require status checks, CODEOWNERS review where applicable, and independent human approval before merge.
6. Require protected environment approval before production deployment.

questions.stem: A repository contains sensitive deployment manifests that Copilot cloud agent should not modify without platform-owner review. The repository already uses Copilot content exclusions for other Copilot surfaces. What should the team do for these files?
questions.scenario: The team is enabling Copilot cloud agent and wants enforceable controls on changes to high-risk repository paths.

options.text: Rely on content exclusions because they prevent cloud agent from seeing and editing excluded files.
Ask the agent in custom instructions to avoid the deployment manifests during routine work.
Move the manifests to a hidden directory so the agent is less likely to discover them.
Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection to require platform-owner review for those paths.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent does not account for content exclusions, so enforce review of sensitive paths with CODEOWNERS and branch protection.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Cloud agent can see and update files despite Copilot content exclusions.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Instructions help guide behavior but do not enforce review before merge.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Obscuring file location is not a governance control.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When content exclusions appear in a cloud-agent question, verify whether they apply; use GitHub governance for acceptance control.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Documentation reviewers may not own agent runtime and governance configuration.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Status checks do not replace human ownership review for sensitive paths.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Agent configuration can directly affect autonomous behavior and setup.

options.text: Allow the agent to deploy after it adds a summary comment to the pull request.

Use a separate agent to approve deployment jobs after verifying the PR description.

Add contents: read permission to copilot-setup-steps.yml so MCP can read the token.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Secret names must not start with GITHUB_, and that prefix is not the MCP requirement.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Setup workflow permissions do not control MCP secret availability.

options.text: Ask the original assignee to recreate the prompt from memory in the pull request.
Review billing export data to infer which tools the agent probably used.
Open the session log linked from the Copilot commit message and review the agent steps.
Search local developer machines for temporary files from the agent environment.

questions.stem: A repository defines a compliance-advisor custom agent that should answer policy questions using repository files but must not edit code or execute shell commands. Which revised front matter best enforces that boundary?
questions.scenario: The agent is meant to support planning and review, not implementation. The team wants tool restrictions rather than relying only on prompt wording.

artifact.title: Current agent profile
artifact.content:
---
name: compliance-advisor
description: Advises on compliance implications of proposed code changes
tools: ['read', 'search', 'edit', 'execute']
---
Use repository policies to advise engineers. Do not modify files unless asked.

options.text: tools: ['read', 'search', 'execute'] so the agent can verify policies with scripts.
tools: ['*'] with prompt text saying edits and shell commands require reviewer approval.
tools: ['read', 'search'] so it can inspect files without editing or running commands.
tools: [] so the agent uses only its model knowledge of compliance policies.

explanation.whyCorrect: The read and search tools support repository inspection while excluding edit and execute capabilities that exceed the advisory role.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Wildcard tool access contradicts the restricted advisory boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Execute allows shell commands, which the scenario explicitly excludes.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Disabling all tools prevents the agent from reading repository policy files.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For custom-agent tool questions, map allowed tools directly to the job the agent is supposed to perform.

questions.stem: A repository has slow and unreliable Copilot sessions because the agent repeatedly discovers how to install dependencies by trial and error. Select TWO changes that improve reliability without expanding repository permissions unnecessarily.
questions.scenario: The project is a standard Node.js application with a lockfile and existing CI tests. The team wants deterministic preparation before agent work begins.

options.text: Remove the lockfile so the agent can choose compatible dependency versions each run.
Keep setup job permissions to contents: read when checkout is needed for installation.
Tell the agent to skip local validation and rely only on reviewers to run tests.
Add copilot-setup-steps.yml with checkout, Node setup, dependency caching, and npm ci.
Grant contents: write to the setup job so dependency installation can update package files.

explanation.whyCorrect: A setup workflow can deterministically install dependencies before work starts, and contents: read follows least privilege for checkout.

whyDistractorsWrong.E: Dependency installation does not require write permission to repository contents.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Removing the lockfile makes dependency resolution less deterministic.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Skipping validation reduces evaluation quality.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Environment reliability questions usually favor deterministic setup steps and least-privilege permissions.

questions.stem: A setup workflow validates private dependencies but sometimes takes longer than expected. Copilot sessions begin with a partially configured environment after the setup fails. Which change is most appropriate?
questions.scenario: The team wants the setup to be deterministic and visible during PR validation without relying on Copilot to recover from missing dependencies.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
jobs:
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 90
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - run: ./scripts/install-private-deps.sh

options.text: Move dependency installation into the agent prompt so the workflow no longer controls setup.
Add continue-on-error to the install step so Copilot can attempt recovery during implementation.
Keep timeout-minutes at 59 or less and make dependency installation fail fast and observable.
Remove timeout-minutes so the setup can run as long as needed for dependency installation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot setup steps support timeout-minutes with a maximum of 59, and setup failures should be surfaced and fixed rather than hidden.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Unsupported or excessive runtime does not create a reliable setup contract.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: continue-on-error hides setup failures and can cause partial environments.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Prompts are less deterministic than setup workflows for environment preparation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: On setup workflows, treat failure visibility as a design goal; do not mask broken prerequisites.

questions.stem: A platform engineer adds a setup workflow so Copilot cloud agent can install dependencies before starting work. The agent still starts without running the setup steps. What is the most likely fix?
questions.scenario: The file is committed to the repository, but the session log shows no setup workflow execution before the agent starts editing files.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  setup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
      - run: npm ci

options.text: Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps and ensure the file is on the default branch.
Grant contents: write permission so the setup job can push the prepared workspace.
Add a pull_request trigger so Copilot can discover the workflow from feature branches.
Move the file to .github/agents so custom agents can load the setup instructions.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot setup steps must be in .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, present on the default branch, and contain a job named copilot-setup-steps.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Triggers help validate workflow changes, but the required job name is still wrong.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: The setup job does not need write permission; least privilege is recommended.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: .github/agents is for custom agent profiles, not setup workflows.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For setup-step artifacts, check the file path, required job name, and default-branch requirement first.

Allowlist only the tracker read tools needed for issue metadata and comments.
Keep all tools enabled and review session logs after the first few agent runs.
Move the same configuration into copilot-setup-steps.yml for better workflow visibility.

questions.stem: A developer asks one Copilot cloud agent task to update a shared library repository and a dependent application repository, then open PRs in both. What is the best architectural response?
questions.scenario: The change requires coordination across repositories, but the team wants to stay within Copilot cloud agent's supported execution model.

options.text: Ask the agent to create multiple pull requests from the same task after completing both changes.
Split the work into separate repository-scoped tasks and coordinate them through issues or PRs.
Give the agent organization write access so it can push related branches in both repositories.
Store both repositories in the same workspace so the task appears as one repository.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent can make changes only in the specified repository and works on one branch with one PR per assigned task, so cross-repo work needs separate coordinated tasks.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Broader write access conflicts with the supported repository-scoped model and least privilege.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: One task cannot open multiple PRs across repositories.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Workspace arrangement does not change the repository limitation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a task exceeds cloud agent limits, decompose it rather than expanding permissions.

options.text: Track Copilot-created PR outcomes, merge rates, and median time to merge using GitHub metrics.
Measure only the number of prompts sent to agents each week across all repositories.
Survey developers about perceived speed and use that as the sole adoption signal.
Count generated lines of code and treat larger diffs as higher delivery throughput.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Prompt counts measure activity, not delivery outcomes or review quality.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Surveys can supplement but should not replace system-of-record outcome metrics.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Generated lines of code can reward large, risky changes rather than useful outcomes.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Outcome questions favor PR lifecycle signals over activity counts or code volume.

questions.stem: A company wants Copilot cloud agent to reach an internal artifact mirror that is inaccessible from GitHub-hosted runners. Security is concerned about long-lived runner state and broad network access. What is the best design?
questions.scenario: The organization can operate Actions Runner Controller and wants to minimize persistence between agent jobs.

options.text: Store internal packages in the repository so the agent does not need network access.
Use a persistent self-hosted runner with cached credentials to reduce setup time.
Disable network controls so the default agent environment can discover internal mirrors.
Use ephemeral single-use self-hosted runners with explicit firewall rules for required hosts.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub recommends ephemeral, single-use self-hosted runners for Copilot cloud agent when self-hosting is needed, with network controls for required access.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Persistent runners increase state and credential reuse risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Open network access conflicts with controlled runtime boundaries.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Vendoring internal packages into the repository can create maintenance and security issues.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Runner questions reward isolation and explicit network boundaries, not persistence or unrestricted access.

questions.stem: Copilot opens a draft PR that modifies owned files. The code owners have not been requested automatically, and the team wants normal review routing to occur. What should happen next?
questions.scenario: The PR is still in draft state. The repository uses CODEOWNERS and branch protection requiring code-owner review before merge.

options.text: Copilot should approve its own PR to trigger code-owner review requests.
The team should disable draft PRs so code owners are requested during planning.
A workflow should merge the draft PR and create a follow-up review issue.
A human with appropriate access should mark the draft PR ready for review.

explanation.whyCorrect: Code owners are not automatically requested on draft PRs; when a draft PR is marked ready for review, code owners are notified.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot cannot approve its own PR and approval is not how draft review routing is triggered.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Draft PRs provide a useful checkpoint; they do not need to be disabled.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Merging before review violates branch protection intent.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Know the difference between draft visibility and ready-for-review enforcement in PR-based governance.

questions.stem: A financial-services team is designing an agent workflow for schema migrations. The agent may research and propose a plan autonomously, but database-impacting code changes require explicit human approval of the plan first. Select THREE design elements that best enforce the boundary.
questions.scenario: The team wants to keep planning fast while preventing unapproved execution on migration files.

options.text: Require a structured plan artifact listing files, migration strategy, rollback, and validation steps.
Use CODEOWNERS or rules for migration paths so database owners review resulting PRs.
Hide migration history from the agent context to reduce the chance of risky edits.
Allow the agent to approve its own plan if the plan contains a rollback section.
Gate execution on a human approval signal before the agent modifies migration paths.
Let the agent edit migration files first, then require approval before tests run.

explanation.whyCorrect: A structured plan makes intent inspectable, an approval gate separates planning from action, and path ownership enforces expert review of database changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.F: Editing first violates the required boundary before action.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Self-approval removes the human checkpoint.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Hiding relevant context can make migrations less safe rather than more controlled.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For high-risk action boundaries, combine structured plans, explicit approval, and path-based governance.

questions.stem: A team reviews an agent workflow after multiple failed PRs. The agent catches test failures and continues committing, and its final PR description says only "updated implementation." Select TWO anti-patterns demonstrated by this workflow.
questions.scenario: Reviewers need to classify the failure modes before revising the agent instructions and required artifacts.

options.text: Overuse of protected environments for low-risk validation tasks.
Silent failure handling that hides failed tests from reviewers.
Excessive least-privilege scoping of repository read access.
Premature human approval before the agent begins planning.
Lack of structured output describing changes, validation, and remaining risks.

explanation.whyCorrect: Continuing after hidden test failures is a silent-failure pattern, and a vague PR description lacks structured review output.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The scenario does not mention environment gates.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: The scenario does not indicate that permissions were too narrow.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: The problem is poor failure surfacing and output, not early approval.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Agent anti-pattern questions often describe symptoms; map them to reliability failures like hidden errors or unstructured artifacts.

questions.stem: During a running Copilot cloud agent session, a maintainer notices the agent is implementing a custom error handler instead of using the repository standard utility. The maintainer wants to correct course without losing useful work. What should the maintainer do?
questions.scenario: The session is still active, and no PR has been opened yet. The agent has already pushed one intermediate commit to its branch.

options.text: Steer the active session with a follow-up instruction to use the existing utility.
Wait for the PR, request changes, and let reviewers handle the rewrite manually.
Create a new issue with the correction and assign it to a second agent session.
Stop the session immediately and delete the branch so the agent starts from a clean slate.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub supports steering an active Copilot cloud agent session with follow-up instructions when it is heading in the wrong direction.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Stopping discards momentum and is unnecessary when steering can correct the active session.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Waiting until review increases rework and delays feedback.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A second session can create coordination overhead for a correction within the same task.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Human intervention does not always mean stopping automation; use the lightest control that corrects direction.

questions.stem: A regulated repository is enabling agent-created implementation PRs. The compliance team requires that agent work cannot be merged without independent human review and successful validation. Select TWO controls that best satisfy the requirement.
questions.scenario: The repository already uses GitHub Actions for build and security checks. The team wants controls that fit normal GitHub review workflows.

options.text: Allow maintainers to bypass required checks for PRs created from copilot branches.
Replace pull requests with direct commits to reduce review overhead during agent runs.
Let Copilot merge its own PR when all files were generated by the same session.
Require approving reviews on the protected target branch before pull requests can merge.
Require status checks for build, tests, and security scans before merging agent PRs.

explanation.whyCorrect: Required reviews and required status checks enforce human review and objective validation before merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot cannot approve or merge its own pull request, and self-merge would violate independent review.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Bypassing required checks weakens the validation requirement for agent changes.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Direct commits remove the PR-based governance path that provides review and traceability.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When asked for governance, combine human approval with automated checks rather than relying on agent judgment.

questions.stem: A product team reports inconsistent results from agent-created PRs because issue descriptions vary widely. What is the best improvement to the agent task intake process?
questions.scenario: Some issues include acceptance criteria and test expectations, while others contain only a short title. Reviewers want predictable outputs.

options.text: Ask reviewers to add missing details only after the agent opens a pull request.
Standardize issue templates with inputs, expected outputs, and success criteria for agent tasks.
Increase the agent token budget so vague issues can include more repository context.
Let the agent choose acceptance criteria dynamically after it reads the repository history.

explanation.whyCorrect: Structured task definitions improve reliability by defining inputs, outputs, and success criteria before execution.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Letting the agent invent criteria can diverge from product intent.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Waiting until PR review delays feedback and creates rework.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: More context does not replace explicit acceptance criteria.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When stems mention inconsistent outcomes, look for better task definition rather than larger context.

questions.stem: A team creates a documentation-review custom agent. Security review flags that the agent can edit source files and invoke all configured tools. Which change best aligns the agent with its intended role?
questions.scenario: The agent should read repository files, search docs, and produce review comments. It should not modify code or call unrelated MCP tools.

artifact.title: .github/agents/doc-reviewer.md
artifact.content:
---
name: doc-reviewer
description: Reviews documentation for clarity and consistency
tools: ['*']
---
You review documentation changes and suggest improvements.
Return concise findings with file paths and rationale.

options.text: Add a sentence asking the agent to request permission before each repository read.
Move the profile to /agents so organization-level governance applies automatically.
Restrict tools to read and search capabilities, excluding edit and unrelated MCP tools.
Keep tools: ['*'] and rely on the prompt to discourage edits to source files.

explanation.whyCorrect: The tools property should match the agent's job; read and search support review while excluding edit and broad tool access.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Prompt-only limits are weaker than tool scoping.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Read approval prompts add friction without addressing edit capability.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Changing profile location does not reduce tool permissions.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When an agent role is narrow, prefer explicit tool scoping over behavioral instructions alone.

questions.stem: A Copilot setup workflow must authenticate to a private package registry. The team stored the token as a normal GitHub Actions repository secret, but Copilot cannot access it. What should the team change?
questions.scenario: The session log shows the registry authentication command receives an empty token value during Copilot cloud agent setup.

artifact.title: copilot-setup-steps.yml excerpt
artifact.content:
jobs:
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Configure registry
        run: npm config set //registry.example.com/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN
      - run: npm ci

options.text: Create NPM_TOKEN as an Agents secret for Copilot cloud agent, not as an Actions secret.
Move the token into copilot-instructions.md so the agent can read it during setup.
Grant contents: write permission so the setup job can read repository-level secrets.
Add secrets: inherit to the copilot-setup-steps job so all repository secrets are passed.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent uses dedicated Agents secrets and variables; it does not receive normal Actions, Codespaces, or Dependabot secrets.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: The setup workflow is not a reusable workflow call, and Copilot does not receive Actions secrets this way.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Putting a token in instructions would expose a secret in source control.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Repository contents permission does not grant access to Actions secrets.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Secret-boundary questions often turn on the difference between Actions secrets and Copilot Agents secrets.

questions.stem: A team wants Copilot cloud agent to handle small bug-fix issues, but reviewers complain that the first visible artifact is a large code diff with no explanation of intended steps. What should the team require before the agent makes code changes?
questions.scenario: The repository already uses pull requests and required CI checks. The team wants faster review without reducing control over autonomous changes.

options.text: Move agent planning notes into a private chat outside the repository workflow.
Require the agent to create an inspectable implementation plan in GitHub before starting execution.
Allow the agent to commit first, then ask reviewers to infer the plan from the diff.
Disable automated tests until the agent has completed its first implementation attempt.

explanation.whyCorrect: A structured plan separates planning from execution and gives reviewers an inspectable artifact before the agent acts.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Reviewing only after code is committed weakens the planning boundary and slows review.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Disabling tests removes an evaluation signal rather than improving plan quality.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Keeping plans outside GitHub reduces traceability and auditability.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For Domain A, prefer answers that create reviewable GitHub artifacts before autonomous action.

questions.stem: A platform team is designing observability for autonomous agent work in GitHub. Select THREE artifacts or signals that should be part of the standard review and audit trail.
questions.scenario: The team wants artifacts that fit normal SDLC tooling and can be inspected by reviewers and administrators after a task completes.

options.text: Private direct messages between developers discussing what they think the agent did.
Uncommitted scratch notes stored only in the agent's ephemeral workspace.
GitHub Actions logs and required status checks produced during validation.
Pull request descriptions that summarize intent, changes, validation, and risks.
Copilot session logs linked from commits and visible in the agents interface.
Local shell history from maintainers who reviewed the pull request.

explanation.whyCorrect: PR descriptions, Actions checks/logs, and Copilot session logs are inspectable GitHub artifacts that support review and audit.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Private messages are not a durable system-of-record artifact.
whyDistractorsWrong.F: Reviewer shell history is not authoritative for agent activity.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Ephemeral scratch notes are not preserved for audit.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Look for artifacts that live in GitHub and survive the agent session.

questions.stem: An organization wants to test a new custom agent privately before releasing it to all organization users. Select TWO steps that align with the documented rollout process.
questions.scenario: The organization has already created a .github-private repository from GitHub's custom agents template. The agent is still experimental.

options.text: Publish the profile as a GitHub Action so Copilot discovers it during workflow execution.
After testing, move the approved profile from .github/agents into the agents directory.
Create the test agent profile under .github/agents in the .github-private repository.
Store the custom agent in each product repository to avoid organization-level visibility controls.
Place the test profile directly in /agents so all organization users can invoke it immediately.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents testing organization custom agents from .github/agents in .github-private, then releasing them by moving the profile into agents.

whyDistractorsWrong.E: The /agents directory is the release location, not the private testing location.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Copying to every repository increases drift and does not use the organization rollout process.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Custom agents are agent profiles, not GitHub Actions.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For custom-agent lifecycle questions, separate private testing location from broad release location.

questions.stem: A backend team uses Copilot cloud agent over several days to modernize a payment service. On the third run, the agent repeats completed refactors and starts changing logging patterns that conflict with the original issue requirements. The team also wants future Copilot code reviews in the same repository to remember the repository's database-connection convention. Which memory and state strategy should the team implement?
questions.scenario: The team needs continuity for the long-running migration, but each new issue must start from a clean task context. Stable repository conventions should be reusable by Copilot features in the same repository.

options.text: Store task progress, issue decisions, and repository conventions only in Copilot Memory, then resume future runs from remembered facts.
Persist checkpoints in the PR, re-anchor each run to the issue criteria, and store only stable repository conventions in Copilot Memory.
Move checkpoints and conventions into a shared external vector store, then make all service repositories read the same memory.
Keep the full chat and tool-call history pinned across related issues, pruning it only after the whole migration completes.

explanation.whyCorrect: B separates durable task state from long-term repository memory. Progress checkpoints in the PR let the agent resume without repeating work, re-anchoring to the issue criteria corrects context drift, and Copilot Memory is appropriate for stable repository-level facts such as coding conventions or architectural decisions that may later be used by cloud agent or code review in the same repository.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot Memory is designed for repository facts and user preferences, not as the only durable execution log for a multi-day task.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Keeping full historical context increases drift and stale-context risk; completed tool history should be pruned instead of carried across task boundaries.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A shared cross-repository memory risks conflicting or stale context; Copilot repository-level facts are scoped to operations on the same repository.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 memory questions, separate execution state from reusable knowledge: checkpoints belong in durable GitHub artifacts, while stable repo conventions belong in scoped Copilot Memory.

questions.stem: A DevOps team wants Copilot cloud agent to implement routine application fixes, but some fixes may update deployment workflows and trigger a staging deployment. The security team wants to preserve delivery speed while adding checkpoints only where risk is meaningful. What should the team configure?
questions.scenario: The repository already requires pull requests for default-branch changes. The team must prevent unreviewed deployment changes without blocking low-risk code edits.

options.text: Allow workflows to run automatically, then review session logs and rollback if the staging deployment fails.
Require security approval for every agent-created commit and prohibit staging deployments until the quarterly access review finishes.
Use rulesets with required checks, CODEOWNERS on agent configuration, and environment approval for staging deployments.
Move all deployment logic outside GitHub Actions so Copilot PRs cannot trigger any deployment workflow.

explanation.whyCorrect: This right-sizes the guardrails: rulesets and required checks apply to Copilot cloud agent like human contributors, CODEOWNERS review protects Copilot and MCP configuration files, and environment approvals create a human checkpoint for deployment risk without slowing routine code changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Requiring approval for every commit over-controls low-risk work and slows delivery without focusing on deployment or configuration risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Reviewing logs after automatic workflow execution is reactive and does not provide a pre-deployment human checkpoint.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Moving deployment outside GitHub Actions adds avoidable architectural complexity instead of using existing rulesets and environment controls.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 guardrail questions, prefer layered preventive controls that match the risk level. Avoid blanket approvals for low-risk work and avoid relying on monitoring after risky actions occur.
