questions.stem: A repository administrator is reviewing an MCP configuration before enabling a Copilot cloud agent for bug triage. The agent needs read-only GitHub context from the current repository and read-only incident details from Sentry. What remediation should the administrator apply before enabling the agent?
questions.scenario: Security requires that the agent avoid broad GitHub access, use Copilot cloud agent secret substitution correctly, and prevent autonomous use of write-capable MCP tools.

artifact.title: Repository MCP configuration draft

options.text: Use built-in read-only GitHub MCP, allowlist Sentry read tools, and reference a COPILOT_MCP_ secret.
Keep the GitHub entry, document the broad tools, and store SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN as an Actions secret.
Change only the GitHub URL to /readonly, keep tools ["*"], and validate after the first run.
Move the MCP setup into copilot-setup-steps.yml and grant contents: read to the setup job.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent has a built-in GitHub MCP server with read-only access to the current repository, so a broader custom GitHub MCP entry is unnecessary for this scenario. MCP configurations should allowlist specific tools, especially read-only tools, because the agent can use MCP tools autonomously. Secret references in MCP configuration must come from Copilot environment variables or secrets with names prefixed by COPILOT_MCP_.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Actions secrets are not the right substitution source for this MCP configuration, and documenting broad access does not reduce autonomous tool exposure.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: The /readonly endpoint is safer than the broad endpoint, but leaving tools as ["*"] and keeping invalid secret substitution is incomplete.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: copilot-setup-steps.yml customizes the agent development environment; it is not where repository MCP server authorization and tool allowlists are configured.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When an artifact mixes environment setup, MCP configuration, and secrets, separate the control planes: MCP tool allowlists belong in MCP config, and MCP credentials must use Copilot environment secret naming.

questions.stem: A platform team is building an incident-review dashboard for a Copilot SDK workflow that delegates research, implementation, and validation work to custom sub-agents. After a failed release candidate, reviewers cannot determine which sub-agent invocation introduced the bad change because the same agent name appears in multiple places. What should the team change?
questions.scenario: The workflow must preserve enough operational evidence to reconstruct each sub-agent execution after the fact without disabling automatic delegation.

artifact.title: Current event subscriber

options.text: Track started, completed, and failed events keyed by toolCallId, including status, error, and timestamps.
Set infer:false on worker agents and require operators to invoke each agent explicitly during incidents.
Preselect the implementation agent at session creation so all emitted events share one parent context.
Group events by agentName and overwrite the previous status whenever the same agent runs again.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents that sub-agent lifecycle events include started, completed, and failed events, and that toolCallId fields let you reconstruct the execution tree. Capturing those events with status, errors, and timestamps gives reviewers the audit trail needed for post-hoc failure analysis.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Disabling inference changes delegation behavior but does not create a reliable execution tree for incident review.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Grouping only by agentName collapses separate invocations of the same agent and can hide the failed execution.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Preselecting one agent narrows the session start context but does not capture lifecycle status across sub-agents.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 observability questions, prefer durable, correlatable artifacts over changes that merely constrain routing. Lifecycle events plus correlation identifiers are stronger than agent names alone.

questions.stem: A platform team is piloting Copilot coding agent for dependency remediation in a regulated repository. Leadership wants the agent to reduce developer effort, but the security team requires traceable work, independent human review, and CI evidence before any change reaches the default branch. Which SDLC design best satisfies these requirements?
questions.scenario: The repository already uses GitHub pull requests, CODEOWNERS, required checks, and protected branches. The team wants to avoid adding a separate approval system outside GitHub.

options.text: Keep Copilot work in pull requests, require status checks and CODEOWNERS review, then have a maintainer approve and merge.
Run Copilot in a staging fork, then have maintainers copy the final patch into the protected repository.
Enable auto-merge for Copilot pull requests after dependency tests pass, then review agent session logs during weekly audits.
Require Copilot to post an issue comment plan, then allow deployment once the package manager test command succeeds.

explanation.whyCorrect: Using pull requests as the control point preserves GitHub as the system of record, allows required status checks and CODEOWNERS review to gate the merge, and aligns with Copilot coding agent behavior: Copilot proposes changes for review and cannot approve or merge its own pull request.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: This shifts control to after-the-fact auditing and allows merge based mainly on tests, rather than requiring independent review before integration.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A plan comment is useful, but it does not provide sufficient PR-based governance, review enforcement, or merge protection by itself.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A staging fork may reduce direct access, but copying patches weakens attribution, review traceability, and normal GitHub PR controls.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 SDLC questions, prefer designs that use GitHub-native checkpoints: PRs, required checks, CODEOWNERS, protected branches, and human approval before merge.

questions.stem: A platform team is creating a custom Copilot cloud agent to investigate flaky test failures. The agent must read source files, search the repository, and retrieve issue metadata from an MCP server, but it must not edit files or call write-capable MCP tools. Which configuration approach should the team use?
questions.scenario: The repository already has an MCP server configured with both read and write tools. The team wants the agent profile itself to enforce least-privilege access.

options.text: Move write-capable MCP tools to a separate server but keep both servers configured.
Set tools to ["*"] and rely on system instructions not to modify files.
Omit tools so the runtime can choose the smallest set needed for each task.
List only read and search aliases plus required server-prefixed read-only MCP tools.

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific tools list filters the built-in and MCP tools made available to the custom agent. Using read/search aliases and server-prefixed read-only MCP tool names enforces the agent's required capability boundary instead of depending on instructions alone.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Omitting the tools property enables all available tools, which can expose write-capable MCP tools already configured for the repository.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Using ["*"] enables all available tools, so the agent profile does not enforce the required read-only boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Separating servers can help organization, but keeping both servers configured does not restrict which tools this agent may call.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 tool-permission questions, prefer an explicit allowlist at the narrowest practical scope. Prompts, comments, or server reorganization do not replace tool filtering.

questions.stem: A backend team uses a custom implementation-planner agent before allowing Copilot cloud agent to modify service code. After three sprints, reviewers report that the final PRs often solve a related problem but do not match the agent's original plan. You review the session log excerpt and agent profile. Which tuning action best addresses the root cause?
questions.scenario: The team wants to improve plan adherence without blocking valid agent work or replacing the agent with a manual review process.

artifact.title: Session log excerpt and current custom agent profile
artifact.content:
SESSION: copilot/plan-order-retry-429
TASK: Add retry handling for order submission timeouts.

[plan]
- Update OrderClient to retry HTTP 429 and timeout responses.
- Add tests for timeout retry behavior.
- Keep checkout API response shape unchanged.

[tool: search]
query: "OrderClient retry timeout"
result: src/payments/PaymentClient.ts has retry helper.

[tool: edit]
files changed:
- src/api/CheckoutController.ts
- src/ui/messages.ts
- package-lock.json

[validation]
npm test -- --filter checkout => passed

[agent note]
Implemented a broader checkout retry UX because the existing retry helper was in payments.

--- .github/agents/implementation-planner.agent.md ---
---
name: implementation-planner
description: Creates implementation plans for backend changes
tools: ["read", "search", "edit"]
---
Create a concise implementation plan. Prefer existing patterns. If tests pass, prepare the result for review.

options.text: Increase the model tier and token budget, then monitor whether plan drift decreases over the next sprint.
Add required CodeQL and secret scanning checks so unrelated PR changes are caught during security validation.
Revise the agent instructions to require success criteria, constraints, risks, and plan-to-diff validation before review.
Remove edit access from the planner agent and require developers to manually translate every generated plan.

explanation.whyCorrect: The log shows a prompt/instruction issue and plan-adherence failure: the agent produced a related implementation that changed files outside the stated plan and lacked explicit success criteria or constraints. The documented implementation-planner pattern includes success criteria, technical approach, phased tasks, assumptions, constraints, and risks; session logs are the right evidence for comparing the plan, tool use, validation, and final changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Security scanning is useful for vulnerabilities and secrets, but it does not directly address plan drift or missing task constraints.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: A larger model or token budget may improve some outputs, but it does not encode the missing evaluation criteria or constraints.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Removing edit access avoids the symptom by disabling useful agent work, rather than tuning the instructions that caused the drift.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 tuning questions, identify the failure class first. If the plan is reasonable but execution drifts because constraints are vague, prefer targeted instruction and evaluation-signal changes over broader monitoring or capability removal.

questions.stem: HelioLedger is defining the standard workflow for routine agent fixes in `ledger-api`. Order the steps to satisfy the required plan, act, and evaluate lifecycle while preserving the required human checkpoint.
questions.scenario: The workflow must define clear task inputs, prevent code changes until the plan is approved, and keep review evidence inside GitHub.

options.text: Create or update the draft pull request with validation results, session evidence, and a human review request.
Publish a structured implementation plan and wait for the required reviewer checkpoint in the issue or pull request.
Extract the issue inputs, affected paths, acceptance criteria, test expectations, and known risky files.
After approval, implement the change on the agent branch and run the applicable checks.

explanation.whyCorrect: The workflow begins by turning the issue into structured inputs and success criteria. The agent then publishes a plan and waits for approval. After that checkpoint, it can act on an agent branch and run validation. The final step is evaluation through pull request review, checks, and traceable evidence.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Creating the review package is an evaluation activity and belongs after implementation and validation, not before planning.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A plan is valuable only after the task inputs and success criteria have been extracted from the issue.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Implementation must occur after the structured plan has been reviewed under HelioLedger's required checkpoint.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Sequence items often test lifecycle boundaries. Identify the earliest input-definition step, then place human approval before any irreversible or code-changing action.

questions.stem: HelioLedger's `support-fix-planner` agent will triage customer-impacting issues in `support-portal`, but auditors require reviewers to see the agent's intended approach before any code changes are made. Which design best satisfies the case study requirements?
questions.scenario: The team wants to keep delivery fast, but the workflow must preserve an inspectable planning artifact and prevent implementation before a human checkpoint.

options.text: Keep the plan in the session log and allow the agent to mark the pull request ready.
Have a project manager write a separate planning document, then let the agent implement from that document.
Let the agent implement the fix first, then require CI and reviewers to catch problems in the pull request.
Require a structured plan comment with inputs, tests, and success criteria, then wait for approval before changes.

explanation.whyCorrect: The correct design separates planning from action, produces a structured artifact in GitHub, defines inputs and success criteria, and adds a human checkpoint before implementation. This aligns with the GH-600 objective to separate planning, reasoning, and execution and with Copilot cloud agent's GitHub-centered review workflow.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: This relies on evaluation after implementation and does not prevent the agent from acting before the plan is reviewed.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: This creates a planning artifact, but it moves the inspectable agent plan outside the agent workflow and weakens traceability.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Session logs help auditing, but the plan is not placed in the normal review surface, and Copilot cannot mark its own pull requests ready.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 planning questions, prefer answers that create an inspectable GitHub artifact before action and insert human approval at the risk boundary.

questions.stem: HelioLedger's compliance team is concerned that agent-created changes could modify workflows, setup steps, or custom agent definitions without the right reviewers. Which control set best satisfies the case study requirements without blocking all agent work?
questions.scenario: The organization wants agents to continue creating routine fixes, but sensitive configuration and deployment paths must require stronger review and validation.

options.text: Add CODEOWNERS entries for sensitive files, but allow agent pull requests to merge when CI succeeds.
Enable the agent firewall and review audit logs weekly for changes to workflows, setup steps, and agent profiles.
Disable automatic workflow runs for agent pull requests and rely on reviewers to inspect session logs.
Use rulesets for `copilot/` branches requiring PRs, checks, CODEOWNERS review, and protected environment approval.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rulesets or branch protection targeted at agent-created branches enforce pull requests, required checks, and human review. CODEOWNERS protects sensitive GitHub configuration files, while protected environments add the manual deployment gate required by the case study.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Firewall and logs help reduce exfiltration risk and support auditability, but they do not enforce merge controls for sensitive files.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: CODEOWNERS identifies reviewers, but without required review and merge rules it does not fully enforce the compliance requirement.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Manual inspection is useful, but session logs alone do not enforce required checks, CODEOWNERS review, or deployment approval.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a scenario asks for governance without stopping delivery, select preventive GitHub controls: PRs, rulesets or branch protection, CODEOWNERS, checks, and environment gates.

caseStudies.title: Case Study: HelioLedger Platform Engineering
caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: HelioLedger is a financial software company that maintains a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization for payment reconciliation, ledger reporting, and customer support tooling. The company is piloting GitHub Copilot cloud agent and custom agents to reduce the backlog of low-risk maintenance issues while keeping regulated repositories auditable.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The organization uses Copilot Business. The pilot repositories include `ledger-api`, `support-portal`, and `reconciliation-workers`. Issues are created by product owners and must include affected service, expected behavior, acceptance criteria, test expectations, and known risky files. The platform team has created a `.github-private` repository from GitHub's custom agents template, but most teams have not yet standardized how agent profiles should separate planning from implementation.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: HelioLedger wants agents to handle routine bug fixes, dependency updates, and internal documentation corrections. Agent work must remain visible in GitHub issues, pull requests, comments, commits, checks, and logs. Reviewers must be able to understand why an agent made a change without opening external systems.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: All agent-created implementation work must use pull requests. The desired workflow is: define task inputs and success criteria, produce an inspectable plan, wait for a human checkpoint when code or workflow changes are involved, make changes on an agent branch, run applicable validation, and request human review. The organization wants to use custom agents for specialized roles such as `support-fix-planner` and `safe-implementation-agent`.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: The compliance team requires independent review before merge, required status checks, CODEOWNERS review for `.github/`, `.github/workflows/`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `copilot-setup-steps.yml`, and agent profile changes. Agent-created `copilot/` branches must not bypass repository rules. Deployments to protected environments must require manual approval. Audit evidence must include the initiating user, agent-authored commits, session logs, and the final pull request review outcome.

questions.stem: A healthcare engineering organization enables MCP servers in Copilot for a pilot group. The security team configures the policy to use Registry only, but the pilot includes repositories with regulated data and local MCP configurations that developers can edit. What should the platform owner do to satisfy the highest-security requirement?
questions.scenario: The organization wants to prevent non-approved MCP servers from being used during the pilot, not merely detect usage after the fact.

options.text: Disable MCP servers for the regulated pilot until stricter enforcement is available, then re-enable approved servers.
Allow local MCP servers when their configured server ID matches an entry uploaded to the registry.
Require developers to rename local MCP servers to match registry IDs before starting Copilot sessions.
Keep Registry only enabled and review Copilot session logs weekly for unexpected MCP server names.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents current MCP allowlist enforcement limitations, including server name or ID matching and lack of strict enforcement that prevents non-registry servers. For the highest-security requirement, disabling MCP servers until strict enforcement is available is the safest preventive control.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Weekly log review is detective, not preventive, and leaves a bypass window during regulated agent runs.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Registry only is more restrictive than Allow all, but documented limitations still leave bypass risk through editable configurations.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Renaming servers to match registry IDs relies on the same name or ID matching behavior that the limitation warns about.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 governance questions, distinguish policy intent from actual enforcement behavior. If a documented limitation leaves a bypass, choose the preventive control over monitoring.

questions.stem: A developer experience team is building an observability panel for an orchestrator-worker workflow that uses Copilot SDK custom agents. During an incident review, two parallel security-auditor sub-agents overwrote each other's status in the panel, and the team could not identify which failed worker caused the parent session to continue with incomplete results. Which change best fixes the implementation?
questions.scenario: The team must preserve enough event data to reconstruct parallel sub-agent execution, detect failed workers, and support a human-in-the-loop recovery checkpoint before integration.

artifact.title: Current sub-agent event handler

options.text: Keep agentName as the key, then compare draft PR branches after all workers finish.
Key nodes by toolCallId from started events, then persist completed and failed outcomes.
Track only selected events, then restart the parent session when any worker reports an error.
Move each worker to a separate session, then disable streaming to reduce telemetry volume.

explanation.whyCorrect: The implementation should correlate each sub-agent execution by toolCallId because parallel invocations of the same custom agent can share the same agentName. Capturing subagent.started, subagent.completed, and subagent.failed outcomes creates an execution tree that supports incident review and recovery decisions.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Branch comparison is useful after code is produced, but it does not reconstruct the event tree or identify the failed invocation reliably.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Selected events show which agent was chosen, but they do not include the execution correlation data needed for parallel workers.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Separate sessions and reduced streaming remove useful orchestration signals instead of improving observability and recovery.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 multi-agent observability questions, prefer answers that preserve correlation identifiers and failure artifacts. Avoid fixes that rely only on final PR state or reduce telemetry.

questions.stem: A SaaS company is introducing an organization-level custom Copilot agent for risky billing-system changes. Architecture leads require the agent to inspect the repository and produce an implementation plan, but they do not want the same agent to modify code or run commands until a maintainer approves the plan in GitHub. Which change best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The platform team wants the plan to be reviewable in normal SDLC tooling and wants to avoid relying only on post-change controls.

artifact.title: agents/billing-implementation-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: billing-implementation-planner
description: Creates implementation plans for billing changes and may implement low-risk fixes
tools: ["read", "search", "edit", "execute"]
---

You are responsible for billing implementation work.

For each assigned issue:
1. Inspect the affected services and tests.
2. Write an implementation plan.
3. Implement low-risk changes immediately when the plan is clear.
4. If tests fail, fix the failures and continue without interrupting the user.

options.text: Keep edit and execute tools, require approval before merge, and rely on branch protection to catch unsafe generated changes.
Limit tools to read and search, require a structured plan artifact, and start implementation only after human approval.
Add CODEOWNERS and required CI, allowing the planner to commit code when its plan meets acceptance criteria.
Publish the agent from .github-private with internal visibility, preserving all tools so organization audit logs capture usage.

explanation.whyCorrect: Limiting the planner to read and search tools enforces the planning boundary before action. Requiring a structured plan artifact supports review in GitHub, and a separate approved implementation step creates the human checkpoint required before code changes or command execution.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Approval before merge is too late for this requirement because the agent can still edit files and execute commands before the plan is reviewed.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Organization-level placement and visibility help distribution and access, but they do not prevent the planner from acting with edit and execute tools.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: CODEOWNERS and CI are valuable PR governance controls, but they evaluate changes after the planner has already modified code.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 plan-versus-act questions, favor answers that remove action capabilities from the planning agent and create a reviewable artifact before implementation begins.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A media streaming company is introducing Copilot cloud agent for dependency modernization work across a regulated monorepo. Architecture leaders want agents to move quickly, but they require planning to be separated from execution, all agent work to remain inspectable in GitHub, and deployment to remain gated by human approval. In which order should the team implement the workflow?
questions.scenario: The repository already uses GitHub Actions, CODEOWNERS, required status checks, and protected deployment environments. The team wants to avoid both unbounded autonomy and approval steps that do not reduce material risk.

options.text: Allow Copilot to implement changes on a branch and open a pull request containing the diff and rationale.
Define task inputs, expected artifacts, acceptance tests, ownership boundaries, and merge-readiness criteria.
Require CI, CODEOWNERS review, and protected-environment approval before merge or deployment.
Have Copilot research the repository and produce a structured implementation plan before writing code.
Have a responsible reviewer approve the plan and authorize Copilot to proceed with execution.

explanation.whyCorrect: The workflow first defines the agent task contract, then uses Copilot cloud agent for research and planning before code changes. A human approval checkpoint separates planning from execution. After Copilot creates the branch and pull request, standard GitHub governance evaluates the output through checks, CODEOWNERS review, and environment approval.

whyDistractorsWrong.A-before-D: Starting with implementation collapses planning and execution, making the agent's reasoning harder to inspect before code is written.
whyDistractorsWrong.C-before-A: Requiring CI and review before a pull request exists gives governance controls no concrete diff, artifact, or workflow run to evaluate.
whyDistractorsWrong.E-before-D: Approving execution before a structured plan exists turns the checkpoint into a generic approval rather than a meaningful risk control.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-B: Planning before defining inputs, outputs, and success criteria increases the chance that the plan optimizes for the wrong task boundary.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 sequence questions, order agent work as contract, plan, human checkpoint, action, then evaluation. If an option lets the agent act before an inspectable plan is approved, it is usually too early.

questions.stem: A retail engineering team uses Copilot cloud agent to continue a multi-week feature-flag migration after several interruptions. The agent previously learned that feature flags must be declared in one TypeScript file and mirrored in a YAML catalog, but several branches have changed since that fact was captured. What should the team configure or require to maintain continuity without using stale context?
questions.scenario: The team wants future Copilot code reviews to detect inconsistent feature-flag updates, but the migration checklist itself must resume from the last completed step in the active PR.

options.text: Rely on Copilot Memory for the migration checklist, because repository memories remain available across agent sessions until manually deleted.
Move all state into an external vector database, and disable Copilot Memory to avoid branch citation validation delays.
Store the flag convention as repository memory, keep migration checkpoints in the PR, and revalidate against branch HEAD before resuming.
Save both the convention and developer-specific decisions as user preferences, so code review can reuse them during later reviews.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository-level Copilot Memory is appropriate for reusable repository facts such as coding conventions and project-specific rules, and Copilot validates repository facts against citations in the current branch before use. Task progress should be captured as a durable artifact, such as the PR description or comments, so the agent can resume from the latest checkpoint rather than relying on transient context.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot Memory is not the right place for step-by-step task progress, and unused facts or preferences can be deleted after 28 days rather than persisting until manual deletion.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: User-level preferences are tied to one user's later interactions, and Copilot code review uses repository-level facts only, not user-level preferences.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: An external store can be useful for some permanent memory needs, but replacing Copilot Memory removes built-in repository scoping and citation validation for repo facts.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 memory questions, separate durable task state from reusable repository knowledge. Checkpoints belong in GitHub artifacts; repository conventions belong in validated repository-level memory.

questions.stem: A support engineering team creates a repository-level custom Copilot cloud agent to summarize GitHub issues and SupportHub tickets. The agent must read repository files and search SupportHub tickets, but it must not create or update tickets or modify source files. Based on the artifact, which change best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The SupportHub MCP server documentation lists three tools: `search_tickets`, `create_ticket`, and `update_ticket`. The token has already been provisioned as an Agents secret named `COPILOT_MCP_SUPPORTHUB_TOKEN`.

artifact.title: .github/agents/support-triage.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: support-triage
description: Drafts issue summaries from repository files and SupportHub tickets.
mcpServers:
  supporthub:
    type: http
    url: https://supporthub.example.com/mcp
    tools: ["search_tickets", "create_ticket", "update_ticket"]
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.COPILOT_MCP_SUPPORTHUB_TOKEN }}
---

You summarize related GitHub issues and SupportHub tickets. Produce a Markdown summary only.

options.text: Move the token to an Actions secret and omit `tools` so the default toolset is available.
Set SupportHub `tools` to `*` and rely on the MCP registry policy for tool restriction.
Keep the configuration and strengthen the prompt to instruct the agent not to call write tools.
Use `mcp-servers`, keep only `search_tickets`, and set `tools` to `read`, `search`, and `supporthub/search_tickets`.

explanation.whyCorrect: Custom agent profiles use the `mcp-servers` frontmatter property. The MCP server configuration should expose only the required SupportHub tool, and the agent-level `tools` list should restrict the agent to read/search plus the specific namespaced MCP tool.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Prompt instructions are not a permission boundary; the write-capable MCP tools would remain available to the agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Using `*` enables all tools from the MCP server, including the write tools the scenario explicitly prohibits.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot cloud agent MCP configuration uses Agents secrets or variables with the required prefix, and omitting `tools` enables all available tools.

explanation.examStrategyNote: On GH-600 configuration artifacts, check both syntax and effective permissions. A valid-looking prompt cannot compensate for an over-broad tool list.

questions.stem: A financial services team is creating a custom Copilot cloud agent to plan database migration work. Compliance requires the agent to inspect the repository and produce an auditable implementation plan, but no code changes, shell commands, or migration execution can occur until a maintainer approves the plan. Based on the agent profile, which change best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The team wants to keep delivery moving by using Copilot for repository analysis and planning, while enforcing a clear boundary between planning and implementation.

artifact.title: .github/agents/migration-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: migration-planner
description: Plans and implements database migration changes for platform services
tools: ["read", "search", "edit", "execute", "github/*"]
---

You are responsible for translating approved issues into production-ready migration changes.

For each assigned issue:
1. Analyze the repository and create an implementation plan in the pull request description.
2. Update migration code immediately after the plan is drafted.
3. Run tests, commit changes, and request review.
4. If requirements are unclear, choose the least disruptive implementation.

options.text: Move the profile to .github-private and monitor session logs for changes made without approval.
Keep the tools and ask the agent to request maintainer approval in the PR description before merging.
Limit tools to read/search and require a structured plan comment approved before a separate implementation assignment.
Remove execute but keep edit, then rely on branch protection and required reviews before merging.

explanation.whyCorrect: Limiting the planning agent to read/search removes code-edit and shell-execution capability during the planning phase, while the structured plan and approval checkpoint preserve the required Plan → Act boundary. GitHub custom agents allow specific tool lists, and the GH-600 study guide explicitly tests separating planning from execution, producing structured plans, validating plans, and preventing action until approval.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A prompt-only approval instruction leaves edit and execute available, so the agent can still make changes before approval.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Branch protection controls merge, not planning-time action; keeping edit still allows unapproved repository changes on the agent branch.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Organization-wide placement improves reuse, and logs help audit, but monitoring after the fact does not prevent unapproved action.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 architecture questions, prefer designs that prevent risky agent actions through tool scope and workflow boundaries. Reviews and logs are important, but they are weaker than separating planning capability from implementation capability.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A platform team pilots a custom Copilot cloud agent intended to create implementation plans before engineers start coding. After 18 sessions, evaluation shows low plan-to-diff adherence, frequent source changes before plan review, and repeated reviewer comments that the agent is acting like an implementation agent instead of a planner. Which change should you make first to tune the agent based on this evaluation?
questions.scenario: Session logs show the agent used shell commands to run migrations and modify application files. The team wants the next sprint's evaluation to measure structured plan quality, risk coverage, and reviewer rework rather than completed feature PRs.

artifact.title: .github/agents/sprint-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: sprint-planner
description: Creates sprint implementation plans and prepares code changes for backlog items
tools: ["*"]
---

You are a sprint planning and implementation specialist.

For each assigned issue:
- Explore the repository and identify the likely files to change.
- Create an implementation plan.
- If the plan is straightforward, make the code changes in the same session.
- Run available tests and linters.
- Open or update a pull request when the work is ready.

Preferred output:
- Summary
- Files changed
- Test results
- Follow-up work

options.text: Switch to a stronger model and require reviewers to comment when the final PR diverges from the plan.
Keep the agent unchanged and add a dashboard for plan adherence, review iterations, and test pass rate.
Restrict tools to read/search/edit and instruct it to write a structured plan artifact, excluding source edits.
Add a post-run CodeQL workflow and ask the agent to fix scan findings after it opens the PR.

explanation.whyCorrect: The evaluation indicates a behavior and tool-scope mismatch: the agent is supposed to plan but has broad tool access and instructions to implement. The best first tuning action is to narrow the tool set and revise the prompt so the agent produces an inspectable structured plan artifact instead of making source changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A dashboard improves visibility but leaves the broad tool access and implementation-oriented instructions unchanged, so it does not address the root cause.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: A stronger model may improve reasoning quality, but the artifact already tells the agent to implement, so model choice is not the primary issue.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: CodeQL is useful for security evaluation, but post-run scanning does not correct the planner-versus-implementer role mismatch.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 tuning questions, map the failure signal to the smallest causal change: revise instructions and tool access when logs show the agent is using the wrong autonomy level.

questions.stem: An insurance company's platform team is enabling Copilot cloud agent for a repository that contains custom agent profiles and a setup workflow. An auditor says an agent must not be able to weaken its own instructions, runner setup, or tool restrictions without accountable human review, but application-code changes should still move quickly. Based on the CODEOWNERS artifact, which change best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The repository already requires one approving review before merge. The team wants a preventive control that applies to Copilot-created pull requests and human pull requests without adding approval gates to ordinary feature files.

artifact.title: .github/CODEOWNERS
artifact.content:
# Current CODEOWNERS
src/payments/** @payments/app-reviewers
src/policies/** @policies/app-reviewers
.github/copilot-instructions.md @platform/ai-governance
.github/workflows/deploy-production.yml @platform/release-governance

options.text: Allow Copilot edits but add a weekly workflow that reports configuration changes.
Require signed commits and CodeQL status checks only on copilot/** branches.
Store custom-agent instructions in Actions secrets and load them during setup steps.
Add CODEOWNERS for .github/agents/* and .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, then require Code Owner review.

explanation.whyCorrect: Protecting custom agent profiles and the Copilot setup workflow with CODEOWNERS, combined with required Code Owner review, creates a preventive human checkpoint for changes that can alter agent behavior or execution context. GitHub guidance recommends protecting important Copilot and MCP configuration files with CODEOWNERS and enabling required Code Owner review.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Signed commits and CodeQL checks improve traceability and security scanning, but they do not stop a pull request from changing agent configuration without the accountable reviewers.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Moving instructions into Actions secrets reduces inspectability and is the wrong boundary; Copilot cloud agent is not intended to access GitHub Actions secrets in its sessions.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: A weekly report is a detective control after changes occur, not a preventive approval path for compliance-sensitive configuration changes.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 governance questions, prefer preventive controls that scope the risky artifact and preserve velocity elsewhere. Monitoring-only answers usually fail human-in-the-loop requirements.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A NovaWorks custom agent opens a pull request that changes application code and modifies .github/workflows/build.yml. GitHub Actions has not run automatically. In what order should the reviewer proceed?
questions.scenario: The repository follows the case study policy for Copilot pull requests and workflow-file changes.

options.text: Complete required human and CODEOWNERS review, then merge only after checks pass.
Click Approve and run workflows for the Copilot pull request.
Open the session log to inspect tools used and validation steps.
Inspect the PR diff, focusing on proposed workflow-file changes.

explanation.whyCorrect: The reviewer should first inspect the pull request diff, especially workflow changes, then use the session log to understand the agent's tool use and validation. Only after becoming comfortable with the changes should the reviewer approve Actions workflows to run. Merge remains last and depends on required checks and human review.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Merging before workflow approval and passing checks would bypass the validation and review gates required by the case study.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Approving workflow execution before inspecting workflow-file changes risks running privileged automation prematurely.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Session logs are valuable, but the PR diff should be inspected first because the workflow file itself changed.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Diff inspection is the correct first step, but it does not replace session-log review, workflow approval, checks, and human review.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For Copilot PR review sequence questions, inspect changes first, validate traceability next, run privileged checks only after review, and merge last.

caseStudies.title: Case Study: NovaWorks Platform Engineering
caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: NovaWorks is a SaaS company that maintains a large GitHub organization with 220 repositories. The platform engineering group is introducing GitHub Copilot cloud agent and custom agents to reduce backlog in maintenance, testing, and documentation work. The first rollout targets the phoenix-api repository, a TypeScript service that handles customer-facing APIs.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The organization uses GitHub Enterprise with Copilot enabled. The phoenix-api repository has a protected main branch, required status checks for build, unit-test, lint, and codeql, and CODEOWNERS for security-sensitive paths. The platform team has created an organization-level .github-private repository from GitHub's custom agents template. Agent profiles are intended to be available across the organization, while repository-specific runtime setup is managed in .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml. Copilot cloud agent sessions are tracked through the agents panel and session logs.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: NovaWorks wants agents to handle dependency modernization, test coverage improvements, and low-risk refactoring. Product teams need faster delivery, but architecture leads want every non-trivial agent task to produce a plan that can be reviewed before implementation. The release team wants agent work to remain visible in normal GitHub workflows: issues, pull requests, comments, checks, reviews, and session logs.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: Custom agents must define clear inputs, expected outputs, and success criteria in their prompts. For tasks estimated above one hour, the agent must produce a structured implementation plan before modifying code. The plan must be stored as a GitHub artifact that reviewers can inspect without leaving the repository. The agent must not begin implementation until a human with write access approves the plan in GitHub. The setup workflow must be deterministic, use least-privilege permissions, and keep the required job name for Copilot setup steps.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Changes to .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/agents/*.agent.md, and CODEOWNERS require review by the platform-governance team. Copilot-authored pull requests must be reviewed like other contributions and must not be merged solely because the agent reports success. GitHub Actions workflows on Copilot pull requests should be run only after a human reviews the proposed changes, especially changes under .github/workflows/. The firewall should remain enabled unless an approved exception is documented.

questions.stem: A mobile backend repository tries to customize Copilot cloud agent's setup workflow as shown. Copilot does not use the intended environment. Which correction should the team make first?
questions.scenario: The repository administrator wants the setup to run before each Copilot task without relying on unsupported runner settings.

options.text: Keep macOS and add a second Linux job that installs the same tools for validation.
Increase timeout-minutes so slow package installation can finish before Copilot starts.
Move the workflow into .github/agents so it is loaded with the custom agent profile.
Use a copilot-setup-steps job on Ubuntu or Windows and set timeout-minutes to 59 or less.

explanation.whyCorrect: The setup workflow must include the required copilot-setup-steps job. Copilot cloud agent supports Ubuntu x64 Linux and Windows 64-bit runners, not macOS, and timeout-minutes has a documented maximum of 59 in this file.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Adding another job does not fix the unsupported macOS job or the required setup job name.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: The documented maximum is 59 minutes, so increasing the timeout moves further from supported configuration.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Agent profiles and setup workflows are different mechanisms stored in different paths.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When setup-step artifacts include runners, verify both the required job name and the limited job settings Copilot actually honors.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent commits are authored by Copilot, list the initiator as co-author, are signed and Verified, and include links from commit messages to session logs containing reasoning and tool-use evidence.

questions.stem: A deprecated incident-remediation custom agent is being retired because a safer replacement is ready. Several old PRs and session logs may be needed for an upcoming audit. Select TWO actions that best preserve workflow continuity and auditability.
questions.scenario: New tasks should use the replacement agent, while historical evidence about the deprecated agent must remain traceable.

options.text: Rewrite old PR descriptions to remove references to the deprecated agent.
Commit the removal or rename of the old agent profile with a clear retirement rationale.
Keep both agents automatically invocable until the audit has fully completed.
Delete historical session logs so reviewers focus on the replacement agent's behavior.
Route new work to the replacement while preserving existing PRs, commits, and log links.

explanation.whyCorrect: A versioned configuration change with a retirement rationale documents lifecycle intent. Preserving PRs, commits, and session log links keeps historical work auditable while new work moves to the replacement.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Removing references from old PRs weakens traceability and can look like history rewriting.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Deleting logs directly conflicts with the requirement to support the upcoming audit.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Keeping a deprecated agent automatically invocable increases the chance of new work using it.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Retirement questions are about versioned change control and preserved evidence, not erasing old artifacts.

questions.stem: A platform engineer is writing a review checklist for MCP configurations submitted by repository administrators. Select THREE checklist rules that correctly reflect Copilot cloud agent MCP behavior.
questions.scenario: The checklist must prevent common validation errors before configurations are saved in repository settings.

options.text: Approve remote MCP OAuth flows when the server presents a browser consent URL.
Permit unprefixed Actions secrets when the repository workflow already uses them.
Require url for remote http or sse MCP server configurations.
Reject MCP resources and prompts because cloud agent supports MCP tools only.
Allow variable substitution in every string field, including tools and type values.
Require command and args for local MCP servers that start a separate process.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent supports MCP tools, not MCP resources or prompts. Local MCP servers require command and args, while remote MCP servers require a url for the server endpoint.

whyDistractorsWrong.E: The documentation excludes tools and type from the fields that support variable substitution.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Remote MCP servers that use OAuth authentication and authorization are not currently supported by Copilot cloud agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: MCP secrets must be Agents secrets or variables with names prefixed COPILOT_MCP_, not ordinary Actions secrets.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Checklist-style items test exact boundaries. Be cautious with options that generalize a rule, such as substitution applying to all fields.

description: Summarizes production incidents, linked issues, and related pull requests

Create a concise incident timeline, identify likely contributing changes, and list follow-up questions for humans.

options.text: Keep the tool list and add prompt text saying not to edit or execute commands.
Remove edit and execute, and use disable-model-invocation true for manual selection.

Remove the description so automatic model invocation is less likely to match it.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Removing the description weakens usability and does not provide a reliable invocation control.

questions.stem: A developer assigns an issue to Copilot cloud agent, then the product owner clarifies an acceptance criterion after the assignment. In which order should the team handle the change with the least rework?

options.text: Wait for Copilot to raise the pull request for the assigned issue.
Add the clarification as a pull request comment directed to Copilot.
Review the agent's revised commits, tests, and updated PR description.
Decide whether the clarification changes scope enough to stop or restart the session.

explanation.whyCorrect: The team should first decide whether the late clarification invalidates the task. If it is still the same task, they should wait for the PR and then provide the new requirement as PR feedback so Copilot can iterate.

whyDistractorsWrong.B-before-A: A pull request comment cannot be used until Copilot has opened the pull request.
whyDistractorsWrong.C-before-B: There are no revised commits to review until the agent receives the clarification and iterates.
whyDistractorsWrong.A-before-D: If the clarification changes the task materially, waiting for the original PR may waste time.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Remember the timing detail: after assignment, new issue comments are not the best way to update Copilot; use the PR once it exists or restart if scope changed.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent creates a pull request that adds a new file-upload endpoint. The session log shows a CodeQL security issue was detected during the agent's validation pass, but the final pull request still contains the vulnerable pattern. What is the best evaluation and tuning response?
questions.scenario: The team wants to keep using the agent for similar endpoint work, but security policy requires vulnerable patterns to be addressed before merge.

options.text: Merge the pull request after filing a follow-up issue because CodeQL already documented the finding.
Treat the finding as a failed evaluation signal and steer Copilot to fix it before review completion.
Approve the pull request if the endpoint tests pass and the vulnerability is not currently exploitable.
Disable CodeQL for agent branches to reduce noise and rely on human review instead.

explanation.whyCorrect: A security finding in the agent's validation path is an evaluation failure for the generated change. GitHub documents that Copilot analyzes its generated code for security issues and that session logs show the analysis and actions taken, so the appropriate response is to have the agent remediate before merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Documenting a finding is not remediation and leaves a known vulnerability in the pull request.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Disabling the scan removes an important automated evaluation signal instead of tuning the workflow.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Passing functional tests does not satisfy a security policy requiring vulnerable patterns to be addressed.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In GH-600, scan findings are not merely informational when they map to the task's success criteria; they are feedback for iteration.

questions.stem: A repository migrated from Mocha to Vitest two weeks ago. A Copilot cloud-agent session now proposes a test change using the old `npm run mocha` command, which appears to come from a previously learned repository fact. Select TWO actions that best address stale memory while preserving useful repository learning.
questions.scenario: The repository owner wants future Copilot sessions to use Vitest, but does not want to disable Copilot Memory for every user.

options.text: Have the repository owner remove the stale repository-level fact if it no longer applies.
Copy the old Mocha command into repository instructions so future sessions see both options.
Verify whether the fact citation still matches the current branch before relying on it.
Keep the proposed change and depend on CI failure to correct the command later.
Disable Copilot Memory for the organization until every historical test command is manually audited.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot Memory repository facts are stored with citations and validated against the current branch before use. Repository owners can review and delete repository-level facts, which is the targeted correction for a stale migration fact.

whyDistractorsWrong.E: Organization-wide disablement is broader than needed and removes useful memory for unrelated repository facts.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Preserving conflicting commands in instructions increases context conflict instead of pruning obsolete information.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Waiting for CI is reactive and leaves the agent operating from stale context during the task.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a memory appears stale, prefer validation and targeted pruning over disabling the feature or adding contradictory context.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants Copilot to learn repository-specific build and architecture facts during cloud-agent work, but compliance also requires certain migration decisions to remain auditable for one year. The tenant uses organization-managed Copilot subscriptions. Select THREE design choices that satisfy the memory and retention requirements.
questions.scenario: Developers with read access should benefit from learned repository facts, while long-term audit records must not depend on Copilot Memory retention.

options.text: Store annual audit decisions as user-level preferences so they travel with each migration lead.
Use write-access users with Copilot Memory enabled to initiate fact-generating repository work.
Have an enterprise or organization admin enable Copilot Memory for the managed subscription.
Persist one-year migration decisions in an external durable store or committed audit artifact.
Ask read-only users to create repository facts during code review because they can see the repository.
Depend on unused Copilot Memory entries remaining available until the annual audit window closes.

explanation.whyCorrect: For organization-managed subscriptions, Copilot Memory is off by default and must be enabled by an admin. Repository facts are created from actions by write-access users with Memory enabled. One-year audit decisions should use external durable storage or committed artifacts because unused Copilot Memory entries are deleted after 28 days.

whyDistractorsWrong.F: Unused facts and preferences are automatically deleted after 28 days, so they do not satisfy a one-year audit requirement.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Repository-level facts are created from actions by users with write access and Copilot Memory enabled.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: User-level preferences are personal workflow signals, not shared auditable migration records.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For mixed retention requirements, separate adaptive Copilot Memory from compliance-grade durable records with explicit retention.

questions.stem: An engineering manager asks why the team should delegate routine cleanup tasks to Copilot cloud agent through GitHub instead of having developers run local AI sessions and manually push the results. Which reason best supports the GitHub-based agent workflow?
questions.scenario: The organization needs reviewers and auditors to understand what the agent did, why it did it, and who started the work.

options.text: GitHub workflows remove the need for developers to review generated changes before merging.
GitHub records agent work through branches, pull requests, signed commits, session logs, and review events.
Local AI sessions provide stronger isolation because they avoid repository-level workflow controls.
Local AI sessions reduce audit scope because only final commits are visible to reviewers.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub is the system of record and control plane for agent activity. Copilot cloud agent work is visible through branches, PRs, session logs, and signed commits that link back to the session.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Avoiding repository controls reduces governance rather than improving SDLC integration.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Showing only final commits loses useful planning and execution context for review and audit.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot-generated work still requires human review and normal repository controls before merge.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For observability questions, favor answers that keep agent activity inside GitHub artifacts and logs.

questions.stem: A repository-level custom agent should run in Copilot cloud agent to update release notes from merged pull request summaries. Developers report that it is not selected on GitHub.com, and the profile would not have enough tools if selected. Which change best fixes the profile?
questions.scenario: The agent should read repository history, search Markdown files, and edit docs/RELEASE_NOTES.md only.

artifact.title: .github/agents/release-notes.md
artifact.content:
---
name: release-notes-writer
description: Writes concise release notes from merged pull request context
target: vscode
tools: []
---

Update docs/RELEASE_NOTES.md using merged pull request summaries. Do not edit application source files.

options.text: Set target to github-copilot and tools to ["read", "search", "edit"].
Keep target as vscode and add a prompt saying the agent is intended for GitHub.com.
Set user-invocable to false and rely on automatic model invocation from GitHub.com.
Remove the tools property so the agent has enough tools in every environment.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Prompt text does not override a target value that limits where the agent is intended to run.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Removing tools enables all available tools, which is broader than needed for release-note editing.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Disabling user invocation does not fix the wrong target or the empty tool list.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a custom agent does not appear or cannot act, check both environment targeting and tool availability; either one can block the intended workflow.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A repository owner reviews a failed Copilot cloud agent task. The requested change was to add validation to one checkout endpoint. The session log shows the agent first planned to update the checkout controller, then called a repository-wide replace command that modified generated clients and unrelated tests. Select TWO root-cause classifications that best fit the evidence.
questions.scenario: The final pull request failed CI because generated files no longer matched the checked-in API schema, and reviewers noted that the initial plan was narrower than the actual diff.

options.text: Context issue, because the agent had no evidence that generated clients existed in the repository.
Memory issue, because stored repository facts should have prevented all generated-file edits.
Reasoning drift, because the final diff diverged from the agent's original task plan.
Environment issue, because CI failed after the agent pushed changes to its branch.
Tool misuse, because the agent used a broad replace command for a narrow endpoint change.

explanation.whyCorrect: The broad repository-wide replace is tool misuse because the wrong tool scope caused unintended edits. The mismatch between the narrow plan and broad final diff is reasoning drift that should be identified by comparing plans, logs, and outputs.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The evidence says the agent modified generated clients, not that it lacked context about their existence.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A CI failure is an observed symptom; the root cause is the agent's broad edit and plan divergence.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Copilot Memory may help with repository facts, but the evidence does not show a stale or missing memory caused the failure.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a stem includes both a plan and a tool trace, classify the failure from the causal evidence, not from the final failing check alone.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A security team adds dependency review as an evaluation gate for agent-created pull requests. The goal is to block runtime dependencies that introduce high or critical vulnerabilities while still allowing development-only moderate findings for now. What change should the team make to the workflow?
questions.scenario: The workflow currently fails inconsistently and reviewers are unsure whether the configuration expresses the intended policy.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/dependency-review.yml
artifact.content:
name: Dependency Review
on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  dependency-review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - name: Dependency Review
        uses: actions/dependency-review-action@v4
        with:
          fail-on-severity: moderate
          fail-on-scopes: development, runtime
          allow-licenses: MIT, Apache-2.0
          deny-licenses: GPL-3.0

options.text: Set fail-on-severity to high, set fail-on-scopes to runtime, and use only one license policy field.
Keep the workflow unchanged and evaluate only the final Dependabot alert count after merge.
Remove dependency review and rely on Copilot code review comments for dependency risk evaluation.
Change fail-on-severity to low and keep both license fields to maximize early detection.

explanation.whyCorrect: The intended gate is high-or-worse runtime vulnerability blocking, so fail-on-severity should be high and fail-on-scopes should be runtime. The dependency review action documentation also states that allow-licenses and deny-licenses are mutually exclusive.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Post-merge alert counts are useful telemetry but do not prevent insecure dependencies entering the default branch.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Failing on low severity and development scope is stricter than the stated policy and keeps a conflicting license configuration.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot review comments can provide feedback, but dependency review is the specific automated enforcement mechanism for dependency changes.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For scan-as-evaluation items, translate the stated policy into the narrowest enforceable check and remove conflicting configuration.

questions.stem: A platform team is evaluating whether a planning custom agent improves implementation quality. Each task should produce a structured plan before code changes, and the team wants to measure whether later pull requests follow that plan. Select TWO artifacts that provide the strongest evidence for this evaluation.
questions.scenario: The team wants a repeatable review process for comparing intent, agent actions, and final code changes.

options.text: The repository star count and number of contributors during the evaluation period.
The structured plan artifact, compared with the final pull request diff and commit history.
The session log showing tool use, validation steps, and reasons for implementation choices.
The number of times developers opened the Agents page during the agent session.
The count of emojis and reactions on the agent-created pull request summary.

explanation.whyCorrect: Plan adherence is evaluated by comparing the structured plan with the final diff and commit history, while session logs show Copilot's approach, tools used, and validation steps. Together they reveal whether execution followed intent.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Opening the Agents page is an engagement signal, not evidence of plan adherence or implementation quality.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Reactions may reflect sentiment but do not connect the plan to the actual implementation.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Repository popularity and contributor count are contextual metrics, not task-level evaluation artifacts.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For evaluation-by-artifact questions, choose artifacts that preserve intent, actions, and outputs in GitHub's system of record.

questions.stem: A governance review finds that a custom Copilot agent for incident triage can call every tool on an internal MCP server. The agent only needs to read incident metadata and link existing issues. What is the best correction?
questions.scenario: The MCP server also exposes tools that can close incidents, page on-call engineers, and modify severity labels in the incident system.

artifact.title: .github/agents/incident-triage.md
artifact.content:
---
name: incident-triage
description: Reads incident context and prepares GitHub issue updates.
tools: ["read", "search", "edit", "incident-mcp/*"]
mcp-servers:
  incident-mcp:
    type: http
    url: https://incidents.example.com/mcp
    tools: ["*"]
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.INCIDENT_TOKEN }}

options.text: Disable the cloud agent firewall because the MCP server already authenticates every request with a token.
Expose only needed read/link tools in the agent tools list and use an appropriately scoped Agents secret.
Replace the MCP server with screenshots from the incident dashboard attached to each GitHub issue.
Keep incident-mcp/* and add an instruction telling the agent to avoid mutating incident records.

explanation.whyCorrect: MCP tools can be invoked autonomously without per-call approval, so the agent should allow only the specific read or linking tools needed for the task and use a scoped secret from the supported agent-secret mechanism.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Natural-language instructions are weaker than tool allowlisting when mutating MCP tools remain available.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: The firewall is not a substitute for MCP tool governance, and disabling it increases exfiltration risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Screenshots reduce automation quality and still do not establish a governed tool permission boundary.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When MCP tools appear in an artifact, inspect the effective tool list. The safest answer usually removes unnecessary tools rather than relying on prompts.

questions.stem: A team wants Copilot cloud agent to use GitHub issue and pull request context while fixing issues in a single repository. The agent does not need information from other repositories. What should the repository administrator choose?
questions.scenario: A developer proposes adding a fine-grained PAT to the GitHub MCP server because it seems more explicit than relying on defaults.

Add an organization PAT with read access to all repositories for simpler future reuse.
Disable the built-in GitHub MCP server and configure a custom local GitHub proxy.
Use a broad PAT but restrict repository writes through branch protection and review rules.

explanation.whyCorrect: The built-in GitHub MCP server for Copilot cloud agent provides read-only tools by default and uses a token scoped to the source repository. That satisfies current-repository context without introducing broader credentials.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: An organization-wide PAT expands repository visibility beyond the stated need and increases credential blast radius.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A custom proxy adds operational complexity without improving the least-privilege posture for this use case.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Branch protection governs merges and some writes, but it does not reduce unnecessary read scope granted to the agent.

explanation.examStrategyNote: If the requirement fits the default scoped GitHub MCP behavior, do not add a broader PAT just because it feels more configurable.

questions.stem: A regulated payments team wants Copilot cloud agent to research a legacy billing module and propose a migration approach before any code changes occur. Developers must approve the approach because the module affects transaction reconciliation. Which workflow best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The team is using GitHub.com agent entry points and wants the approval step to be visible in normal development tooling.

options.text: Move the planning discussion to chat, then paste the final decision into the pull request afterward.
Ask Copilot to research and create a structured plan on a branch, then approve before requesting implementation.
Let Copilot open a pull request immediately, then ask reviewers to ignore the initial implementation commit.
Assign the full migration issue to Copilot and depend on branch protection to catch unsafe changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Branch protection is important, but it evaluates changes after execution rather than approving a plan first.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Opening an implementation PR immediately mixes planning and action, which weakens the required checkpoint.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: External chat may help collaboration, but it reduces traceability compared with GitHub-hosted plan artifacts.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For planning-boundary questions, prefer workflows that separate research and plan approval from implementation.

questions.stem: A repository administrator reviews a proposal to fix blocked dependency downloads for Copilot cloud agent. The proposal disables the firewall because one private package host is blocked. Which action best meets the runtime boundary requirement with the least additional risk?
questions.scenario: The agent only needs access to packages.internal.example.com in addition to GitHub and the recommended dependency hosts.

artifact.title: Proposed Copilot cloud agent network policy
artifact.content:
Internet access:
  firewall: disabled
  recommended_allowlist: enabled
Reason: npm install fails because packages.internal.example.com is blocked during Copilot setup.

options.text: Disable the recommended allowlist and let package managers retry until they find a reachable mirror.
Move package installation into setup steps because the firewall does not apply there.
Disable Copilot cloud agent for the repository until dependencies are made public.
Keep the firewall enabled and add packages.internal.example.com to the custom allowlist.

explanation.whyCorrect: The firewall limits internet access to reduce data exfiltration risk. Adding the specific required host to the allowlist preserves the boundary while enabling required dependency downloads.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Removing the recommended allowlist makes dependency installation less reliable and does not add the needed private host.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Setup-step processes are outside the firewall's coverage, so moving access there weakens the intended boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Disabling the agent is disproportionate when a scoped allowlist entry satisfies the requirement.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For firewall questions, prefer narrow allowlisting over disabling controls or moving work to a less-governed path.

questions.stem: An organization defines an Agents variable NPM_REGISTRY_URL for all repositories. One repository must use a different internal registry for Copilot cloud agent setup steps. What should the repository administrator do?
questions.scenario: The team wants the exception to apply only to this repository and not affect other services in the organization.

options.text: Store the URL as COPILOT_MCP_NPM_REGISTRY_URL so setup steps can read it.
Create a repository-level Agents variable with the same name and the repository-specific value.
Create an Actions repository variable with the same name and update the setup workflow.
Rename the organization variable so the repository can define a different unscoped name.

explanation.whyCorrect: Agents secrets and variables can be configured at organization and repository levels. When the same name exists at multiple levels, the lower-level repository value takes precedence for that repository.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot cloud agent receives Agents secrets and variables, not Actions variables, for its own environment.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Renaming the organization variable disrupts other repositories and is unnecessary because precedence handles the exception.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: COPILOT_MCP_ values are only available to MCP servers, not general setup-step environment usage.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Secret-scope questions often hinge on the dedicated Agents store and precedence. Do not switch to Actions secrets unless the scenario is Copilot CLI in Actions.

questions.stem: A team uses a planning-only custom agent to produce implementation plans for senior review. In three recent runs, the agent executed build scripts and edited source files before writing the plan. Which configuration change best tunes the agent to the intended evaluation workflow?
questions.scenario: The team wants the agent to inspect the codebase, search for patterns, and write a Markdown plan file, but not execute commands or modify application code.

artifact.title: .github/agents/implementation-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: implementation-planner
description: Creates implementation plans for review before coding
tools: ["read", "search", "bash", "edit"]
---

You are a planning specialist. Analyze the requested feature, inspect the repository, and create a Markdown implementation plan with risks, assumptions, constraints, phases, and dependencies.

Before finishing, validate that the proposed approach is feasible.

options.text: Keep all tools and require a reviewer to inspect the session log after each run.
Keep bash and add an instruction telling the agent to avoid source edits unless reviewers object.
Remove read and search so the agent cannot inspect files before creating the plan.
Remove bash, keep read/search/edit, and specify that edit is only for writing the plan document.

explanation.whyCorrect: The implementation planner pattern uses read, search, and edit to inspect the repository and create structured Markdown plans. Removing bash narrows tool access to the intended workflow, while constraining edit to the plan file addresses the observed failure.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A soft instruction leaves the unnecessary execution tool available and does not directly remove the misuse path.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Removing read and search prevents the agent from grounding the plan in repository evidence.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Reviewing logs after the fact helps diagnosis but does not tune the agent's tool access.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When tuning tool misuse, remove or constrain the tool that enabled the failure while preserving the minimum tools needed for the task.
