questions.stem: A documentation-maintenance team is creating a custom agent that should inspect Markdown, locate broken internal links, and propose documentation-only edits. The repository already has MCP servers configured for issue management and deployment status. Which tool configuration best fits the requirement?
questions.scenario: The agent must not run build commands, change application code, or call unrelated external tools during autonomous execution.

options.text: Omit the tools property so the agent can choose any available built-in and MCP tool.
Set tools to ["read", "search", "edit"] and instruct the agent to edit documentation files only.
Set tools to ["read", "search", "execute"] so it can verify links with shell scripts.
Set tools to ["*"] and rely on branch protection to catch inappropriate repository changes.

explanation.whyCorrect: The agent needs repository read/search plus edit capability, but not shell execution or unrelated MCP tools. Custom agent tool lists can explicitly enable only specific aliases, and omitted tools or ["*"] enables all available tools.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Omitting the tools property grants all available tools, including configured MCP tools that are not needed for documentation edits.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Shell execution adds unnecessary capability for a documentation-only task and increases the execution surface.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Branch protection is a review control, not a least-privilege tool configuration for autonomous execution.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 tool-scope questions, start from the smallest tool set that can complete the task, then reject options that defer prevention to review controls.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A team measures agent quality by requiring the full CI workflow to pass on every agent-created pull request. A recent pull request was merged after reviewers saw only the agent's local test summary, and a deployment regression occurred. What is the best diagnosis and remediation?
questions.scenario: The team reviews the pull request timeline and finds the following workflow output.

artifact.title: Pull request workflow output
artifact.content:
Pull request: copilot/fix-cache-invalidation
Author: Copilot
Timeline:
  - Copilot pushed commit 4f1a9c2
  - pull_request workflow: not started
  - reviewer comment: "Agent says unit tests passed locally"
  - pull request merged

Actions note:
  Workflows from this actor were not run automatically for this pull request.

options.text: Classify this as a reasoning error because the agent chose an incorrect cache invalidation strategy.
Replace local tests with Copilot code review comments as the primary merge signal.
Tune Copilot Memory so future summaries include more detail about locally executed tests.
Classify this as an evaluation gap and require CI workflow evidence before merge.

explanation.whyCorrect: The stated quality gate was full CI, but the workflow never ran and reviewers accepted a local-test summary. GitHub documents that Actions workflows do not run automatically by default when Copilot pushes changes to a pull request, so the remediation is to require CI evidence or explicitly manage workflow execution before merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The artifact does not show the agent's implementation reasoning; it shows a missing evaluation signal.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A more detailed local summary still would not satisfy the required CI workflow gate.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Copilot code review can provide feedback, but it is not a substitute for the required workflow validation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Do not confuse an agent's self-reported validation with an enforced GitHub check. Evaluation evidence should come from the required artifact or status check.

questions.stem: A platform team is building a dashboard for multi-agent incident repair sessions. The dashboard must reconstruct which sub-agent ran, whether it succeeded, and which execution span produced each result. Select TWO telemetry design choices the team should implement.
questions.scenario: Several instances of the same custom agent may run during one parent session, and reviewers need a post-hoc execution tree.

options.text: Suppress selected and deselected events because only final PR status affects review.
Group all events only by agent display name to simplify the dashboard model.
Treat a completed event as proof that the resulting code is safe to merge.
Stream sub-agent lifecycle events from the parent session into a durable review artifact.
Correlate started, completed, and failed events by toolCallId when building the execution tree.

explanation.whyCorrect: The lifecycle events include toolCallId on started, completed, and failed events, which lets the dashboard correlate spans. Persisting streamed events creates an artifact suitable for audit and post-hoc analysis.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Agent names are not unique execution spans, especially when the same agent runs more than once.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Selection and deselection events help explain delegation and context switches during the session.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Successful execution is an operational signal, not a substitute for code review and validation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Observability questions usually reward correlation IDs and durable artifacts, not summaries that collapse execution detail.

questions.stem: A financial services organization must prove which human initiated a Copilot cloud agent change, why the agent made the change, and whether agent activity occurred outside normal hours. Which accountability design best satisfies the requirement?
questions.scenario: The organization already requires pull request review, but auditors need evidence after merge for quarterly controls testing.

options.text: Create a bot that labels Copilot pull requests and exports the labels to a spreadsheet each month.
Use Copilot-authored signed commits, session-log links, and enterprise audit-log queries or streaming for agent activity.
Ask reviewers to add a signed comment confirming they read the diff and approve the agent behavior.
Require developers to paste a summary of every Copilot session into the pull request description before merge.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent commits identify Copilot as author, mark the human initiator as co-author, include session-log links, and appear signed. Enterprise audit logs can be queried for Copilot and agent activity and streamed for longer-term monitoring.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Manual summaries are useful context but are weaker evidence than system-generated commit, session, and audit records.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Labels help filtering but do not show who initiated work, why a change was made, or detailed activity history.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Reviewer comments document approval, but they do not replace agent session logs or enterprise audit events.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Accountability questions favor system-of-record evidence: signed commits, session logs, and audit logs. Manual notes are usually supplemental.

questions.stem: An enterprise platform team wants to introduce a custom database-migration agent but must prove it is safe before broad availability. In which order should the team run the pilot and release process?
questions.scenario: The agent will eventually be available organization-wide, but early tests must be limited to a small set of maintainers and repositories.

options.text: Create or prepare the .github-private repository with restricted visibility for the pilot.
Author the agent profile with scoped instructions, tools, and migration boundaries.
Test the agent on representative low-risk tasks and review session evidence.
Move the validated profile into the organization release location and document usage rules.

explanation.whyCorrect: A safe rollout prepares the controlled repository first, then authors the scoped agent profile, then validates behavior with representative tasks, and only then releases the profile for wider organization use with guidance.

whyDistractorsWrong.B-before-A: Authoring can happen locally, but controlled organization release requires the correct repository and visibility foundation.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-C: Publishing before representative testing expands risk before evidence exists.
whyDistractorsWrong.C-before-B: There is no meaningful pilot until the custom agent profile has scoped behavior to test.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Pilot sequencing items reward controlled exposure first and broad release last. Avoid options that publish before validation.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A platform review finds that several autonomous agent runs completed with confusing results: some errors were hidden, some tasks changed scope mid-run, and some outputs were hard to review. Match each observed behavior to the best architectural mitigation.
questions.scenario: The team wants to reduce operational risk without disabling agent workflows across the organization.

options.text: The agent catches tool failures and continues without reporting degraded output.
The agent keeps applying unrelated historical context from earlier work items.
The agent produces only narrative summaries instead of reviewable artifacts.
The agent attempts high-risk changes without a decision checkpoint.

matchChoices: Require structured outputs such as plans, PR descriptions, and test evidence
Add escalation paths that surface failures in logs, PR comments, or checks
Scope memory and context to the current task and prune stale information
Insert human approval before irreversible or compliance-sensitive actions
Increase token limits so the agent can retain more repository history
Move the work outside GitHub to reduce pull request noise

pairs.row1: Add escalation paths that surface failures in logs, PR comments, or checks
pairs.row2: Scope memory and context to the current task and prune stale information
pairs.row3: Require structured outputs such as plans, PR descriptions, and test evidence
pairs.row4: Insert human approval before irreversible or compliance-sensitive actions

explanation.whyCorrect: The mitigations map to the underlying failure modes: hidden failures need escalation, context leakage needs scope control, unreviewable prose needs structured artifacts, and risky autonomy needs approval checkpoints.
explanation.examStrategyNote: Matching questions often pair symptoms with controls. Identify whether the failure is about visibility, context, output structure, or autonomy.

questions.stem: A team notices that its multi-agent incident dashboard sometimes marks the wrong worker as failed when two instances of the same custom agent run during one parent session. What is the most important fix?
questions.scenario: The dashboard code below was written when only one instance of each agent ran per session.

artifact.title: event-handler.ts

options.text: Key run state by toolCallId and keep agentName as metadata for display.
Replace the event listener with polling of final pull request status only.
Ignore failed events until all agents emit completed or deselected events.
Store events by agentDisplayName because display names are intended for UI rendering.

explanation.whyCorrect: The same agent can have multiple execution spans, so toolCallId is the correct correlation key for started, completed, and failed events. agentName remains useful display metadata.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Final PR status loses the execution-tree detail needed to diagnose which worker failed.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Display names are not execution identifiers and can collide across repeated runs.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Ignoring failed events delays incident response and can overwrite the true failure state.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When telemetry includes an explicit correlation identifier, use it; human-readable names are usually labels, not keys.

questions.stem: A developer has used Copilot CLI for a long refactor involving planning, implementation, and repeated test fixes. After several hours, Copilot starts proposing changes that conflict with an earlier decision to keep the public API stable. Select THREE actions that best manage continuity and drift.
questions.scenario: The developer wants to preserve useful work, understand what context may have been summarized, and continue safely if the session is still recoverable.

options.text: Use `/context` to inspect context usage and determine whether compaction likely affected continuity.
Delete local session state so Copilot cannot reference any earlier incorrect direction.
Increase tool-call verbosity so later context contains every command and file-read result.
Re-anchor the session to the original requirement or restart from a reliable checkpoint.
Review the session checkpoints to see whether the API-stability decision survived compaction.
Continue accepting the proposed edits because automatic compaction preserves every prior detail.

explanation.whyCorrect: Checkpoints help review what was preserved during compaction, `/context` shows context usage, and re-anchoring or restarting from a reliable checkpoint corrects drift without discarding all valid work.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: More raw tool output consumes context and can worsen drift by retaining low-value details.
whyDistractorsWrong.F: Compaction summarizes important information but may lose fine-grained details, so review is warranted.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Deleting session state removes continuity and makes recovery harder than checkpoint-based correction.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For long-running execution questions, look for deliberate compaction awareness, checkpoint review, and re-anchoring to original requirements.

questions.stem: An organization owner wants to pilot a new security-remediation custom agent with only the platform team before releasing it to all repositories in the organization. Which repository and path strategy best supports this rollout?
questions.scenario: The organization has prepared a .github-private repository from the custom agents template. The platform team needs to test and then release the same profile broadly.

options.text: Place the agent in every target repository under .github/agents, then delete copies after testing.
Test under .github-private/.github/agents, then move the profile to .github-private/agents for release.
Create the agent in a public repository so all members can discover and test it easily.
Store the agent in .github-private root until testing ends, then move it to each repository.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents testing organization or enterprise custom agents in the .github/agents directory of .github-private, then releasing by moving the profile into the root agents directory for broad availability.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copying to every repository creates drift and is not the documented organization-level release pattern.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A public repository is inappropriate for an organization-scoped custom agent and may expose internal guidance.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: The root agents directory is the release location, not the private pilot location.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For organization custom-agent rollout, remember the distinction between test location and release location inside .github-private.

questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent pull request is ready after implementing a requested change to a service module. The repository requires an approving review and required checks before merge. In which order should the team complete the review workflow?
questions.scenario: The developer who initiated the agent task wants the change merged quickly but must preserve the independent review requirement.

options.text: Inspect the pull request diff, session log link, and generated test evidence.
Request agent revisions with a pull request comment if review issues remain.
Wait for required checks and an eligible independent approval to complete.
Merge the pull request only after required repository protections are satisfied.

explanation.whyCorrect: Review starts with the diff and trace evidence, then uses PR comments for any agent iteration, then relies on required checks and an eligible independent reviewer, and only then permits merge.

whyDistractorsWrong.B-before-A: Requesting revisions before inspecting the diff and session evidence risks vague or incorrect feedback.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-C: Merging before checks and independent approval violates the repository protection model.
whyDistractorsWrong.C-before-B: Waiting for final approval before asking for needed fixes can waste reviewer time and produce stale approvals.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For Copilot PR questions, remember that Copilot output is reviewed like any contribution, and the initiator's approval may not satisfy required approval rules.

questions.stem: A release team allows an agent to update deployment manifests, but production promotion must stay under human control. In which order should the team design the acceptance path?
questions.scenario: The repository uses GitHub Actions deployments and has a production environment with required reviewers.

options.text: Require CODEOWNERS review for deployment manifests and workflow-related files.
Let the deployment workflow request production environment approval after merge.
Have the agent create changes in a pull request branch rather than production.
Merge only after required checks and reviews satisfy branch protections.

explanation.whyCorrect: Agent work should enter through a PR branch, sensitive file ownership should be reviewed, branch protections should be satisfied before merge, and production deployment should wait for environment approval.

whyDistractorsWrong.B-before-D: Requesting production approval before merge bypasses the intended PR-based acceptance sequence.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-A: Branch protection should include the required owner review for sensitive deployment files.
whyDistractorsWrong.A-before-C: Owner review is triggered by a concrete pull request changing owned files.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Separate code acceptance from deployment approval. PR governance decides whether code can merge; environment protection decides whether deployment can proceed.

questions.stem: A team adds Copilot setup steps so the agent can install project dependencies before working. Copilot sessions still show the default environment and do not run the setup job. What is the best fix?
questions.scenario: The file has been merged to the default branch at the expected path. The team wants the smallest configuration change that makes Copilot pick up the setup steps.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  setup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

options.text: Move the workflow to .github/copilot-setup-steps.yml so it is outside normal Actions workflows.
Grant contents: write permission so Copilot can push dependency cache updates from setup.
Add pull_request to the workflow triggers so Copilot can validate the setup file during review.
Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps while keeping the file at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml.

explanation.whyCorrect: The setup workflow must be located at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml and contain a single job named copilot-setup-steps. The current job name setup prevents Copilot from using it.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: pull_request is useful for validation, but the missing required job name is the pickup blocker.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: The documented location is under .github/workflows, not directly under .github.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: The setup job should use least privilege; write permission is unnecessary for installing dependencies.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For setup-step artifacts, check the required file path and required job name before tuning triggers or permissions.

questions.stem: An agent connected to an internal issue-tracking MCP server is asked to link a pull request to the corresponding incident. The trace shows it called the issue search tool with the pull request number instead of the incident ID, then created a link to an unrelated incident. Select TWO actions that best address the root cause.
questions.scenario: The MCP server worked correctly when called manually with the incident ID, and the agent had read access to the pull request body where the incident ID appeared.

options.text: Classify the failure as tool misuse and refine instructions to extract the incident ID before linking.
Broaden MCP permissions so the agent can inspect all incidents before choosing a link.
Classify the failure as an environment outage because the created link was incorrect.
Disable the MCP server for all agents until the issue-tracking vendor changes the API.
Add a verification step that reads the incident title before committing the pull request link.

explanation.whyCorrect: The tool call used the wrong parameter even though the needed incident ID was available, so the root cause is tool misuse. Refining instructions and adding a verification step tune tool use without expanding permissions.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: The MCP server behaved correctly with valid input, so disabling it globally is disproportionate.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: An incorrect output is not evidence of an environment outage when the trace shows wrong parameters.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Broader access increases risk and does not fix the parameter-selection failure.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For tool failures, distinguish bad tool behavior from bad tool invocation. The fix is usually parameter guidance, verification, or least-privilege tool refinement.

questions.stem: A platform group is deciding how to redesign incident rollback automation. The decision affects reliability, cost, and compliance, and the team wants multiple independent proposals before choosing. Which orchestration pattern best fits this decision?
questions.scenario: The agents should not edit code yet. The desired output is a set of competing designs with trade-offs for a human architecture review board.

options.text: Use a pipeline where each agent rewrites the previous proposal into its preferred style.
Use debate or consensus so agents independently propose designs for human selection.
Use parallel fan-out where agents implement separate modules before the design is approved.
Use a single implementation agent with broad tools to converge quickly on one design.

explanation.whyCorrect: Debate or consensus fits situations where multiple agents independently produce alternatives and a human or orchestrator selects the best option based on trade-offs.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: A pipeline would make each proposal depend on the previous one, reducing independence.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Implementation before design approval creates unnecessary change risk for a governance decision.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A single broad agent does not provide the independent viewpoints requested by the review board.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When the stem asks for competing viewpoints before action, choose debate or consensus rather than execution-oriented patterns.

questions.stem: A team adds the following setup workflow so Copilot cloud agent can install dependencies before editing a service. The agent still starts without dependencies installed. Select TWO changes that best align the workflow with Copilot setup-step requirements and least privilege.
questions.scenario: The workflow file is intended to run before Copilot starts work and is stored at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
jobs:
  setup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4

          node-version: "22"

options.text: Rename the job from setup to copilot-setup-steps so Copilot can pick it up.
Add a second job named validate-dependencies that runs after the setup job completes.
Move dependency installation into a separate deployment workflow triggered after pull_request.
Add issues: write permission so Copilot can report dependency installation failures.
Change contents: write to contents: read because checkout only needs read access.

explanation.whyCorrect: The setup workflow must contain a single job named copilot-setup-steps to be used by Copilot cloud agent. Since the setup steps only check out code and install dependencies, contents: read is the least-privilege permission.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Additional jobs do not satisfy the required Copilot setup job name and may be ignored for this purpose.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: A separate deployment workflow runs at the wrong point in the lifecycle and does not configure the agent environment before work starts.

questions.stem: A monorepo team asks Copilot cloud agent to update an API client in Repository A and simultaneously patch the matching service implementation in Repository B. The agent creates changes only in Repository A. What should the architect recommend?
questions.scenario: Both repositories are hosted on GitHub. The organization wants traceability and does not want an agent run to make uncontrolled cross-repository changes.

options.text: Use a broader custom agent prompt that names both repositories and asks Copilot to infer coordination.
Grant the agent organization-owner permissions so it can push branches across both repositories.
Split the work into coordinated repository-scoped tasks with separate branches, PRs, checks, and reviews.
Disable branch protection temporarily so the two repository changes can be merged as one operation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent can make changes only in the repository specified when the task starts and can work on one branch at a time. Coordinated repository-scoped tasks preserve traceability and review controls.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Over-permissioning does not change the documented single-repository task boundary and increases risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Prompting cannot safely override repository execution boundaries.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Disabling protection weakens governance and does not solve cross-repository traceability.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For scope-limit questions, do not choose answers that bypass governance; decompose work into bounded, auditable tasks.

questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent pull request includes a warning that a command attempted to reach downloads.vendor.example and was blocked. The dependency is legitimate and required by tests, but the security team wants to preserve exfiltration controls. What should the repository administrator do?

options.text: Move the dependency download into an MCP server because the firewall blocks Bash commands.
Store the vendor URL as an Agents secret so the firewall treats it as trusted.
Disable the firewall for the repository until the dependency installation process is stable.
Add the specific vendor host to the custom allowlist and keep the firewall enabled.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: MCP servers are not the right workaround for dependency downloads and are not covered by the same firewall limitation.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Secrets and variables provide environment values; they do not automatically grant network access through the firewall.

questions.stem: A service team is responding to a checkout incident. One agent must inspect logs and historical PRs, another must make a minimal code fix, and a third must validate tests after the fix. Which orchestration approach best fits the situation?

Ask each agent to produce a full independent fix and let CI determine the final choice.
Use a single broad agent with all tools so it can switch tasks without handoff overhead.
Run all three agents against the same branch and merge whichever output finishes first.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: A platform team is preparing an organization-level custom agent for high-risk database migration work. The security review requires the agent to produce an inspectable design artifact before any repository edits occur, and a human must approve that plan before implementation begins. Which revision best satisfies the requirement while preserving delivery velocity?
questions.scenario: The organization stores shared custom agents in a private `.github-private` repository. The draft agent profile is intended to be released as `agents/migration-planner.agent.md`.

artifact.title: agents/migration-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: migration-planner
description: Designs database migration work and opens implementation pull requests
tools: ["read", "search", "edit", "runCommands"]
target: github-copilot
---

When assigned an issue:
1. Inspect the schema and application code.
2. Decide the migration approach.
3. Apply required edits, run tests, create a pull request, and mark it ready for review.
4. If CI passes, summarize the outcome and ask for merge.

options.text: Split this into a planning-only custom agent with read/search tools, structured plan output, and a human approval gate before invoking an implementation agent.
Move it to each repository’s .github/agents folder and rely on repository visibility to limit use.
Keep one agent, but add CODEOWNERS and required checks so unsafe edits are blocked during pull request review.
Allow edit tools, but instruct the agent to self-review and request human review only when tests fail.

explanation.whyCorrect: The requirement is to separate planning from execution, produce a structured and reviewable plan, and prevent action until a human approves. A planning-only agent with read/search tools limits autonomy at the design stage, creates an inspectable artifact, and still preserves velocity by allowing an implementation agent after approval.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: CODEOWNERS and checks help govern pull requests, but they act after edits occur. They do not enforce the required plan-before-action boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Self-review and test-gated review leave execution in the agent’s hands before approval. This keeps the risky edit capability inside the planning phase.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Repository-level placement can narrow availability, but it does not solve the core issue: the agent still mixes planning, editing, and execution.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 architecture questions, identify where the risk occurs in the lifecycle. If the requirement says approval before action, choose the design that removes action tools from the planning phase rather than relying only on downstream PR controls.

questions.stem: A compliance reviewer asks how the team will prove which agent introduced a risky dependency during a multi-agent remediation effort. What evidence design best supports the investigation?

options.text: Store a screenshot of the agents dashboard at the end of each workday.
Require session logs, commit links to those logs, and PR handoff notes for each agent.
Rely on the final merged diff because intermediate agent decisions are rarely needed.
Ask agents to summarize their own quality in a final comment after merging.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: The final diff does not explain which agent made a decision or why it used a tool.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A post-merge self-summary is weaker than source evidence collected during execution.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Screenshots are incomplete, hard to correlate to commits, and poor substitutes for logs.

artifact.title: Repository MCP configuration

options.text: Replace resources and prompts with a tools allowlist such as ["search_experiments"].
Add a prompt that instructs Copilot to call compare-runs before changing files.
Move resources and prompts under headers so they are sent with each request.
Convert the resources array to a string so Copilot can load the latest experiments resource.

questions.stem: A release engineering team wants Copilot cloud agent to update deployment manifests and trigger a staging deployment for review apps. The deployment can modify shared test data but cannot affect production customers. What autonomy level and guardrail best balances velocity and control?
questions.scenario: The repository already requires CI checks before merge, and the team wants to avoid approvals for simple code edits that do not deploy anything.

options.text: Let Copilot deploy to staging automatically, then rely on audit logs to identify problematic changes later.
Disable Copilot cloud agent for the repository whenever deployment manifests are part of the requested change.
Require a security manager approval before Copilot can create any commits or open a draft pull request.
Allow code changes autonomously, but require a protected staging environment approval before the deployment job proceeds.

explanation.whyCorrect: Staging deployment is a higher-risk action than editing code, so the efficient guardrail is to keep artifact creation autonomous while placing the human checkpoint at the protected environment boundary.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Approving every commit or draft PR slows low- and medium-risk work that can be controlled by reviews and required checks.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Monitoring after deployment is weaker than a pre-deployment approval for an action that can affect shared data.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Disabling the agent removes useful delivery velocity instead of scoping the human checkpoint to the risky action.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 guardrail questions, place approvals at the risk boundary. Code generation usually needs artifact review; deployments need environment protection.

questions.stem: A repository needs Copilot cloud agent to install private build tools before editing code. The security team requires least privilege and does not want the agent to access deployment credentials. Select TWO configuration decisions that satisfy the requirement.
questions.scenario: The current proposal grants broad GITHUB_TOKEN permissions in copilot-setup-steps.yml and reuses GitHub Actions secrets used by release workflows.

options.text: Provide only required build credentials through Copilot agent secrets or variables, separate from release credentials.
Grant actions: write and contents: write so Copilot can repair failed setup workflows during the same run.
Move deployment secrets into repository-level Actions secrets so Copilot can read them when setup needs authentication.
Use a long-lived personal access token with organization-wide write access to avoid repeated permission changes.
Disable the setup workflow on pull_request events to prevent validation from exposing dependency installation failures.
Set only the minimum GITHUB_TOKEN permissions needed by setup steps, such as contents: read for checkout.

explanation.whyCorrect: The setup workflow should use the lowest token permissions required for setup, and secrets needed by the agent should be provided through the Copilot agent secrets or variables mechanism rather than reusing unrelated release credentials.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Broad write permissions increase blast radius and are not needed for dependency installation or checkout.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot cloud agent does not access GitHub Actions secrets during runtime or environment setup steps, and deployment credentials should remain outside the agent boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Disabling validation hides setup failures and does not improve least-privilege design.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: An organization-wide write token is over-scoped for installing build tools and increases credential risk.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In multi-select least-privilege questions, choose both sides of the boundary: minimal token permissions and the correct secret mechanism.

questions.stem: A dependency-update agent creates a branch, edits four files, and then encounters repeated 429 responses from a package registry during validation. The team requires safe execution paths and auditable recovery. Select TWO actions the workflow should take.
questions.scenario: The issue is likely transient, but the agent has already made partial changes that should not be silently abandoned.

options.text: Retry the registry calls with bounded exponential backoff and record each attempt.
Merge the branch after unit tests pass locally and rerun registry validation later.
Increase the agent's package-registry permissions so rate limiting is less likely.
Escalate with a comment and roll back or preserve the branch as a draft for inspection.
Continue with the pull request and let maintainers discover validation gaps during review.

explanation.whyCorrect: Transient failures should be retried with bounded backoff and logged. If retries fail or confidence is low, the agent should surface the failure to humans and either roll back partial work or preserve it in an inspectable draft state.

whyDistractorsWrong.E: Proceeding without surfacing the validation failure hides an important tool error from reviewers.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Permission expansion does not address a transient 429 safely and may violate least privilege.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Passing local tests does not substitute for the failed registry validation required by the workflow.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For safe-execution questions, combine bounded automation with human-visible escalation; avoid options that hide partial failures or expand permissions reactively.

questions.stem: A product team wants Copilot cloud agent to handle small accessibility fixes across a React repository. The first pilot issue says only: "Improve accessibility on the settings page." The agent produced a broad refactor that passed tests but changed unrelated navigation behavior. What should the team do before assigning similar issues to the agent?
questions.scenario: The team wants to keep the agent in the SDLC, but reviewers need predictable scope and reviewable outputs.

options.text: Assign only senior developers as reviewers and keep the issue format unchanged for velocity.
Rewrite issues with explicit inputs, affected paths, expected diff artifacts, tests to run, and acceptance criteria.
Require the agent to create fewer commits, so reviewers can inspect a smaller commit history.
Increase the agent model capability and allow it to infer missing acceptance criteria from repository history.

explanation.whyCorrect: The scenario shows an underspecified task. Domain A expects agent tasks to define inputs, outputs, and success criteria so the agent can produce bounded, inspectable work inside normal GitHub review workflows.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: A stronger model does not replace explicit task boundaries; it can still infer scope incorrectly.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Reviewer expertise helps catch problems, but it does not prevent the agent from starting with vague goals.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Commit count affects review ergonomics, not whether the task is scoped to the right work.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a GH-600 question describes an agent doing too much, look for the answer that improves task definition before execution.

artifact.title: .github/CODEOWNERS

.github/workflows/* @octo-org/devops
.github/dependabot.yml @octo-org/security
mcp.json @octo-org/platform

Keep the file unchanged because .github/workflows/* already covers every Copilot and MCP configuration path.

questions.stem: A platform team is creating a repository-level custom agent for documentation-only changes. A reviewer notices the agent can edit source files and run shell commands even though its prompt asks it not to. Which change best aligns the configuration with the intended boundary?
questions.scenario: The team wants the custom agent to inspect repository files and update Markdown documentation, but not execute commands or invoke every configured MCP tool.

artifact.title: .github/agents/docs-maintainer.agent.md

name: docs-maintainer
description: Updates README files, ADRs, and Markdown guides for the service
---
You are a documentation specialist. Update only Markdown documentation.
Do not modify application code, workflow files, or package manifests.

options.text: Set user-invocable to false and rely on automatic routing to select the agent only for docs tasks.
Move the agent into the organization .github-private repository so fewer repository users edit it.
Add a tools list limited to read, search, and edit, and keep the prompt scoped to Markdown.
Add more prompt text explaining that application files are confidential and should be avoided.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Prompt guidance helps behavior, but it does not reduce available tools.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Changing storage location can affect availability, but it does not narrow tool access.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Invocation settings affect selection, not what the agent can do after it runs.

questions.stem: A repository owner finds that Copilot cloud agent repeatedly proposes changes using a legacy database helper that was removed during a migration. The session log shows Copilot citing a stored repository fact about that helper, and reviewers confirm the fact is no longer accurate. What should the owner do first to tune future agent behavior?
questions.scenario: The team wants to reduce repeated rework without disabling Copilot for the repository.

options.text: Ask developers to mention the new database helper in every future Copilot prompt.
Disable all custom instructions until Copilot relearns the codebase from new pull requests.
Add a branch protection rule requiring two approvals for any database-related pull request.
Review Copilot Memory for the repository and delete the misleading stored fact.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository owners can view and delete stored Copilot Memory entries that are inappropriate, misleading, or incorrect. Removing the stale fact tunes the context source causing repeated wrong proposals.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Custom instructions are not identified as the faulty context source, so disabling them is overbroad.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Additional approvals may catch the issue but do not remove the stale context causing repeated failures.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Repeating corrective context in every prompt increases manual burden instead of fixing the repository-level memory issue.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When repeated errors trace to stored context, tune the memory source rather than adding review friction or relying on every prompt to compensate.

questions.stem: A team adds a cleanup sub-agent to an SDK-based orchestrator used during incident response. Reviewers worry that routine incident prompts could accidentally invoke the cleanup agent and delete useful diagnostic files. Which change best addresses the risk?

artifact.title: orchestrator.ts

options.text: Set infer to false and replace tools null with an explicit minimal tool list.
Keep tools null and add stronger natural-language warnings in the cleanup prompt.
Remove the description so the runtime has less information for intent matching.
Preselect the cleanup agent at session creation so invocation is predictable.

explanation.whyCorrect: In the SDK, infer false prevents automatic selection, and an explicit tools array avoids inheriting all session tools when tools is null or omitted.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Prompt warnings do not remove automatic selection or broad inherited tool access.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A missing description can reduce routing quality without enforcing explicit invocation or tool scope.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Preselecting the cleanup agent makes it active at session start, increasing the accidental-use risk.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a sub-agent is sensitive, prefer configuration controls such as explicit invocation and scoped tools over prompt-only safeguards.

questions.stem: An organization owner is preparing organization-level custom agents so multiple repositories can use a standardized refactoring agent. In which order should the owner set up and release the agent repository?

options.text: Choose internal or private visibility based on who should read and use agents.
Create the custom agent repository from GitHub's template under the organization.
Name the repository .github-private and add organization-specific authoring guidance.
Place the tested organization agent profile in the root agents directory for release.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub directs organization owners to create the custom agents repository from the template, name it .github-private, choose internal or private visibility, and use the organization-level agents directory for agent profiles.

whyDistractorsWrong.A-before-B: Visibility is selected as part of creating the repository, after choosing the organization and repository purpose.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-B: An organization-level agent profile cannot be released until the .github-private repository exists.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-A: Releasing an agent before setting repository visibility can expose it to the wrong audience.

Keep required checks and human review before merge, especially for changes under .github/workflows.
Ask Copilot to approve and run the workflows after it explains the workflow file changes.
Disable workflow approval for Copilot pull requests so required checks start immediately.
Merge the pull request with pending checks because Copilot commits are signed and verified.

explanation.whyCorrect: By default, Actions workflows do not run automatically when Copilot pushes changes. A write-access user should inspect the changes, especially workflow changes, and explicitly approve running workflows; required checks and review remain merge gates.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Automatic workflow execution may be configurable, but it weakens the checkpoint described in the scenario.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Signed commits improve traceability; they do not replace required checks or review.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot cannot supply the human authorization needed for privileged workflow execution.

questions.stem: A release-engineering agent in repo apps/api needs read-only GitHub context from repos apps/web and platform/contracts to prepare compatibility notes. The default GitHub MCP access only covers the source repository. Select THREE actions that meet the requirement with the narrowest practical access.
questions.scenario: The agent must not create issues, update files, or access unrelated repositories through the GitHub MCP server.

options.text: Remove all tool restrictions and rely on the prompt to request read-only behavior.
Create a fine-grained PAT limited to read access on apps/web and platform/contracts.
Set github/* in the custom agent tools list to simplify GitHub MCP selection.
Store the PAT as an Agents secret named COPILOT_MCP_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN.
Use GitHub MCP toolsets and tool filtering to expose only required read operations.
Use an organization classic PAT with repo scope so future agents can reuse it.

explanation.whyCorrect: For context outside the current repository, GitHub documents using an appropriately scoped PAT, preferably fine-grained. The credential must be stored as a COPILOT_MCP_ Agents secret, and toolsets plus tool filtering should constrain which GitHub MCP operations are available.

whyDistractorsWrong.F: A classic PAT with broad repo scope grants more repository access than the two named repositories require.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: github/* enables all available GitHub MCP tools rather than limiting to required read operations.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Prompt instructions do not enforce permission boundaries for autonomously callable MCP tools.

questions.stem: A repository administrator adds the following MCP configuration for Copilot cloud agent to read deployment incidents. The configuration fails validation and would be over-permissive even if it loaded. Which remediation best addresses both issues?
questions.scenario: The remote service supports static bearer-token authentication and exposes separate read and write tools.

artifact.title: Repository MCP configuration

options.text: Change the server type to local, keep OAuth, and run the server through npx.
Remove OAuth, reference $COPILOT_MCP_INCIDENTS_TOKEN, and list only required read tools.
Move the token into a repository Actions secret and reference it as $INCIDENTS_TOKEN.
Keep tools as ["*"], remove the header, and rely on the server's default anonymous read access.

explanation.whyCorrect: Remote MCP configuration supports url and optional headers, but Copilot cloud agent does not support remote OAuth flows. Secret references for MCP must use Agents secrets or variables prefixed with COPILOT_MCP_, and the tools list should allowlist only required read tools.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Anonymous access does not solve least privilege or authentication and keeps every exposed MCP tool enabled.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Actions secrets are not passed to Copilot cloud agent MCP configuration, and the name lacks the required prefix.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Changing to a local server adds unnecessary runtime complexity and keeps the unsupported OAuth configuration.

questions.stem: A security team reviews the following custom agent profile before enabling it for dependency advisory triage. The agent should read advisories and repository files, then create a Markdown plan without running commands or changing application code. What is the best change?
questions.scenario: The repository has a vulnerability-intelligence MCP server configured with both read and mutation tools.

artifact.title: .github/agents/advisory-planner.md
artifact.content:
---
name: advisory-planner
description: Reviews dependency advisories and drafts remediation plans
mcp-servers:
  vuln-intel:
    type: http
    url: https://vuln-intel.contoso.example/mcp
    tools: ["*"]
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer $COPILOT_MCP_VULN_INTEL_TOKEN
---

Create a remediation plan in docs/security/remediation-plan.md.

options.text: Keep the profile unchanged because the instructions restrict the agent to Markdown output.
Add execute so the agent can verify package-manager behavior before drafting the plan.
Remove the MCP server and ask developers to paste advisory data into the issue.
Set tools to ["read", "search", "edit", "vuln-intel/advisory-read"] and restrict MCP tools.

explanation.whyCorrect: The profile currently omits the top-level tools property, which enables all available tools, and the MCP server enables every server tool. Explicitly listing read, search, edit, and the one required MCP read tool matches the task while avoiding command execution and mutation tools.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Natural-language instructions do not remove tool capabilities that the agent is configured to use.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Shell execution is not required for drafting a remediation plan and expands the allowed action surface.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Removing MCP access reduces useful context and shifts manual work to developers instead of scoping the tool correctly.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In GH-600 config artifacts, instructions and tool permissions are separate controls; do not treat prompt wording as a substitute for tool scoping.

questions.stem: A team automates release-note generation after incidents. A triage agent must first identify merged incident PRs, a summarizer must convert them into user-facing notes, and a reviewer agent must check tone and policy wording. Which orchestration pattern should the team choose?
questions.scenario: Each step depends on the previous step's output, and running later agents before earlier outputs are complete causes inaccurate notes.

options.text: Use parallel fan-out so each agent produces release notes independently from the repository.
Use orchestrator-worker so the parent agent assigns every step at the same time.
Use a pipeline so each agent transforms the prior agent's output in sequence.
Use debate consensus so all agents argue for the most complete final summary.

explanation.whyCorrect: A pipeline fits sequential transformations where agent N's output becomes agent N+1's input, such as triage to summary to policy review.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Parallel fan-out is better for independent subtasks, not ordered dependent transformations.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Debate consensus is useful for comparing alternatives, not enforcing a fixed processing chain.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Concurrent delegation risks later agents working before required intermediate artifacts exist.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When the stem emphasizes ordered dependencies, choose pipeline rather than fan-out or debate.

questions.stem: Two Copilot cloud agent sessions are repairing the same incident from different issues. One PR changes authentication middleware to fail closed, while another PR changes a caller to retry unauthenticated requests. Both PRs pass their local tests. What should the incident orchestrator do next?
questions.scenario: The incident commander needs a defensible decision trail and cannot merge changes that encode contradictory security behavior.

options.text: Close both PRs and restart the entire incident fix as one new agent session.
Pause merging, request human review of both designs, choose one, and document the rejection.
Merge the PR with the larger test suite because passing tests indicate the safer behavior.
Ask both agents to rebase repeatedly until GitHub reports no merge conflicts.

explanation.whyCorrect: Contradictory outputs are not just textual conflicts; they require human judgment, an explicit choice, and an auditable rationale before work continues.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: More tests do not resolve conflicting security intent or prove the architecture is correct.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A clean rebase can hide semantic disagreement while leaving incompatible behavior in the system.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Restarting discards useful work and evidence that can support a human-in-the-loop decision.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Semantic conflicts require judgment. Do not confuse passing CI or clean merges with resolved design disagreement.

questions.stem: An SDK-based orchestrator should not run shell commands itself, but it must delegate test execution to a specialized sub-agent. Which change best implements that boundary without blocking the test sub-agent?
questions.scenario: The current configuration uses a session-wide exclusion and the test-runner agent cannot execute npm test.

artifact.title: Copilot SDK session configuration

options.text: Remove execute from availableTools and let test-runner request it during execution.
Keep excludedTools unchanged and add execute twice in the test-runner tools array.
Move execute restriction to defaultAgent.excludedTools and keep execute session-available.
Give the main agent execute access and depend on prompt instructions not to use it.

explanation.whyCorrect: In Copilot SDK, session-level availableTools and excludedTools apply globally before default-agent restrictions. defaultAgent.excludedTools can hide a tool from the main agent while leaving it available to sub-agents when the tool remains session-available.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Removing execute from availableTools prevents every agent from using it, including the test-runner sub-agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A session-level excluded tool remains unavailable regardless of how often the sub-agent lists it.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Granting execute to the main agent violates the intended separation between orchestration and execution.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For SDK filtering questions, determine whether a filter is global or main-agent-only; global exclusions override sub-agent tool lists.

questions.stem: A product infrastructure group asks Copilot cloud agent to modernize deprecated logging calls across several services. The goal is to reduce human cleanup while avoiding behavior changes. Which success criteria set is most appropriate?
questions.scenario: The work is repetitive but touches production services, so the team wants evaluation signals that detect both correctness and unnecessary churn.

options.text: A successful merge, positive pull request emoji reactions, and no comments after the first hour.
Maximum number of replaced logging calls, shortest session duration, and the fewest prompt tokens used.
No behavior-test regressions, limited diff scope, fewer reviewer cleanup comments, and unchanged public API snapshots.
A larger refactor that removes logging wrappers, updates dependencies, and rewrites service initialization.

explanation.whyCorrect: The stated intent is modernization without behavior changes and with less cleanup. The best criteria combine quantitative regression and API checks with qualitative reviewer feedback and diff-scope control.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Replacement count and speed can reward broad churn rather than safe, behavior-preserving modernization.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Merge status and reactions are weak proxies and do not verify behavior or scope control.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Expanding the task into a larger refactor conflicts with the intent to avoid behavior changes.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Align evaluation criteria with intent: for safe repetitive changes, look for low churn, passing tests, stable interfaces, and reduced review rework.

questions.stem: A maintainer notices that an issue assigned to Copilot cloud agent contains a visible bug report and an HTML comment with instructions to exfiltrate repository files. A contractor without write access added the comment after the issue was created. What should the maintainer rely on first?
questions.scenario: The team wants to keep using Copilot for normal issue work, but it must prevent untrusted prompt content from steering the agent.

options.text: Move the repository to self-hosted runners so the hidden comment cannot reach the agent environment.
Run the agent and inspect the final diff because PR review is enough to catch prompt injection effects.
Use Copilot's trigger restrictions and hidden-character filtering, then review the session log and PR normally.
Add a repository secret containing a trusted system prompt that overrides user comments during execution.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent limits who can trigger it, does not present comments from users without write access, and filters hidden content such as HTML comments before passing input to the agent. Normal review and session-log inspection remain part of accountability.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: Reviewing only the final diff is reactive and ignores built-in input filtering and trigger restrictions.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Changing runner infrastructure does not address malicious prompt text in GitHub issues or comments.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A secret-based prompt override is not the documented control and risks exposing policy content in the wrong mechanism.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Prompt-injection items often test whether you know the built-in input boundary. Do not replace it with unrelated runner or secret patterns.

questions.stem: A DevOps team wants a nightly GitHub Actions workflow to ask Copilot to summarize the day's repository changes into the workflow summary. The job should be noninteractive and limited to reading git history and writing a local summary file. Which implementation is best?
questions.scenario: The team is using GitHub Copilot CLI in CI, not Copilot cloud agent assigned from an issue.

options.text: Use GITHUB_TOKEN as the Copilot credential and omit tool flags for faster setup.
Run copilot -p with COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN, --allow-tool for git and write, and --no-ask-user.
Run Copilot CLI with --allow-all so it can decide which tools the summary needs.
Assign the default branch to Copilot each night and let it open a summary pull request.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents running Copilot CLI programmatically in Actions with copilot -p, COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN, explicit --allow-tool permissions, and --no-ask-user for noninteractive workflows. Allowing git and write matches the stated task.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: This changes the workflow into a cloud-agent branch and PR task instead of a CI summary job.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: --allow-all grants broader tool access than the summary task requires and is discouraged outside sandbox scenarios.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot CLI authentication uses its documented credential variable, and omitting tool flags weakens permission control.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When the scenario says Copilot CLI in Actions, answer with programmatic CLI patterns and scoped flags; do not substitute cloud-agent issue assignment.

questions.stem: A backend team repeatedly asks Copilot cloud agent and Copilot code review to follow the same repository-specific rule: every new repository class must use the existing UnitOfWork wrapper and the `make test-integration` command. The rule is documented in code patterns but not in a single policy file. What should the team use to reduce repeated prompting while keeping the information scoped to this repository?
questions.scenario: The team wants later cloud-agent sessions and code reviews in the same repository to benefit from the learned rule without exposing it to unrelated repositories.

options.text: Use Copilot Memory repository-level facts, supported by citations to current code in the repository.
Keep the rule only in the active chat context for each cloud-agent assignment.
Store the rule as a user-level preference so code review can apply it for every reviewer.
Add the rule to an external vector store shared across all repositories in the organization.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository-level Copilot Memory is designed for coding conventions, architectural decisions, build commands, and project-specific rules. It is scoped to the same repository and can be used by cloud agent and code review when validated.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: User-level preferences are personal and code review applies repository-level facts, not user-level preferences.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A broad external store increases governance burden and risks cross-repository leakage for a repository-specific rule.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Short-term chat context disappears after the session and would force the team to repeat the rule.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 memory questions, choose the smallest durable scope that matches the reuse need: session, repository/user memory, or external storage.

questions.stem: A repository requires one approving review before merge. A developer assigns a bug issue to Copilot cloud agent, reviews the resulting pull request, and approves it. The pull request remains blocked. What is the correct governance interpretation?
questions.scenario: The developer who assigned the issue has write access and believes their approval should count because they understand the bug best.

options.text: The pull request is blocked because Copilot must mark it Ready for review before approvals count.
The initiator can review, but their approval does not count; another reviewer must approve before merge.
The approval is blocked because Copilot-created branches require two reviews regardless of branch rules.
The approval is ignored because Copilot pull requests can only be approved by repository administrators.

explanation.whyCorrect: When a user asks Copilot to create a pull request and branch protection requires approvals, the initiating user's approval does not count toward the required approvals. Someone else must approve.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot does not create a universal two-review requirement; repository rules define the required count.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot cannot mark its own pull requests Ready for review, but that is not why the initiator approval is excluded.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A separate eligible reviewer is required; the reviewer does not have to be an administrator.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For Copilot PR governance, distinguish who can comment or review from whose approval counts toward protected-branch requirements.

questions.stem: A multi-agent workflow is repairing a flaky deployment. The validator agent stopped producing progress after running tests, while the fixer agent already pushed commits to its PR branch. Select TWO recovery actions that preserve useful work and support auditability.
questions.scenario: The incident policy requires reviewers to understand what happened before any rerun or rollback.

options.text: Restart or steer validation from the last known checkpoint rather than discarding fixer commits.
Disable session logging temporarily to reduce overhead during the recovery attempt.
Inspect the stalled session log to determine the last completed tool call and validation state.
Merge the fixer PR immediately because the validator is the only stalled component.
Delete the validator PR branch so the next run starts from a clean repository state.

explanation.whyCorrect: Session logs reveal the agent's approach, tool usage, and progress. Restarting or steering from a checkpoint preserves valid commits while addressing the stalled validation path.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Merging without completed validation bypasses the quality gate that the stalled agent was meant to provide.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Deleting the branch removes potentially useful state and weakens the recovery trail.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Disabling logging undermines the auditability required by the incident policy.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For failure recovery, preserve evidence first, then resume from the smallest reliable checkpoint.

questions.stem: A team is designing an autonomous agent workflow for dependency upgrades. The agent should keep delivery fast while reducing unbounded autonomy and silent failures. Select TWO controls the team should implement.
questions.scenario: The repository has required status checks and CODEOWNERS for package manifests. The team wants agent activity to be inspectable without adding manual approval to every low-risk command.

options.text: Disable CI on Copilot branches to avoid blocking the agent during iterative dependency fixes.
Use required checks and CODEOWNERS review on package manifests before any upgrade merges.
Move dependency-update decisions to an external ticket queue and sync results weekly.
Let the agent merge patch-level dependency updates when local tests pass in its environment.
Require the agent to publish a plan and test summary as PR artifacts before human review.

explanation.whyCorrect: Publishing a plan and test summary creates inspectable artifacts, while required checks and CODEOWNERS review enforce human and automated gates at merge time.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Agent self-merge is excessive autonomy for dependency changes and bypasses PR governance.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Disabling CI removes an evaluation signal and increases the chance of silent failure.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: An external queue can track work, but it reduces GitHub as the primary control plane for review.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For autonomy questions, the best answers usually add targeted checkpoints and artifacts rather than approving every action or bypassing controls.

questions.stem: A team wants Copilot cloud agent to resume an interrupted database-migration task without repeating discovery. A developer proposes writing progress checkpoints from setup steps to `/tmp/agent-state.json`. Which change best aligns the artifact with durable state requirements?
questions.scenario: The checkpoint must survive runner replacement and be visible to maintainers reviewing the agent's work.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
jobs:
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Record previous migration phase
        run: |
          echo '{"phase":"schema discovery","status":"complete"}' > /tmp/agent-state.json

options.text: Keep `/tmp/agent-state.json` and add longer setup-step timeouts for interrupted agent sessions.
Persist the checkpoint in a PR comment, issue comment, or committed branch state file.
Move the checkpoint into a shell variable exported during setup-step execution.
Store the checkpoint in Copilot Memory so it becomes permanent task execution state.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent works in an ephemeral GitHub Actions-powered development environment. Durable task state should be captured in reviewable GitHub artifacts such as PR comments, issue comments, or committed state files.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: A longer timeout does not make `/tmp` state durable across runner replacement.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: An environment variable is less durable than `/tmp` and is not reviewable after interruption.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Copilot Memory stores reusable facts and preferences, not per-run checkpoint state for task execution.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Differentiate environment setup from durable workflow state; setup steps prepare execution, while checkpoints must live in GitHub-visible artifacts.

questions.stem: A monorepo team wants an agent workflow that can be resumed after failures without repeating earlier analysis. In which order should the team design durable handoffs between planning, implementation, and evaluation?
questions.scenario: The team has seen long-running agent sessions lose focus after dependency installation failures and repeated test retries.

options.text: Start implementation from the approved artifact and write changes to a pull request branch.
Capture task inputs, constraints, and success criteria in the issue or prompt.
Persist the plan, assumptions, and selected files as a reviewable GitHub artifact.
Record test results and unresolved failures in PR comments or check outputs.

explanation.whyCorrect: Reliable handoffs begin with a clear task contract, then persist the plan and assumptions, then implement from the approved artifact, and finally record evaluation evidence for continuation or review.

whyDistractorsWrong.A-before-C: Implementing before the plan artifact is persisted makes recovery and review harder after failures.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-A: Evaluation artifacts depend on implementation and test execution.
whyDistractorsWrong.C-before-B: A durable plan needs the task inputs and success criteria as its foundation.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For reliability questions, prefer workflows that externalize state into GitHub artifacts rather than relying on the agent's transient context.

questions.stem: A platform group split a monolith into `checkout-api` and `pricing-api`. Copilot cloud agent learned a repository-level fact in `checkout-api`: service-to-service clients must include the `X-Trace-Id` header. The group expects Copilot code review in `pricing-api` to apply the same learned fact automatically. What should the architect recommend?
questions.scenario: The header rule is now an organization-wide integration standard, but it was originally learned from code in one repository.

options.text: Wait for the 28-day memory timer to synchronize the fact into related repositories.
Rely on user-level preferences so every reviewer carries the header rule across repositories.
Document the standard separately or use governed external memory; repository facts remain repo-scoped.
Ask a write-access user in `pricing-api` to trigger memory creation from `checkout-api` citations.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository-level facts can be used only in operations on the same repository. An organization-wide standard should be captured in an appropriate shared artifact or governed external memory rather than relying on cross-repository memory bleed.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The 28-day behavior is retention for unused entries, not cross-repository propagation.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Repository facts require supporting citations in the same repository context where they are used.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: User-level preferences are personal and are not applied by Copilot code review.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a fact must cross repository boundaries, Copilot Memory repository scope is the limitation; choose shared documentation or external memory.

questions.stem: A healthcare SaaS team wants Copilot cloud agent to prepare hotfix pull requests, but production deployment requires change-manager approval and access to production environment secrets. Which control should enforce the human decision point?
questions.scenario: The team wants Copilot to keep producing fixes quickly, while ensuring production credentials are not available before approval.

options.text: Use a protected production environment with required reviewers and prevent self-approval for deployment jobs.
Let Copilot merge the hotfix after CI succeeds, then require manual verification in the production service.
Allow automatic production deployment from copilot branches, but require signed commits on those branches.
Store production credentials as repository variables and ask Copilot to deploy only after a reviewer comments.

explanation.whyCorrect: A protected environment with required reviewers gates the deployment job before it proceeds or accesses environment secrets. Preventing self-approval strengthens the human-in-the-loop requirement for production changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: A comment convention is not an enforceable deployment protection rule and repository variables are not the right boundary for production secrets.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Copilot cloud agent cannot approve or merge its own pull request, and verification after deployment is too late for production approval.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Signed commits improve traceability, but they do not provide production approval or protect environment secrets.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For irreversible or production-sensitive actions, prefer GitHub environment protection rules over conventions, comments, or post-deployment monitoring.

Allow file changes only after approval, using a pull request branch.
Let the agent inspect context and post a structured migration plan.
Evaluate the pull request with migration tests, checks, and human review.

whyDistractorsWrong.B-before-A: Changing files before plan approval violates the required planning and execution boundary.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-B: Pull request evaluation cannot occur until the agent creates reviewable changes.

questions.stem: A repository team wants to add a database-migration specialist agent to an existing multi-agent workflow. Several Copilot sessions are already open for unrelated documentation and test tasks. What is the best rollout action?
questions.scenario: The team wants the agent available for new database tasks while avoiding disruption to active sessions and preserving review history.

options.text: Replace the default cloud agent globally until all migration-related work is finished.
Cancel active sessions so they restart with the newly available database-migration agent.
Add a new agent profile under .github/agents, merge it, and use it for new sessions.
Edit every open Copilot PR to include the new agent instructions in its description.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository custom agents are added as agent profile files under .github/agents and become available after the file is committed and merged; active work does not need to be disrupted.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: PR descriptions are review artifacts, not the configuration source for adding a reusable custom agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Cancelling unrelated sessions loses progress without being required for adding a new profile.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Replacing the default agent is broader than needed and can affect unrelated task routing.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Lifecycle questions favor additive, versioned changes for new sessions rather than disrupting in-flight work.

questions.stem: A backend team wants Copilot cloud agent to implement a noncritical validation change, but the security lead requires the team to separate planning from execution and keep the workflow auditable in GitHub. In which order should the team structure the agent workflow?
questions.scenario: The repository already requires pull requests and status checks. The team wants the agent to move quickly while avoiding unapproved code changes.

options.text: Create a GitHub issue that includes inputs, expected outputs, and merge success criteria.
Require the agent to publish a structured plan as an inspectable GitHub artifact.
Have a human validate the plan before allowing the agent to modify code.
Let the agent create a pull request, then evaluate CI results and review feedback.

explanation.whyCorrect: The safest architecture starts by defining the task contract, then makes the plan inspectable, then gates execution on human validation, and finally uses PRs, checks, and review as the evaluation surface.

whyDistractorsWrong.C-before-B: A human cannot meaningfully validate an agent plan until the plan exists in an inspectable form.
whyDistractorsWrong.D-before-C: Letting the agent act before plan approval weakens the planning and execution boundary.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 sequencing items, look for the order that moves from task contract to inspectable plan to approval to PR-based execution.
