questions.stem: A risk committee asks which Copilot cloud agent protections are built in before the organization adds custom rulesets and environment protections. Select THREE statements the platform owner can accurately present.
questions.scenario: The committee is deciding whether additional controls are needed for agent-created pull requests in repositories with sensitive application code.

options.text: Copilot can approve its own pull request after CodeQL and secret scanning complete successfully.
Copilot-generated code is checked with CodeQL, secret scanning, and advisory database dependency checks.
Copilot commits are authored by Copilot, signed, and linked to session logs for traceability.
Copilot can read GitHub Actions secrets when setup steps run in the copilot environment.
Copilot can merge its draft pull request if the human requester has repository administrator access.
Actions workflows from Copilot pull requests are blocked by default until a write user approves them.

explanation.whyCorrect: GitHub documents built-in validation using CodeQL, secret scanning, and GitHub Advisory Database checks; Copilot commits are signed and traceable to session logs; and workflows in Copilot PRs are blocked by default until approved by a user with write access.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot cloud agent cannot approve its own pull requests.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Copilot cloud agent does not have access to GitHub Actions secrets or variables during runtime or setup steps.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Draft pull requests created by Copilot must be reviewed and merged by a human; Copilot cannot merge them.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Built-in protection questions mix true safety controls with exaggerated autonomy. Eliminate answers that let the agent approve, merge, or read Actions secrets.

questions.stem: An internal orchestration service stores a Copilot agent checkpoint in the feature branch so a replacement agent can resume after runner failure. The next agent reads the following file before making changes. Which improvement best prevents stale context and repeated work?
questions.scenario: The branch has received human commits since the checkpoint was written, and the issue acceptance criteria are still the source of truth.

artifact.title: .github/agent-state/payment-retry.json
artifact.content:
{
  "issue": 842,
  "agentRunId": "run-17",
  "baseSha": "31b4c9a",
  "completed": [
    "located retry policy",
    "updated RetryPolicy defaults"
  ],
  "next": "add regression tests",
  "decision": "use exponential backoff with jitter"

options.text: Append full tool-call logs to the JSON file so every command result remains in context.
Move the checkpoint to the agent prompt so it travels with the next session.
Compare `baseSha` with branch HEAD, then reconcile completed steps against the issue criteria.
Delete the checkpoint at startup and ask the replacement agent to rediscover prior decisions.

explanation.whyCorrect: A durable checkpoint should be validated against branch HEAD before acting, then re-anchored to the issue or acceptance criteria so the resumed agent avoids repeating completed work or drifting from current requirements.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Deleting the checkpoint discards durable state and increases the chance of redoing completed analysis.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Keeping full tool logs bloats context and can preserve stale details after the step is complete.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Prompt-only state is less durable than a branch artifact and can diverge from branch changes.

explanation.examStrategyNote: State-resume questions usually reward checkpoint validation against the current branch and original task, not larger prompts or raw history.

questions.domainName: Prepare agent architecture and SDLC processes
questions.stem: An architecture board is classifying agent actions by autonomy level. Match each action category to the most appropriate control pattern.
questions.scenario: The board wants delivery speed for low-risk work while preserving human judgment for changes that affect security, production, or compliance.

options.text: Read repository files and produce a proposed implementation plan.
Modify code in a feature branch and open a draft pull request.
Change deployment workflow files or security-sensitive policy configuration.
Promote changes into a protected production environment.

matchChoices: Allow autonomous planning with logged, inspectable output
Require PR review, checks, and branch protection before merge
Require CODEOWNERS or designated owner approval before acceptance
Require environment approval before the deployment job proceeds
Allow direct default-branch commits when the agent is trusted
Disable session logging to reduce reviewer cognitive load

pairs.row1: Allow autonomous planning with logged, inspectable output
pairs.row2: Require PR review, checks, and branch protection before merge
pairs.row3: Require CODEOWNERS or designated owner approval before acceptance
pairs.row4: Require environment approval before the deployment job proceeds

explanation.whyCorrect: Autonomy should increase only where risk is low. Planning can be autonomous when logged, code changes should go through PR governance, sensitive files need owner review, and production deployment needs an environment gate.

questions.stem: FinEdge must keep agent work auditable in GitHub while avoiding unnecessary approval delays for routine iterations. Select TWO controls that best meet the case study requirements.

questions.stem: FinEdge needs the `risk-refactor` pilot to analyze a poorly understood risk-model package before making changes. Which initiation approach best satisfies the requirement to separate planning from execution?

Assign the issue to Copilot immediately and rely on the created pull request to reveal the plan.

After approval, moving the profile to the root agents directory and merging releases it broadly.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Creating the profile before the organization custom-agent repository exists skips the required setup location.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Moving the profile to the root agents directory releases it broadly, so this belongs after the pilot succeeds.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: This is the first enabling step because organization-level custom agents are prepared through .github-private.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Testing belongs after the test profile is merged and before the release-scope change.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For custom-agent lifecycle questions, distinguish private testing location from organization-wide release location.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: FinEdge is a regulated lending company that hosts its core loan-decision services in GitHub Enterprise Cloud. The platform organization wants to adopt GitHub Copilot cloud agent and custom agents to reduce routine refactoring work, update test coverage, and improve documentation for risk-model APIs.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The main repository is named `decision-engine`. The organization uses GitHub Copilot Enterprise. The default branch is protected and requires pull requests, two approving reviews, passing CI, dependency review, secret scanning, and CODEOWNERS review for `.github/**`, `risk-models/**`, and deployment workflow files. The team has created an organization-owned `.github-private` repository with private visibility for custom agent testing.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: The first pilot agent, `risk-refactor`, must help senior engineers modernize old Java service code and add tests. The team wants the agent to work quickly, but all regulated code changes must remain reviewable in GitHub. Engineering managers want agent sessions, plans, pull requests, comments, workflow logs, and review outcomes to serve as the system of record.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: For ambiguous or high-risk work, Copilot must first research the repository and produce a structured implementation plan before code changes begin. Engineers must be able to review and refine the plan, inspect the diff, and decide when to open a pull request. Routine low-risk fixes may create pull requests directly after an issue is assigned. The custom agent profile must use explicit tools rather than inheriting all available tools.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Copilot must not deploy software, approve its own pull requests, or bypass required reviews. Private package installation requires access to Artifactory using a token scoped only to `decision-engine`. The team must use Copilot cloud agent secrets and variables rather than GitHub Actions, Codespaces, or Dependabot secrets. Network access should remain restricted to the minimum required package and GitHub endpoints.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Fabrikam Health builds patient scheduling, claims-routing, and analytics software. The platform engineering group is piloting GitHub Copilot coding agent and organization-level custom agents to reduce routine backlog work while maintaining health-data compliance controls. The pilot covers the `care-portal`, `claims-api`, and `ops-automation` repositories.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The organization uses GitHub Enterprise Cloud with GitHub Copilot Business. Copilot coding agent is enabled only for the three pilot repositories. The `care-portal` repository uses required pull requests, required CI status checks, and CODEOWNERS review for `.github/**`, `.github/workflows/**`, `src/auth/**`, `db/migrations/**`, and `deploy/**`. Copilot-created branches are expected to use the `copilot/` branch prefix and be reviewed through the normal pull request workflow.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: The organization wants agents to handle low-risk work such as documentation updates, test coverage improvements, lint fixes, and small accessibility defects. Higher-risk work, including authentication changes, database migrations, deployment workflow changes, and changes to agent instructions, must have a human-approved plan before implementation. Agent output must remain visible in standard GitHub artifacts such as issues, pull requests, comments, status checks, and logs.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: Agent tasks must define clear inputs, expected outputs, and success criteria. For implementation work, the expected outputs are a pull request, commit diff, test results, and a PR description explaining the approach. For planning-only work, the expected output is a structured plan comment that includes affected files, risks, proposed tests, and a human approval checkpoint. Custom agents for the organization must be released from the organization's custom agent repository rather than copied independently into every product repository.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Agents must use least-privilege tools and avoid broad repository or external-service access. The platform team must preserve independent human review for agent-authored code. Copilot must not approve, merge, or mark its own pull requests ready for review. Compliance reviewers want a repeatable process that prevents silent failures, prevents unapproved high-risk actions, and limits stale or unrelated context from influencing later tasks.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Contoso Health operates a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization that hosts a regulated claims-processing platform. The organization wants to use Copilot cloud agent and custom agents to accelerate routine engineering work while preserving auditability, review discipline, and deployment safety.

sections.body: The platform is split across a monorepo named claims-platform and several service repositories. Copilot cloud agent is enabled only for selected repositories. The claims-platform repository uses branch protection on main, required pull requests, required status checks, and CODEOWNERS review for .github/**, database migrations, billing calculation code, and deployment workflows. The organization has created a .github-private repository from GitHub's custom agents template, but it has not yet released any organization-level custom agents.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: The engineering organization must reduce cycle time for well-scoped maintenance work such as test updates, documentation updates, small defect fixes, and dependency cleanup. Teams must be able to pilot specialized agents with a small reviewer group before making them broadly available. Product owners want issues to be assignable to Copilot only when the task has clear acceptance criteria and a bounded implementation scope.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: For high-risk tasks, Copilot must research the repository and produce a structured implementation plan before changing files. The plan must identify the inputs, affected paths, expected outputs, validation steps, and success criteria. A human reviewer must approve the plan in GitHub before implementation begins. Agent work must result in inspectable artifacts in normal GitHub workflows, such as issue comments, pull request descriptions, commits, session logs, status checks, and review comments.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Agent changes must be traceable to the triggering user and the Copilot session. Copilot-created changes must be reviewed by humans before merge. Deployment to regulated environments requires an environment approval gate. Teams must avoid agent anti-patterns including silent failures, unbounded autonomy, stale context reuse, and prose-only outputs that are difficult to validate.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Orion Retail operates a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization for its e-commerce platform. The platform engineering team is introducing GitHub Copilot cloud agent to reduce lead time for routine engineering work while keeping regulated payment, tax, and deployment changes under human governance. The team wants agents to behave like supervised contributors, not independent release authorities.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The organization has Copilot Enterprise enabled. Copilot cloud agent is enabled in the checkout-service, tax-rules-service, inventory-api, and storefront-web repositories. The default branch in each repository is protected and requires pull requests, CI status checks, and at least one approving review. CODEOWNERS already covers application directories, but platform-owned files such as .github/workflows, .github/copilot-instructions.md, and agent profile files are not yet consistently owned. Production deployment workflows use GitHub Actions environments, but the current production environment does not prevent deployment self-review.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: Orion Retail wants agents to handle small implementation tasks, dependency hygiene, test fixes, and documentation updates. For compliance-sensitive tasks, agents must produce an inspectable plan before implementation. The plan must identify intended files, validation commands, expected outputs, and success criteria. Human intervention should be targeted to meaningful risk points so that low-risk delivery is not slowed by unnecessary approvals.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: All agent activity must remain visible through GitHub issues, pull requests, comments, commits, checks, and session logs. Agent work must follow a plan, act, evaluate lifecycle. Copilot-generated implementation work must be delivered through pull requests with CI evidence. The platform team is also preparing an organization-level custom security-remediation agent. They will pilot the agent with AppSec engineers before releasing it broadly to Orion Retail developers.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Agent-generated changes to production deployment workflows, custom agent profiles, Copilot setup steps, and repository-wide Copilot instructions require platform review. Copilot must not be treated as a merge authority or production deployment approver. Production deployment must require a protected-environment approval from a human reviewer other than the user who initiated the deployment. Audit reviewers must be able to trace why Copilot made a change by using GitHub-native evidence.

questions.stem: A payments platform team wants Copilot cloud agent to handle low-risk developer-experience fixes, but recent agent runs mixed exploration, implementation, and review into one opaque session. The team redesigns the workflow so each run produces reviewable evidence before moving to the next stage. In what order should the workflow steps occur?
questions.scenario: The goal is to preserve delivery speed while making planning distinct from execution and using GitHub PRs, comments, and checks as the standard system of record.

options.text: Have a human merge after reviewing the PR diff, plan alignment, and completed checks.
Capture the task contract from the issue: scope, inputs, constraints, and success criteria.
Allow the agent to create commits on its branch and update the pull request description.
Require the agent to publish a structured implementation plan as a comment or draft PR section.
Run automated checks and request review so the output is evaluated through the PR workflow.
Validate the plan against the task contract and resolve missing assumptions before implementation begins.

explanation.whyCorrect: The correct sequence starts with a defined task contract, then produces a structured plan, validates that plan before action, performs implementation on an agent branch, evaluates the result with checks and review, and finishes with a human merge decision. This preserves the plan, act, and evaluate lifecycle while keeping GitHub as the inspectable control plane.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Merging belongs at the end because it depends on reviewed changes and completed evaluation signals.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Implementation should not precede a structured plan and validation of assumptions against the issue contract.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Planning should occur after the task scope is known, not before inputs and success criteria are captured.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Checks and review evaluate the agent output after commits exist, not before implementation starts.
whyDistractorsWrong.F: Plan validation requires a plan and the original task contract, so it cannot be first.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Sequence questions in this domain usually reward explicit stage boundaries. Put task definition before planning, plan validation before action, and evaluation before merge.

questions.stem: A team reviews several Copilot agent sessions and notices two recurring patterns: failures are described only as vague final summaries, and reviewers cannot tell which validation steps actually ran. Select TWO workflow changes that directly mitigate these SDLC anti-patterns.
questions.scenario: The team wants reviewers to detect agent failure modes earlier while keeping GitHub issues, pull requests, and session logs as the primary artifacts.

options.text: Require unrecoverable setup or test failures to be surfaced as explicit PR comments or checklist failures.
Ask reviewers to inspect only the final diff because logs may contain too much detail.
Require the agent to record attempted validation steps and outcomes in the pull request.
Increase the maximum issue description length so users can include more background context.
Route all low-risk agent tasks through a weekly manual planning meeting before assignment.

explanation.whyCorrect: B creates a structured validation artifact reviewers can inspect. E prevents silent failures by making unrecoverable errors visible in standard GitHub review surfaces.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: More input context may help some tasks, but it does not make validation results or failures inspectable.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Reviewing only the final diff hides tool use and validation behavior that session logs and PR artifacts can expose.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: A weekly meeting slows delivery and does not directly solve silent failures or missing structured output.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For anti-pattern questions, match the remedy to the failure mode. Silent failures require explicit surfacing; unstructured work requires structured artifacts.

questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent pull request modifies application code and also changes a deployment workflow under .github/workflows. The team needs CI results, but the repository uses the default setting that blocks Actions workflow runs on Copilot-created PRs. What should the reviewer do?
questions.scenario: The workflow can access repository secrets during normal deployment jobs, and the reviewer has write access.

options.text: Disable validation tools temporarily so Copilot can mark the pull request ready faster.
Merge the agent branch into main and let protected-branch checks run afterward.
Inspect the workflow changes, then click Approve and run workflows for the PR.
Enable automatic workflow runs for future Copilot PRs to reduce reviewer interruptions.

explanation.whyCorrect: The default workflow approval gate exists because Actions workflows can be privileged and access sensitive secrets. The correct path is to inspect the proposed workflow changes and then explicitly approve the run.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Disabling validation reduces security review rather than addressing the privileged workflow execution risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Merging before checks and review bypasses the intended pull request and protected-branch control path.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Automatic workflow runs may expose repository write access or Actions secrets to unreviewed agent-authored workflow changes.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For Copilot PRs that change workflows, look for an answer that keeps the approval gate and asks a human to inspect before running privileged automation.

questions.stem: A repository owner is designing the standard workflow for issues assigned to Copilot cloud agent. The team wants Copilot to make routine code changes but preserve the same contributor model used for human developers. Which workflow should the owner document?
questions.scenario: The repository requires pull request approval before merge, and the team wants to avoid special bypasses for agent-created branches.

options.text: Let the issue assigner approve the Copilot PR after CI passes, then merge through the normal button.
Have Copilot push to the default branch only for small fixes, and use PRs for larger changes.
Have Copilot open a draft PR, then require human readiness and an independent approval before merge.
Let Copilot mark the draft PR ready, request its own review, and merge after required checks pass.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent works through draft pull requests and must be reviewed like any other contribution. GitHub documentation states that Copilot cannot mark its PRs ready for review, approve, or merge them, and that the person who initiated the Copilot PR cannot count as the required approving reviewer.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The initiating user's approval does not count toward required approval for a Copilot-created pull request.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Copilot cannot mark its own pull requests ready for review, approve them, or merge them.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Direct default-branch changes would bypass the PR-based agent workflow and reduce traceability.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a question mentions the Copilot contributor model, look for independent human review and PR-based flow rather than self-approval or direct branch updates.

questions.stem: A repository team is retiring a custom incident-summary agent because a newer agent now creates better postmortem summaries. The team must prevent future use while preserving evidence from previous incident responses. What should the team do?
questions.scenario: The retired agent was defined as a repository custom agent profile and has been used in several completed outage reviews.

options.text: Remove the agent profile in a reviewed commit and reference the retirement reason in the commit message.
Keep the agent file but blank out its prompt so old sessions remain easier to recognize.
Rename the old file randomly so Copilot stops matching it during future incident tasks.
Leave the agent enabled and tell users to avoid selecting it in future incident reviews.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository custom agents are profile files committed under the agents directory. Removing the profile through normal Git history prevents future selection while preserving prior commits, PRs, and session evidence for audit.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A blank prompt keeps a misleading profile present and can create confusing behavior instead of cleanly retiring the agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A random rename obscures intent and weakens auditability because reviewers cannot easily understand why the agent changed.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Relying on user convention leaves a deprecated agent available and increases the chance it is selected again.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Lifecycle questions often reward normal Git-based change control: add, update, replace, or remove the agent definition with an auditable commit rather than hiding or informally discouraging use.

questions.stem: A compliance team is approving Copilot cloud agent for repositories that include regulated application code. The engineering director wants feature work to keep moving quickly, but deployment and secrets-related changes require clear accountability. Which autonomy model should the platform team recommend?
questions.scenario: The repositories already use pull requests, required checks, protected environments, and standard GitHub review workflows.

options.text: Allow Copilot to merge after successful CodeQL and secret scanning on its working branch.
Permit reads and draft PRs autonomously; gate deployments and secret changes with human approval.
Disable cloud agent outside sandbox repositories until a manual security review finishes quarterly.
Require approval before every file read, test run, and draft PR creation in regulated repositories.

explanation.whyCorrect: The best model right-sizes autonomy: low- and medium-risk actions can proceed through draft PR artifacts and required checks, while irreversible or compliance-sensitive actions use explicit human approval.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: This adds approvals to low-risk work and slows delivery without materially reducing compliance risk.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot cloud agent cannot approve or merge pull requests, and human review remains part of the control model.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A broad sandbox-only restriction is more restrictive than necessary when GitHub controls can gate higher-risk actions.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For autonomy questions, classify the action by risk first. The strongest answer usually preserves velocity for reversible work and adds checkpoints only where risk justifies them.

questions.stem: A platform engineer reviews a custom agent profile before enabling it for production incident triage. The agent only needs to read incident records from an internal MCP server and summarize related repository files. Which change best fixes the configuration?
questions.scenario: Security policy allows this agent to read repository files and incident records, but it must not execute commands or update external incident data.

artifact.title: .github/agents/incident-reader.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: incident-reader
description: Reads incidents and summarizes related code context
tools: ["*"]
mcp-servers:
  incident-mcp:
    type: "http"
    url: "https://incidents.contoso.example/mcp"
    tools: ["*"]
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer ${{ secrets.COPILOT_MCP_INCIDENT_TOKEN }}"
---
Use incident data and repository context to prepare concise incident summaries.

options.text: Remove mcp-servers from the profile and configure the incident server at repository level.
Move the incident token to Actions secrets and keep the same Authorization header.
Keep all tools, but add prompt instructions prohibiting command execution and incident updates.
Limit agent tools to read, search, and incident-mcp/get_incident; allowlist only that MCP tool.

explanation.whyCorrect: The custom agent tools list filters built-in and MCP tools available to the agent. The MCP server configuration also supports listing enabled tools, so both layers should expose only the repository read/search tools and the required read-only incident tool.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Prompt instructions do not remove the ability to call write-capable or execute tools.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Copilot cloud agent uses dedicated Agents secrets and variables, not Actions secrets.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Repository-level configuration would make the server broadly available during agent tasks rather than restricting this profile.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In artifact questions, inspect both the outer agent tools list and the MCP server tools list. A wildcard at either layer may overexpose capabilities.

questions.stem: A developer uses Copilot CLI to run a refactoring task in a shared repository. The developer expects their personal formatting preference to influence the task, but does not want that preference to affect teammates' later CLI runs or code reviews. What should the team rely on?
questions.scenario: The organization has enabled Copilot Memory. The preference is about the developer's preferred interaction and coding style, not a repository-wide convention.

options.text: Keep it as a user-level preference because Copilot CLI applies preferences for the initiating user.
Promote the preference to a repository-level fact so all Copilot features apply it consistently.
Put the preference in the repository README so Copilot code review can enforce it.
Disable Copilot Memory and pass the preference manually in every CLI prompt.

explanation.whyCorrect: User-level preferences capture an individual's coding style and workflow patterns and are available only to that user. Copilot CLI applies stored facts and preferences for the user who initiated the operation.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A personal preference should not be promoted to repository-level memory because repository facts become available to users with memory access for that repository.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: A README change would turn an individual style preference into project documentation and could incorrectly influence repository behavior.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Disabling memory removes the feature that provides the desired scoped persistence and forces repetitive prompting.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a scenario says the knowledge should follow one person but not the repo, choose user-level memory rather than repository facts or documentation changes.

questions.stem: An enterprise governance board is assigning autonomy levels for Copilot cloud agent across repositories that support a customer-facing SaaS product. Match each governance requirement to the best GitHub control pattern.
questions.scenario: The board wants autonomy for low- and medium-risk development tasks, explicit authorization for sensitive operational actions, and traceability for agent-generated work.

options.text: Allow routine code edits to move quickly, but prevent agent-authored code from merging without independent human review.
Support audits that need to determine which changes were agent-generated and which person initiated the work.
Permit the agent to prepare a staging deployment, but require a human decision before the deployment proceeds.

matchChoices: Require a human approval before every read, search, and local test command performed by the agent.
Use environment protection with required reviewers on the staging deployment job, not on ordinary coding steps.
Let the agent create a draft pull request, then rely on human readiness, approval, and merge controls.
Use Copilot-authored signed commits, session-log links, and enterprise audit events for traceability.
Use Copilot content exclusions as the primary control for cloud agent access to protected workflow files.
Disable validation tools and depend on post-merge audit sampling to find agent-generated policy violations.

pairs.row1: Let the agent create a draft pull request, then rely on human readiness, approval, and merge controls.
pairs.row2: Use Copilot-authored signed commits, session-log links, and enterprise audit events for traceability.
pairs.row3: Use environment protection with required reviewers on the staging deployment job, not on ordinary coding steps.

explanation.whyCorrect: Routine code edits fit an autonomous-with-artifact-review model: Copilot cloud agent can work on a branch and open a draft pull request, while GitHub prevents it from approving or merging its own PR and blocks the initiator from approving it. Auditability is supported by Copilot-authored signed commits, session-log links, and enterprise audit events. A staging deployment is higher risk than code exploration or editing, so an environment protection gate with required reviewers places human judgment on the deployment action rather than on every low-risk step.
explanation.examStrategyNote: When classifying autonomy, choose the narrowest human checkpoint that materially reduces risk. GH-600 questions often penalize both extremes: approving every harmless action and relying only on audits after risky actions complete.

questions.stem: A repository recently migrated its test framework from Jest to Vitest. Copilot code review is still making suggestions that reference the old Jest workflow, and the repository owner wants to correct repository-level memory without disabling Copilot Memory for the whole organization. In which order should the owner proceed?
questions.scenario: The team wants future Copilot cloud agent and code review activity to rely on current repository evidence while preserving useful memories that still match the codebase.

options.text: Trigger later Copilot work from the current branch so replacement facts can be grounded in current citations.
Delete misleading repository-level memories instead of disabling Copilot Memory across unrelated repositories.
Open the repository settings and view Copilot Memory entries for the affected repository.
Identify memory entries whose cited evidence no longer matches the current test framework documentation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository owners can review stored repository memories and delete entries they consider misleading or incorrect. Because Copilot validates repository facts against citations in the current branch before using them, the owner should inspect the affected repository's memories, remove obsolete entries, and allow later Copilot activity on the updated codebase to establish replacement facts.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Starting new Copilot work before removing the obsolete memory can preserve the same misleading review behavior.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Deleting memory entries is appropriate only after identifying which stored facts are stale or misleading.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Citation review requires first opening the repository's Copilot Memory management view.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a memory is stale, prefer targeted curation and current-branch validation. Broadly disabling memory is usually an overcorrection unless the requirement is organizational policy.

questions.stem: A documentation agent in repo-a must read issue labels and pull request metadata from repo-b when drafting release notes. The default GitHub MCP server only returns data from repo-a. What should the administrator configure?
questions.scenario: The agent does not need write access to repo-b, and the organization wants the smallest possible expansion of access.

options.text: Grant the repository GITHUB_TOKEN organization-wide read access so both repositories are visible.
Copy repo-b issues into repo-a so the default GitHub MCP token can read them.
Provide a fine-grained PAT with read-only access to repo-b through the GitHub MCP configuration.
Enable all GitHub MCP toolsets and rely on the default token to expand repository scope.

explanation.whyCorrect: The built-in GitHub MCP server uses a specially scoped token with read-only access to the current repository by default. GitHub documents using an appropriately scoped fine-grained PAT when Copilot needs GitHub data outside the current repository.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The default repository token is not the documented mechanism for expanding GitHub MCP access across repositories.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Duplicating issue data creates stale context and avoids the supported MCP access configuration.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Toolsets control available GitHub MCP tools, not the repository scope of the default token.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Separate tool breadth from data scope. Enabling more tools does not automatically grant access to more repositories.

questions.stem: A platform team is defining which Copilot cloud agent actions require human-in-the-loop approval rather than ordinary artifact review. The policy should preserve velocity for reversible development work while protecting critical operational assets. Select TWO actions that should require explicit human approval.
questions.scenario: The team uses GitHub pull requests for code review and protected environments for deployments.

options.text: Running npm test in the agent's ephemeral GitHub Actions development environment.
Changing repository agent secrets used by deployment or incident-response tooling.
Deploying a database migration to production using an environment-protected workflow.
Reading repository files to summarize ownership boundaries before creating an implementation plan.
Updating unit tests and opening a draft pull request on a copilot branch.

explanation.whyCorrect: Production migrations and secret changes are compliance-sensitive and potentially irreversible. They should follow controlled paths with explicit authorization rather than relying only on post-hoc review.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Read-only inspection is low risk and can normally proceed without a human checkpoint.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Draft PRs and test updates are reviewable artifacts that fit standard PR review and CI checks.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Running tests in the agent environment is reversible and usually does not require a separate approval gate.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In autonomy classification, do not equate all agent action with high risk. Reserve human-in-the-loop approval for production, secrets, billing, policy, or other sensitive changes.

questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent pull request in a regulated payment-service repository modifies `.github/copilot-instructions.md` and `copilot-setup-steps.yml`, expands `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions, and asks a maintainer to approve workflow execution. Put the response steps in the correct order.
questions.scenario: The organization requires evidence preservation, least-privilege remediation, and a path to resume the work without giving the agent broader autonomy than the task requires.

options.text: Restart the implementation under the tightened guardrails, using a new task description and normal review path.
Keep the pull request draft, do not approve workflow execution, and block merge during triage.
Review session logs, signed commits, and audit events to identify the initiator and agent actions.
Add CODEOWNERS review for Copilot configuration files and rulesets requiring relevant checks to pass.
Replace broad setup permissions with minimum required permissions and remove unnecessary agent secrets or tools.

explanation.whyCorrect: The safest sequence is to contain the immediate execution risk first by withholding workflow approval and preventing merge. Next, use the agent session logs, signed commits, and audit events to preserve accountability. Then remediate the concrete over-permissioning in setup steps and agent-accessible resources. After that, add durable governance controls such as CODEOWNERS protection and rulesets for required checks. Once the control path is fixed, the work can resume through the normal agent PR workflow.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Restarting first can reproduce the same governance gap before containment, evidence review, or permission remediation is complete.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: This is the correct first step because unreviewed agent workflow changes can access privileged Actions behavior if approved too early.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: This belongs after containment; evidence review is essential, but it should not leave workflow execution available during triage.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: This is a durable prevention step, but it should follow immediate remediation of the active over-permissioned change.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: This should occur after audit review identifies what changed, and before adding longer-term ruleset and ownership controls.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Sequence questions in Domain F often reward containment, evidence, remediation, prevention, then resumption. Options that resume work before closing the guardrail gap are usually premature.

questions.stem: An incident-response team wants one Copilot SDK session to triage a production regression, delegate log analysis to a read-only investigator, delegate a minimal patch to an editor, and then summarize the outcome for the incident commander. Which orchestration pattern best fits this workflow?
questions.scenario: The team wants a single coordinating agent to keep the overall plan coherent while specialized agents execute bounded subtasks with different tool access.

options.text: Use a pipeline pattern so each agent transforms the previous agent's full output sequentially.
Use an orchestrator-worker pattern so one parent coordinates specialized sub-agents and integrates results.
Use independent fan-out so each agent works without a shared coordinating session.
Use a debate pattern so all agents propose competing patches before any triage occurs.

explanation.whyCorrect: The orchestrator-worker pattern fits because one parent session decomposes the incident task, delegates to specialized sub-agents, receives lifecycle events, and integrates their outputs into a final response.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: A pipeline is better when each agent performs a single sequential transformation, not when one coordinator must route work by expertise.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Debate is useful for comparing alternatives, but it delays triage and does not provide bounded worker execution.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Uncoordinated fan-out risks duplicated work and inconsistent outputs because no parent agent integrates the results.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 orchestration items, identify whether the scenario needs coordination, sequential transformation, parallel independence, or independent comparison. A named coordinating parent usually signals orchestrator-worker.

questions.stem: A team wants to add a new performance-investigator sub-agent to an existing Copilot SDK incident workflow. Existing investigator and editor agents are already used by live sessions. Select TWO actions that support safe addition of the new agent.

options.text: Add a new customAgents entry with a distinct name, specific description, scoped tools, and prompt.
Remove descriptions from older agents so the new performance agent receives more tasks.
Update observability handling so selected, started, completed, and failed events show the new agent.
Give the new agent tools:null so it can handle any unexpected incident diagnostic task.
Reuse the existing investigator name so the runtime automatically replaces it mid-session.

explanation.whyCorrect: A distinct custom agent definition with a clear description helps the runtime match user intent and keeps capabilities scoped. Updating lifecycle-event handling ensures the new agent is visible in operational dashboards and post-hoc reviews.

whyDistractorsWrong.E: Reusing a name risks ambiguity and does not provide a controlled replacement strategy for live work.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: tools:null grants all session tools, which weakens isolation for a diagnostic-only agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Removing useful descriptions from existing agents makes routing less predictable across the workflow.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When adding an agent, think in two tracks: routing quality and operational visibility. Avoid changes that blur identities or broaden tools just to make adoption easier.

artifact.content:
name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

  prepare-agent:

options.text: The workflow must include a pull_request trigger before Copilot can run setup steps.
The checkout action must set fetch-depth to zero for setup steps to run.
The job must be named copilot-setup-steps for Copilot to pick it up.
The workflow must grant contents: write so Copilot can modify repository files.

explanation.whyCorrect: The setup workflow must contain a single job named copilot-setup-steps. If the job uses another name, Copilot cloud agent will not pick it up as its setup job.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: The pull_request trigger is useful for validation but is not the reason Copilot ignores this setup job.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: GitHub overrides checkout fetch-depth as needed; this is not required for setup execution.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Setup steps should use the lowest required permissions, and Copilot receives its own token for operations.

questions.stem: A long-running agent task is paused after implementing half of a migration. The team needs another agent session to resume without repeating completed work or drifting from the original acceptance criteria. Select TWO actions the team should include in its state strategy.
questions.scenario: The repository uses pull requests as the system of record. The new session will start after several commits have been pushed by humans.

options.text: Preserve the full tool-call history in context so the agent can replay prior commands exactly.
Rely on the previous chat transcript because it contains the most complete record of reasoning.
Ask the new session to infer progress from file timestamps and recent commit messages.
Store a structured checkpoint in the PR description listing completed steps, open decisions, and remaining work.
Require the agent to compare its current plan with the original issue acceptance criteria before acting.

explanation.whyCorrect: A structured PR checkpoint is a durable artifact that survives session boundaries and helps resume without repeating work. Comparing the current plan to the original issue and acceptance criteria detects context drift and re-anchors the agent before additional changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: A chat transcript may be inaccessible, too verbose, or not treated as the durable repository artifact for later sessions.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Timestamps and commit messages are weak proxies for decisions and can cause the agent to redo or skip important steps.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Keeping full tool-call history increases context noise; completed-step history should be pruned into a concise durable checkpoint.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For resume-and-drift questions, choose durable checkpoints plus re-anchoring to the original requirement; avoid relying on raw transcripts or replaying every prior tool call.

Key execution nodes by toolCallId and update status from completed or failed events.

Key the map by agent display name and overwrite older entries when the same agent repeats.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Display names are human-readable labels and can repeat, so they are weak identifiers for execution correlation.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: The selected event is useful for tool visibility, but it does not by itself represent execution completion or failure.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Splitting sessions removes useful parent orchestration context and avoids the event-correlation problem instead of solving it.

questions.stem: A repository frequently uses Copilot cloud agent for dependency update tasks. The agent wastes time rediscovering the build environment, even though the team added a setup workflow. What is the minimal fix to make the setup workflow part of the agent SDLC path?

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: Copilot Setup Steps

on:

      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

options.text: Rename the workflow file to setup.yml and reference it from each agent prompt.
Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps and keep the workflow on the default branch.
Move dependency installation into the issue template so Copilot repeats it per task.
Add a matrix strategy so Copilot can choose the best runtime during execution.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: A matrix strategy does not address the required job name and is outside the supported minimal fix.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Putting setup commands in issue text is slower and less reliable than preconfiguring the agent environment.

Place the token directly in the MCP JSON so the header is not empty.

questions.stem: Copilot cloud agent opens a pull request but reports that npm install failed because requests to https://packages.contoso.example/npm/internal were blocked by the agent firewall. Store the registry hostname in an Agents variable and rerun the same task.
Add a custom allowlist rule for the required registry URL or domain only.
Move npm install into a normal CI workflow after the agent creates the pull request.

Keep tools:null on rollback so it can choose whatever incident tool seems useful.

explanation.whyCorrect: Setting infer:false prevents automatic selection for vague prompts. Explicit tool scoping applies least privilege to the rollback sub-agent, and defaultAgent.excludedTools hides the rollback tool from the main coordinator while keeping it available to the specialized sub-agent.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Weakening the description makes routing less predictable and does not prevent automatic invocation reliably.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Putting the rollback tool directly in the parent agent's visible tool set undermines the desired coordinator-executor separation.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Using tools:null gives the rollback agent all session tools, which increases blast radius during incident response.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For custom-agent orchestration items, combine selection control with tool isolation. The best answer usually changes both when an agent can be invoked and what it can do.

questions.stem: A mobile repository's Copilot agent repeatedly reformats generated localization files while fixing small UI bugs. Reviewers spend most of their time reverting unrelated diffs. Which tuning change best addresses the observed failure without blocking useful agent work?
questions.scenario: Session logs show the agent used broad shell commands to run a formatter across the repository after editing one component.

options.text: Disable Copilot cloud agent for the repository until localization file ownership is redesigned.
Add instructions limiting edits to task files and require targeted validation before creating the pull request.
Ask reviewers to leave more comments so the agent can repair localization files afterward.
Measure total changed lines per pull request and reject sessions above the monthly average.

explanation.whyCorrect: The observed failure is overly broad tool behavior and missing operational constraints. Targeted instructions and validation tune behavior while preserving the agent's ability to make useful scoped changes.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Disabling the agent removes productive work instead of correcting the specific failure pattern.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Changed-line thresholds are a coarse evaluation signal and may reject legitimate refactors without preventing the root cause.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Relying on reviewer comments shifts the cost to humans after the avoidable diffs are already created.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Tuning questions reward narrow, evidence-based adjustments to instructions, constraints, memory, or tools instead of broad shutdowns.

questions.stem: A healthcare software group is writing its minimum control baseline for Copilot cloud agent. The baseline must reduce vulnerable code risk, prevent bypass of required approvals, and preserve traceability for audits. Select THREE controls that satisfy the baseline.
questions.scenario: The group wants to use GitHub's built-in controls where they are sufficient instead of building a separate approval portal.

options.text: Allow the triggering developer to satisfy required approval after checking session logs.
Keep Copilot's security validation tools enabled for agent-generated code before PR completion.
Store production tokens as Actions secrets and reference them from agent instructions.
Disable default workflow approval so CI findings appear before reviewers inspect changes.
Preserve human review and merge for draft PRs created by Copilot cloud agent.
Use session logs and audit events to trace agent actions during reviews.

explanation.whyCorrect: Security validation helps catch vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets, and insecure dependencies. Human review and merge preserve approval controls. Session logs, signed commits, and audit events support traceability.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Removing workflow approval increases exposure to privileged workflow execution before human inspection.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: GitHub prevents the user who triggered the agent from approving its PR, preserving separation of duties.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Agents should not access Actions secrets; Copilot cloud agent has a separate secrets and variables mechanism.

questions.stem: A team is enabling Copilot cloud agent in a repository with existing Actions workflows. They want the agent to create draft PRs quickly, but they do not want workflows from agent pushes to run before a human has looked at the proposed work. Which workflow design best fits this requirement?
questions.scenario: The team is optimizing the agent SDLC path, not changing network restrictions, secrets access, or compliance policy.

options.text: Use the default approval flow: review the draft PR, then approve and run workflows from the PR.
Disable Actions on Copilot branches and ask the agent to summarize expected test results.
Require Copilot to merge only after workflows pass and skip the draft PR stage.
Enable automatic workflow runs for every Copilot push so CI feedback arrives before human review.

explanation.whyCorrect: By default, GitHub Actions workflows do not run automatically when Copilot pushes changes to a pull request. A human can review the draft PR and then use the Approve and run workflows control, preserving a lightweight checkpoint without blocking PR creation.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Automatic workflow runs prioritize speed but remove the requested human checkpoint before workflows run.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Disabling Actions entirely loses automated validation and relies on unverifiable summaries.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot cannot merge its own pull requests, and skipping drafts conflicts with the normal agent workflow.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For autonomy-level questions in Domain A, choose the option that places the checkpoint at the specific risky transition rather than disabling the workflow or removing automation.

questions.stem: A platform team runs three Copilot-assisted remediation agents in parallel after an outage. Two agents independently edit the same retry middleware, while the third updates documentation. The orchestrator detects incompatible code changes before merge. Select TWO actions the team should take.
questions.scenario: The organization wants to preserve useful work while preventing contradictory changes from entering the default branch.

options.text: Merge the first completed remediation PR and close the second without reviewing its session evidence.
Discard all three branches because one conflict makes the overall incident workflow unreliable.
Allow the documentation PR to continue if it does not depend on the disputed code decision.
Pause the conflicting code PRs and have a human compare the branches and session artifacts.
Ask both agents to continue editing the same middleware until one branch passes CI.

explanation.whyCorrect: Pausing the conflicting code PRs preserves the competing work while requiring human resolution of contradictory outputs. Letting the independent documentation PR continue avoids unnecessary cancellation of unaffected work.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Closing one PR without reviewing evidence can discard the better fix and weakens post-incident auditability.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Continuing simultaneous edits to the disputed middleware can deepen the conflict instead of resolving the dependency.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Discarding all branches loses unrelated valid work and treats a localized conflict as a total workflow failure.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In multi-agent conflict questions, avoid extremes: do not merge blindly, and do not cancel unaffected work. Preserve evidence, isolate the conflict, and resolve the disputed decision explicitly.

questions.stem: A team creates a custom agent to produce implementation plans before a coding agent starts work. Reviewers find that the agent sometimes edits application code while planning. Which change best preserves planning-versus-execution separation while still producing an inspectable plan?
questions.scenario: The team wants the planning agent to create a Markdown plan in the repository and leave implementation to a separate coding agent after review.

artifact.title: .github/agents/implementation-planner.agent.md
artifact.content:
---
name: implementation-planner
description: Creates implementation plans for medium-risk feature work
tools: ["read", "search", "edit", "execute"]
---

You analyze the issue, decide on an implementation approach, update files as needed, and summarize the changes in a pull request.

options.text: Limit tools to read, search, and edit, and prompt the agent to create only a plan document.
Remove the description so Copilot infers the agent's role from the filename and prompt.
Add disable-model-invocation: true so the agent cannot reason about implementation details.
Set tools to ["*"] so the agent can validate the plan using every available tool.

explanation.whyCorrect: A planning agent still needs to inspect the repository and write a planning artifact, but it should not execute commands or implement code. GitHub custom agent configuration supports specifying a subset of tools, and the official implementation-planner example uses read, search, and edit to create structured Markdown plans.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: The description is required for a custom agent profile and helps define the agent's purpose.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Enabling all tools expands the agent's action surface and weakens planning-versus-execution boundaries.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: disable-model-invocation controls automatic selection behavior, not whether the agent can reason once selected.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For planning-agent questions, do not remove all capability. Give the agent enough access to create the plan artifact, but remove execution-oriented tools.

questions.stem: A repository team is redesigning how Copilot agents retain information after several incidents involving stale assumptions and repeated work. Match each requirement to the most appropriate memory or state mechanism.
questions.scenario: The team uses Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, and Copilot CLI. Some information should help future repository work, while other information is only useful during one task or must be retained permanently for audit purposes.

options.text: A coding convention discovered during a Copilot cloud agent session should later help Copilot code review in the same repository.
A user's preferred command-line explanation style should apply only to that user's later Copilot CLI interactions.
A regulatory decision about an API migration must survive longer than Copilot Memory retention limits.
The agent needs to remember the files it has opened while completing one uninterrupted refactoring session.

matchChoices: Session log only, used after completion for human inspection
External durable memory such as a committed state file or system of record
User-level Copilot Memory preference scoped to the initiating user
Short-term context window for the active session
Repository-level Copilot Memory fact scoped to the same repository
Organization-wide repository memory shared across unrelated repositories

pairs.row1: Repository-level Copilot Memory fact scoped to the same repository
pairs.row2: User-level Copilot Memory preference scoped to the initiating user
pairs.row3: External durable memory such as a committed state file or system of record
pairs.row4: Short-term context window for the active session

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository-level Copilot Memory stores repository facts such as coding conventions and can be used by supported Copilot features in that repository. User-level preferences are tied to the individual user. Decisions that must persist beyond Copilot Memory's retention behavior belong in an external durable artifact. Active-session working context is short-term memory and should not be treated as durable state.
explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 memory questions, first identify scope and lifespan. Repository facts, user preferences, task-local context, and permanent external records solve different problems.

Makes the agent produce a structured planning artifact suitable for review

pairs.row2: Defines a reusable specialized agent profile that Copilot can load from the catalog

questions.stem: A team adds a lightweight GitHub Actions check to prevent an agent from resuming work from an outdated checkpoint. Review the workflow artifact. What change best improves continuity without turning the check into a general CI gate?
questions.scenario: The agent writes a JSON checkpoint to .github/agent-state/current-task.json in its working branch. The checkpoint includes the issue number, last processed branch HEAD, and acceptance-criteria hash.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/agent-state-continuity.yml
artifact.content:
name: Agent state continuity
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, edited]

jobs:
  check-agent-state:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Read checkpoint
        run: |
          test -f .github/agent-state/current-task.json
          cat .github/agent-state/current-task.json
      - name: Validate issue binding only
        run: |
          ISSUE=$(jq -r '.issue' .github/agent-state/current-task.json)
          test "$ISSUE" != "null"

options.text: Replace the checkpoint file with a full transcript so every prior command remains available.
Run the entire unit-test suite in this job before allowing any checkpoint to be read.
Remove the workflow and trust Copilot Memory validation to detect all resume-state problems.
Also compare stored branch HEAD and acceptance-criteria hash to current PR state before resuming.

explanation.whyCorrect: The workflow currently verifies only that a checkpoint exists and is linked to an issue. To prevent stale context and drift, the resume check should validate that the checkpoint corresponds to the current branch HEAD and original acceptance criteria before the agent continues.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: A full transcript adds context noise and may still omit a concise statement of current progress, branch state, and decisions.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot Memory validates repository facts, but a task checkpoint is execution state that should be checked separately.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Unit tests are useful quality signals, but they do not prove the agent is resuming from the correct checkpoint.

explanation.examStrategyNote: In artifact questions, identify what the config already checks, then add the narrow missing state validation rather than replacing it with broad logging or unrelated CI.

questions.stem: A Windows-only repository needs Copilot cloud agent to build with an internal compiler installed on self-hosted runners. The security team requires controlled outbound internet access through the corporate proxy. Select TWO configuration actions the platform team should take.
questions.scenario: The repository cannot build on the default Ubuntu runner, and the organization already manages ephemeral self-hosted Windows runners.

options.text: Use a macOS self-hosted runner label because it has stronger isolation for agent tasks.
Configure proxy environment variables as Agents variables, Agents secrets, or runner settings.
Keep the integrated cloud agent firewall enabled to enforce outbound controls on Windows.
Disable the integrated firewall and enforce network controls on the self-hosted runner network.
Store proxy credentials in Dependabot secrets so all automation shares the same proxy.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot cloud agent supports Ubuntu x64 and Windows 64-bit self-hosted runners, but its integrated firewall is not compatible with self-hosted runners. For proxy use, GitHub documents proxy environment variables that can be set through Agents variables, Agents secrets, or directly on the runner.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: The integrated firewall is not compatible with self-hosted runners and would block use of the cloud agent.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Copilot cloud agent does not support macOS runners for this use case.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Copilot cloud agent does not read Dependabot secrets, and proxy values should be provided through supported agent or runner mechanisms.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Runner-environment questions test compatibility boundaries. Look for the supported OS, firewall compatibility, and where environment variables actually come from.

questions.stem: Two specialized agents propose different architectural fixes for the same incident. One changes retry behavior in the API gateway, while the other changes idempotency handling in the worker. Both PRs pass their isolated tests, but applying both would duplicate retries and increase load. What should the orchestrator do next?
questions.scenario: The incident commander needs a defensible recovery decision and an audit trail explaining why one approach was accepted.

options.text: Escalate both PRs for human comparison, accept one approach, and document the rejected alternative.
Select the smaller diff automatically to minimize review time during the incident.
Merge both PRs because each passed its isolated checks and addresses the outage symptom.
Ask both agents to rewrite their patches until Git can merge the branches cleanly.

explanation.whyCorrect: Contradictory outputs require an explicit decision, not just a clean merge. Human comparison of the competing PRs preserves auditability and prevents incompatible architectural decisions from being combined.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Passing isolated checks does not prove the combined behavior is safe when the fixes duplicate retry semantics.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: A clean Git merge does not resolve the higher-level architectural contradiction between the two approaches.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Diff size is a weak proxy for correctness and does not explain the incident recovery decision.

explanation.examStrategyNote: GH-600 conflict questions may describe tests passing. If the conflict is semantic or architectural, the correct answer resolves the decision explicitly rather than relying only on merge mechanics.

questions.stem: A repository owner reviews Copilot Memory after several abandoned pull requests and finds facts that may no longer match the codebase. The team wants to reduce stale influence while preserving useful validated knowledge. Select TWO actions that best align with Copilot Memory behavior.
questions.scenario: Some facts were learned from pull requests that were closed without merging. Other facts are still supported by files on the default branch.

options.text: Rewrite every stale fact into repository custom instructions to make its source explicit.
Manually delete repository-level facts that are misleading, inappropriate, or no longer useful.
Disable Copilot Memory for the repository so existing facts stop being created for that repo only.
Keep all learned facts indefinitely because closed pull requests cannot affect future Copilot behavior.
Rely on citation validation and 28-day unused-entry deletion to limit stale memory over time.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository owners can review and delete repository-level facts they consider inappropriate, misleading, or incorrect. Copilot validates facts against the current codebase before using them, and stored facts or preferences that go unused are deleted after 28 days.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Facts may be captured from closed pull requests, so the correct safeguard is validation against current code, not assuming no future effect.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Copilot Memory is enabled per user or by organization and enterprise policy, not as a per-repository toggle that only stops one repo.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Moving stale facts into custom instructions can make outdated guidance more persistent and bypass the memory validation model.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When memory may be stale, prefer documented curation and validation mechanisms. Be cautious of answers that make stale information more permanent.

questions.stem: A payments team asks Copilot cloud agent to add missing unit tests for a legacy refund module. Which evaluation approach best aligns with the team's development intent?

A Copilot-authored pull request adds a GitHub Actions workflow and the merge box prompts for workflow approval.
The agent needs a private package-registry token, and a developer proposes reusing an existing Actions secret.

Create a narrowly scoped Agents secret for the registry and keep Actions secrets outside the agent environment.
Disable built-in security validation temporarily so the agent can complete the pull request before policy review.

pairs.row1: Rely on hidden-character filtering for the HTML comment, review the visible request, and retain the session record for audit.

The information is stable, repository-specific, and supported by source files in the repo. Which memory strategy should the team use first?
questions.scenario: The team wants Copilot cloud agent and Copilot code review to benefit from the same validated repository knowledge without introducing a separate storage service.

options.text: Create an external vector store and require every agent task to query it before coding.
Use Copilot Memory repository-level facts so validated repo knowledge can be reused across supported features.
Save the pattern as a user-level preference so code review applies each developer's style.
Store the pattern only in the current prompt so each session starts with fresh context.

explanation.whyCorrect: Copilot Memory is intended for repository-level facts such as coding conventions, architectural decisions, build commands, and project-specific rules. whyDistractorsWrong.A: An external store can be appropriate for permanent or custom memory, but it adds unnecessary complexity for supported repository facts.

questions.stem: An operations dashboard shows parent Copilot SDK sessions as successful even when a delegated incident-investigation sub-agent fails. The team needs the dashboard to expose failed, partial, and stalled sub-agent executions. Select THREE implementation changes the team should make.
questions.scenario: The dashboard is used during live incidents and during post-hoc review meetings.

Group event records by agent description so related incident skills appear together.
Treat the parent response text as the single source of truth for all sub-agent outcomes.

Persist toolCallId, agentName, status, timestamps, and error details for later analysis.
Subscribe to subagent.started, subagent.completed, and subagent.failed events from the parent session.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Suppressing sub-agent failures hides degraded behavior that the parent may partially recover from or fail to mention.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Descriptions help routing, but they are not reliable correlation keys for execution status or incident forensics.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: A retail platform reviews three failed Copilot cloud agent sessions for the same bug fix. In each session, the plan identified the correct service, but the commits changed a deprecated helper and the tests failed because the agent ran a package script from the wrong workspace. Select TWO root causes that best explain the failures.
questions.scenario: The session logs show successful repository search calls, followed by shell commands executed from the repository root instead of the service directory.

options.text: Evaluation gap, because the team measured merge rate instead of total token usage.
Reasoning error, because the agent chose the wrong service during its initial planning step.
Prompt issue, because the user did not specify every test command in the initial issue description.
Tool misuse, because the agent invoked the test command from the wrong working directory.
Context issue, because the agent edited deprecated code despite finding the correct active service.

explanation.whyCorrect: The wrong working directory is tool misuse because the command was invoked with the wrong execution context. Editing deprecated helper code after identifying the correct service indicates a context issue in how repository information was applied.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: A prompt can be improved, but the logs show a concrete command-location problem and stale code selection.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: The plan found the correct service, so the initial planning step was not the primary failure.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Merge rate and token usage may be poor evaluation choices, but they do not explain this execution failure.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a scenario includes logs or command history, classify the observed failure directly before proposing broader prompt or metric changes.

questions.stem: A repository team is creating a custom Copilot agent that answers architecture questions by inspecting source files and README content. The agent must not modify files, run commands, or call external systems. Which tool configuration best meets the requirement?
questions.scenario: The agent will be available to developers during design reviews and must follow least-privilege access.

options.text: Set tools to an empty list and rely on prompt instructions for repository access.
Set tools to execute, read, and search so the agent can verify findings.
Omit the tools property so the agent can decide which built-in tools are needed.
Set tools to read and search aliases only, such as read and search.

explanation.whyCorrect: A read-only inspection agent needs only file reading and search capabilities. GitHub custom agent configuration supports limiting tools to specific aliases, while omitting tools enables all available tools.

whyDistractorsWrong.C: Omitting tools grants all available tools, which exceeds the read-only requirement.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Adding execute enables shell access, which is unnecessary for answering architecture questions.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: An empty tools list disables all tools, preventing the agent from inspecting repository content.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For GH-600 tool-scope questions, map the task to the minimum concrete tool set. Prompt instructions are not a substitute for configured tool restrictions.

After four sessions, reviewers find the agent frequently edits unrelated styling files and invokes external package managers even when the requested change is in one component. How should the agent profile be tuned?

You fix accessibility issues quickly. Explore the repository, update the code,

options.text: Add a larger prompt describing WCAG guidance but keep the current unrestricted tool list.
Restrict tools to needed aliases and add instructions for scoped edits plus targeted validation.
Remove edit access so the agent can only produce a written accessibility remediation plan.
Keep all tools enabled and ask reviewers to downvote comments on unrelated styling changes.

explanation.whyCorrect: The evidence points to tool overuse and vague constraints. A tuned profile should limit the tool surface to the task and add explicit instructions for scoped edits and validation.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Feedback after the fact does not reduce the repeated unnecessary tool use or unrelated diffs.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Removing edit access changes the agent's purpose from fixer to planner and blocks useful work.

questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent session learned that service clients must be created through src/platform/clientFactory.ts. A later pull request changes the factory pattern on a feature branch. Before applying the old fact during new work on that branch, what behavior best prevents stale context?
questions.scenario: The team wants repository knowledge to persist when it is still true, but not override code that has legitimately changed on the current branch.

options.text: Copy the stored fact into custom instructions so it survives branch-level code changes.
Delete all repository-level memory whenever a branch changes the referenced files.
Validate the fact's code citations against the current branch before using the memory.
Apply the stored fact first, then let CI determine whether the pattern still compiles.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repository-level facts in Copilot Memory are stored with citations to supporting code. When a fact is relevant, Copilot checks those citations against the current branch and uses only validated facts.

whyDistractorsWrong.D: Relying on CI after applying stale context can cause unnecessary or misleading changes before validation occurs.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Custom instructions are not a substitute for citation validation and may preserve outdated guidance after code changes.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: Deleting all memory on any referenced-file change is excessive because validation can distinguish current facts from stale ones.

explanation.examStrategyNote: For stale-memory scenarios, look for validation against the current branch or current codebase, not broad deletion or post-hoc detection.
