questions.stem: A Copilot cloud agent session was interrupted during a multi-step refactor. When the agent resumes, reviewers want it to avoid redoing completed work and to detect whether its current plan has drifted from the original issue. In which order should the recovery workflow run?
questions.scenario: The repository stores progress checkpoints in the pull request description and a committed JSON state file. Human reviewers added steering comments after the first failed attempt.

options.text: Update the PR checklist or state file after the next validated unit of work completes.
Read the original issue, acceptance criteria, and reviewer steering comments defining the intended outcome.
Compare the current diff and in-progress plan against the original requirements to identify drift.
Fetch branch HEAD and load the latest durable checkpoint from the PR or state file.
Prune irrelevant tool history, re-anchor on the spec, and restart from the valid checkpoint if needed.

explanation.whyCorrect: The agent should first re-establish intent from the issue and human steering, then load the latest branch and durable checkpoint. Only after comparing current work against the original requirements can it determine whether drift occurred. If drift exists, it should re-anchor and resume from the last valid checkpoint, then persist the next completed state update.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Writing a new checkpoint before validating intent and branch state can persist drift or duplicate incomplete work.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Drift comparison is useful only after both the original requirements and current branch state are loaded.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Loading branch state before reading the source requirements gives the agent state without a correctness baseline.
whyDistractorsWrong.E: Pruning and restart decisions should follow drift detection, not precede the comparison.

explanation.examStrategyNote: Sequence questions in this domain reward recovery flows that re-read intent, load durable state, validate for drift, then resume. Avoid options that persist state too early.

questions.stem: A repository team needs Copilot cloud agent to consult a vendor incident system during bug-fix tasks. The vendor exposes a remote MCP endpoint and supports PAT-based authorization. Put the configuration steps in the safest order.
questions.scenario: The agent should read incident summaries and links, but it must not acknowledge incidents, mutate ticket state, or use unrelated vendor tools. The team wants to validate the integration without exposing broader repository or vendor access.

options.text: Create a repository-level Agents secret for the vendor PAT using a COPILOT_MCP_ prefixed name.
Identify the exact read-only MCP tools, transport type, endpoint URL, and minimum PAT permissions.
Add repository MCP JSON with explicit tools, URL, type, and Authorization header substitution.
Save and validate the configuration, then run a low-risk task and inspect the session evidence.

explanation.whyCorrect: The safest sequence starts by defining the required tools and minimum permissions, then provisioning the secret in the Agents secret store with the MCP prefix, then adding a repository MCP configuration that allowlists only those tools and uses header substitution. Validation should occur after the configuration exists and should use a low-risk task with session evidence review.

whyDistractorsWrong.A: Creating the secret before defining required scopes can lead to over-permissioned PATs or naming that does not match the final MCP configuration.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: This is the first step because least-privilege tool and token design should precede secret creation and JSON configuration.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Adding MCP JSON before the secret and permission design risks validation failures or broad tools such as an asterisk wildcard.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: Validation is necessary, but it belongs after the MCP server and secret configuration are in place.

explanation.examStrategyNote: On sequence questions, put discovery and least-privilege design before implementation. Then configure secrets, wire the MCP JSON, and validate with traceable evidence.

questions.stem: A platform engineer reviews a Copilot setup workflow for a repository that only needs to install dependencies before Copilot starts. The workflow currently grants write permissions even though the setup job only checks out code and runs npm ci. Which change best enforces least privilege?
questions.scenario: The organization requires that agent execution contexts receive only the permissions needed for the task.

artifact.title: .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
artifact.content:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
      actions: write
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

options.text: Change job permissions to contents: read only and keep the setup steps unchanged.
Keep permissions unchanged because Copilot receives a separate token for its repository operations.
Move permissions to workflow scope and add id-token: write for future package access.
Remove checkout and grant packages: write to avoid repository reads during setup.

explanation.whyCorrect: The setup job only needs to clone the repository and install dependencies. GitHub's Copilot setup guidance recommends using the lowest permissions possible and notes that checkout-style setup requires contents: read.

whyDistractorsWrong.B: The separate Copilot token does not justify over-permissioning the GITHUB_TOKEN used by setup steps.
whyDistractorsWrong.C: Adding id-token: write expands the trust boundary without a current requirement for OIDC authentication.
whyDistractorsWrong.D: packages: write is unnecessary for installing dependencies and increases the impact of a compromised setup step.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When a GH-600 question shows a setup workflow, inspect what the job actually does. Least privilege usually means reducing GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, not relying on downstream reviews.

options.text: A setup step runs npm ci against a private package registry and needs a registry token available to the shell command.
Copilot reports that a dependency download host is blocked while running on the default GitHub-hosted cloud agent environment.
A Windows-only build requires Copilot cloud agent to use a self-hosted Windows runner inside the corporate network.
A repository setup workflow adds a job named prepare-copilot, but Copilot does not run the setup steps before starting.

matchChoices: Create an Agents secret or variable for the token so setup steps can consume it as an environment variable.
Add only the required host to the Copilot cloud agent firewall allowlist or approved network path.
Use an appropriate Windows runner strategy and implement runner-level network controls because the integrated firewall is not compatible there.
Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps in .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml on the default branch.
Disable the firewall for all repositories so the dependency manager can resolve future hosts.
Move the token into a Dependabot or Actions secret because Copilot automatically inherits those values.

pairs.row1: Create an Agents secret or variable for the token so setup steps can consume it as an environment variable.
pairs.row2: Add only the required host to the Copilot cloud agent firewall allowlist or approved network path.
pairs.row3: Use an appropriate Windows runner strategy and implement runner-level network controls because the integrated firewall is not compatible there.
pairs.row4: Rename the job to copilot-setup-steps in .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml on the default branch.

explanation.whyCorrect: Agents secrets and variables are the correct mechanism for values that Copilot cloud agent and setup steps need. Windows and self-hosted runner scenarios require runner-level network controls because the integrated firewall is not compatible. Copilot setup steps must be defined in the special workflow file on the default branch and the job must be named copilot-setup-steps.
explanation.examStrategyNote: Environment-permission questions usually test the narrowest control that restores execution. Prefer Agents secrets, precise firewall entries, supported runner constraints, and exact setup-step conventions over broad disablement.

explanation.whyCorrect: The wrong component choice is a reasoning failure because the agent's plan diverged from the issue intent. The forced audit command is tool misuse because the tool choice and ordering caused unrelated changes. The unavailable PAYMENT_SIM_URL is a context or environment issue because the failure depends on the agent's runtime environment rather than the code diff alone.

questions.domainName: Evaluation, telemetry, error analysis, and tuning
questions.stem: Meridian Grocery's latest evaluation report shows that Copilot repeatedly uses a stale repository fact, edits generated lockfiles during unrelated pricing changes, and invokes broad shell commands where read/search would be safer. Select THREE tuning actions the team should take.
questions.scenario: The team wants to reduce repeat failures without disabling Copilot cloud agent for low-risk pricing tasks.

artifact.title: Evaluation excerpt
artifact.content:
Recurring signals:
- Stored memory: "Pricing rules are defined in src/rules/*.json"
- Current architecture: pricing rules migrated to config/pricing/*.toml six weeks ago
- Session traces: frequent broad shell search and forced dependency updates
- Review pattern: unrelated lockfile churn and missing tests for TOML rule changes
- Security checks: dependency review sometimes flags newly introduced high-severity advisories

options.text: Require senior engineers to manually rewrite every Copilot pricing PR before running repository checks.
Increase the prompt token budget so Copilot can infer the migration from a larger context window.
Add repository instructions that require pricing TOML tests and discourage unrelated generated-file changes.
Narrow the agent's expected tool pattern toward read/search before editing and verification before PR readiness.
Delete the stale Copilot Memory entry and add the current TOML pricing-location fact if needed.
Disable dependency review and secret scanning for agent-authored branches to reduce noisy evaluation failures.

explanation.whyCorrect: Deleting or correcting the stale memory addresses the repeated context error. Repository instructions can encode project-specific constraints, such as testing TOML pricing changes and avoiding unrelated generated-file churn. Tool-pattern guidance addresses the observed misuse by steering the agent toward repository inspection before editing and validation before PR readiness.

whyDistractorsWrong.F: Disabling scans hides security and dependency signals that the evaluation program explicitly needs.
whyDistractorsWrong.B: A larger context window may not correct a validated stale memory or unsafe tool sequence.
whyDistractorsWrong.A: Manual rewrites add review burden without tuning the agent behavior that caused the failures.

explanation.examStrategyNote: When telemetry shows repeat failures, tune the root cause: memory for stale facts, instructions for recurring constraints, and tool guidance for unsafe execution patterns.

caseStudies.title: Case Study: SkyHarbor Robotics Agentic Maintenance Platform
caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: SkyHarbor Robotics operates autonomous inspection drones for port authorities. The engineering organization uses GitHub Enterprise Cloud and is piloting Copilot cloud agent to repair non-flight-critical maintenance software. The pilot focuses on a single repository, skyharbor/maintenance-console, which contains a TypeScript dashboard, Python simulation tests, and infrastructure templates for non-production environments.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The repository already has Copilot cloud agent enabled. A custom agent named maintenance-triage is stored under .github/agents/maintenance-triage.agent.md. The agent needs to read repository files, run tests, and call an internal FleetOps MCP server that exposes drone status and maintenance-ticket tools. Developers also have a working VS Code MCP configuration for Sentry-based issue triage, but it uses inputs and a local envFile. The platform team wants to adapt the configuration for Copilot cloud agent without copying workstation-specific assumptions.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: The team must reduce mean time to prepare non-production maintenance-console fixes while preserving a controlled execution path. The agent must be able to create draft pull requests with code changes, validate changes with simulation tests, and link relevant FleetOps or Sentry context in the pull request description.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: The FleetOps MCP server is a remote HTTP server. It supports bearer-token authentication but does not provide a Copilot-compatible remote OAuth flow. The simulation tests call https://sim.skyharbor.example/api/v2 from shell commands executed by the agent. The repository uses a private npm registry and a Python package mirror, both reachable through company-controlled hostnames. MCP tools must be enabled explicitly instead of exposing every available tool from a server.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Secrets used by MCP servers must not be available to arbitrary setup scripts or general shell commands unless specifically required. MCP access should be restricted to approved servers through organization-level controls where possible. Network access should be limited to the minimum domains or URL paths required for agent-driven validation. The team must be able to confirm from Copilot session logs whether MCP servers started and which tools were exposed.

caseStudies.title: Case Study: Northstar Transit Analytics Agentic Delivery Program
caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Northstar Transit Analytics builds route-planning and ridership-forecasting software for regional rail and bus agencies. The engineering organization uses GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Actions, and GitHub Copilot Enterprise. The company is expanding its use of Copilot cloud agent beyond documentation fixes into routine service changes, test scaffolding, and low-risk refactoring tasks.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: Northstar has 68 repositories across four product groups. Product teams currently start agent work from issues, the agents panel on GitHub.com, and occasional pull request comments. Several teams copied custom agent profiles into individual repositories, which has caused inconsistent prompts and uneven release practices. A platform team owns a shared `.github-private` repository but has not yet moved organization-level agents into a formal release workflow.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: Northstar wants agents to reduce backlog latency without reducing code review quality. Ambiguous work items should be explored before a pull request is created, while clearly scoped work may proceed directly to a pull request. Engineering managers want agent work to remain visible inside GitHub rather than in private local chat sessions or external spreadsheets.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: Agent work must produce inspectable artifacts in standard GitHub tooling, including branches, pull requests when appropriate, session logs, and commit history. Teams must be able to steer an active agent session if the approach is wrong. Organization-level custom agents must be reusable across repositories after they are tested, and repository-specific experiments must not appear as broadly available agents until released.

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: The compliance team requires traceability from agent-authored commits to the human who initiated the task and to the agent session that explains the change. The company prefers built-in GitHub controls and auditability over creating a separate tracking system unless a requirement cannot be met through GitHub-native artifacts.

caseStudies.intro: This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided. To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Meridian Grocery operates a regional online grocery platform. The engineering team is piloting GitHub Copilot cloud agent for small pricing-service changes, such as promotion rule updates, tax-calculation fixes, and checkout-message corrections. The organization wants to evaluate agent quality using evidence from GitHub pull requests, session logs, automated scans, workflow artifacts, and human review outcomes.

sections.heading: Existing Environment
sections.body: The pricing-service repository is hosted on GitHub Enterprise Cloud and uses Copilot Business. Copilot cloud agent is enabled for the repository. The repository has unit tests, integration tests, linting, CodeQL, secret scanning, and dependency review checks. Copilot Memory is enabled for the organization. Repository owners periodically review stored memories, but no one has yet established a formal memory-curation process.

sections.heading: Business Requirements
sections.body: The pricing team wants agent-authored pull requests to preserve checkout correctness, reduce reviewer rework, and avoid introducing security or dependency risk. The team wants metrics that distinguish between fast but low-quality output and changes that satisfy the original development intent. Evaluation results must be actionable enough to tune agent instructions, memory, workflow expectations, or tool access.

sections.heading: Technical Requirements
sections.body: Each Copilot task should produce a branch and pull request that are traceable to the associated agent session. Evaluation must compare the agent's stated approach with the final diff and workflow artifacts. The team tracks test pass rate, coverage delta, CodeQL findings, secret scanning alerts, dependency-review findings, lint error count, review iterations, and session-log tool-call patterns. The team also stores qualitative reviewer tags, including 'wrong component,' 'unrelated churn,' 'missing test,' 'stale assumption,' and 'tool sequence issue.'

sections.heading: Security and Compliance Requirements
sections.body: Security findings introduced by agent-authored changes must be visible before a pull request is considered ready for merge. The team must preserve enough telemetry to reconstruct why Copilot made a change. Tuning changes should address the observed root cause rather than masking symptoms. The team prefers preventive configuration changes, such as tighter instructions, memory cleanup, and narrower tool usage, over adding manual review effort for every low-risk task.

artifacts.title: Recurring evaluation observations
artifacts.content:
Run set: pricing-service Copilot pilot, 42 sessions
Observation 1: 9 sessions opened PRs within SLA but needed two or more human review rounds.
Observation 2: 6 sessions touched generated lockfiles or unrelated dependency versions.
Observation 3: 5 sessions followed a stale assumption that pricing rules live under src/rules/*.json.
Observation 4: 4 sessions passed unit tests but failed dependency review due to newly introduced high-severity advisories.
Observation 5: Reviewer comments frequently mention that the agent selected the wrong service boundary before coding.
